Nephew wants change after killings of uncles

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:25:54 GMT

A nephew of twin brothers killed by a man suffering a psychotic episode who was released from custody hours before says he has little confidence similar cases could be prevented.

The deaths of Roger and Dick Carter, both 84, and Anthony Payne, 80, in Exeter by Alexander Lewis-Ranwell on 10 February 2019 followed a catalogue of failings by police, healthcare professionals and G4S-employed staff, an inquest jury found.

Alex Carter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that "any number of people could have said releasing this guy is not right".

"What I want to see is visible improvements," he said. "I want somebody to tell me this has happened. I want to be able to see it or hear it."

The jury found Lewis-Ranwell, who had a history of paranoid schizophrenia, was released from custody without a Mental Health Act (MHA) assessment despite warnings about his deteriorating mental state.

Within hours, he killed Mr Payne and later the Carter brothers.

Carter said the inquest had revealed more problems than he had expected and he remained unconvinced enough had changed since 2019, despite hearing during the inquest that some improvements had been introduced.

He also said agencies should examine in particular how information was recorded, shared and acted upon.

He said: "Police, Devon County Council, G4S have all got to look at the processes that are in place because it fell down in so many different places."

He added: "I'm not seeking apologies. Apologies don't mean anything to me.

"We've gone through this really lengthy process. If nothing changes, then this will happen for nothing."

The inquests heard evidence of the then 28-year-old Lewis-Ranwell's interactions with various health professionals and police officers during his arrests between 8 and 10 February, which included:

Lewis-Ranwell was released from Barnstaple police station at about 09:30 on 10 February. He travelled to Exeter, where about three hours later he killed Payne with a hammer at his home on Bonhay Road.

Less than three hours after that, he scaled the wall of the Carter brothers' home in Cowick Lane, took a spade from the garden and killed them both with it.

Lewis-Ranwell, who had a history of paranoid schizophrenia and had been sectioned under the Mental Health Act twice before, was arrested again on 11 February following an incident at an Exeter hotel, the inquests heard.

This time, an MHA assessment was completed and he was found to be acutely psychotic.

Lewis-Ranwell was charged with murdering Payne and the Carters, but found not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a direct hospital order.

Coroner Philip Spinney said he would be considering writing Prevention of Future Deaths reports.

Such reports are sent when a coroner thinks action is needed to protect lives.

Devon and Cornwall Police said its Professional Standards Department liaised with the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) on 13 February 2019 and requested that the matter be considered as a voluntary referral.

The force also said: "Areas of learning and change identified during the inquest and prior reviews are being, and have been, addressed."

An IOPC spokesperson said: "We received a complaint referral from Devon and Cornwall Police in March 2020, in relation to the contact the force had with Alexander Lewis-Ranwell prior to the deaths of three men, in Exeter, in February 2019.

"After assessing all the available information provided by the force, we decided that an investigation was required and it was appropriate for the investigation to be carried out by Devon and Cornwall's Professional Standards Department.

"The complainant would have had the right of review to the IOPC should they have been dissatisfied with the investigation outcome.

"To date, we have not received a request to carry out a review."

G4S Health Services no longer operates. A G4S spokesperson said: "We offer our condolences to the families affected by these tragic events."

The Devon Partnership NHS Trust said: "We would like to extend our sympathies to the families of Richard and Roger Carter and Anthony Payne.

"Our organisation will reflect on the jury's conclusions and we remain committed to continuous learning and ensuring that improvements are embedded in our systems and practice."

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:16:09 GMT

Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title

Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.

With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.

Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.

That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.

Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.

In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.

A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."

The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".

"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.

"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."

Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".

The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.

'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final

'The longest VAR check in history' - the fallout from shock Afcon decision

Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at ⁠a ​referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This new rule will also apply ​to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match ​to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.

Referee Ndala was at the centre of the controversy during the Afcon final

A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.

First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.

The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.

Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.

Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.

Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.

The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.

Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.

Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved by Edouard Mendy after Senegal's walk-off led to a delay of over 15 minutes before he was able to take the spot-kick

Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.

It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's appeal days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.

Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.

The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.

The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.

The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of ​law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.

Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.

But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

This video can not be played

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners

In its appeal, the FSF argued that the decision of referee Ndala to resume the match in the 19th minute of added time - and to allow it to be concluded with a sporting result - could not be reviewed, pursuant to the 'field of play' doctrine.

Cas has a long-standing practice where it refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".

The FRMF argued, on the contrary, that the referee's decision did not fall under the field of play doctrine because Senegal should have faced disciplinary consequences for walking off the pitch.

The Moroccan federation went on to argue that, according to Afcon tournament rules, the referee should have brought the match to an early conclusion.

It added that Ndala "erred in law" and that his decision was "arbitrary".

However, in the view of the panel, the referee's decisions were limited to the pitch and the relevant Afcon regulations regarding withdrawals were not applicable.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," the Cas statement added.

"However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'. On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

This video can not be played

Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstates Senegal as Afcon winners

Despite Cas being the highest authority in sport, and its decision coming 10 months on from the final, there could yet be a further twist.

The FRMF raised a grievance with the process before the panel's judgement was announced on Tuesday.

It alleged that German attorney Haas, the arbitrator on the panel nominated by the Senegalese, held a telephone call with FSF president Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.

Fall "categorically" denies that any such phone call ever took place.

The FRMF says that any unauthorised communication between a member of the panel and one of the interested parties would constitute a serious breach of Cas regulations.

It has demanded that "appropriate legal consequences be applied to actions that compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process".

The Moroccans could appeal against the ruling by taking the case to the Swiss Federal Tribunal, and the country's highest court could set Cas' judgement aside.

The case would then likely be heard again at Cas, with a different panel in place.

A precedent would be the case of Chinese swimmer Sun Yang, who had an appeal against the decision by Cas to impose an eight-year doping ban upheld by the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

A new panel heard his case at Cas, and his ban was reduced to four years and three months.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:16:09 GMT

Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title

Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.

With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.

Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.

That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.

Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.

In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.

A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."

The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".

"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.

"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."

Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".

The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.

'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final

'The longest VAR check in history' - the fallout from shock Afcon decision

Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at ⁠a ​referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.

"This new rule will also apply ​to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match ​to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.

Referee Ndala was at the centre of the controversy during the Afcon final

A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.

First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.

The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.

Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.

Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.

Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.

The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.

Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.

Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved by Edouard Mendy after Senegal's walk-off led to a delay of over 15 minutes before he was able to take the spot-kick

Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.

The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.

The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of ​law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.

Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.

But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

Government probe into housing scheme 'exploitation'

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:10:40 GMT

The government has announced an independent inquiry into allegations rogue landlords in Birmingham are making huge profits by exploiting a housing scheme.

BBC Panorama reported last month that some companies in the city were taking advantage of the Supported Exempt Accommodation (SEA) system, intended to provide housing along with care and support for vulnerable people.

There have been claims of fraud, crime, poor housing and firms receiving housing benefits on behalf of residents but not giving them the support they are meant to.

A government spokesperson said an eight-week investigation would begin immediately, with initial findings and recommendations reported to ministers in the new year.

Sir David Pearson, chair of the Supported Housing Advisory Panel and social care expert, has been appointed to lead the investigation.

The government added the investigation would examine the scale of the problems in the city's SEA sector, including the quality of accommodation and support, use of public money, and effectiveness of oversight and regulation.

In a letter confirming the appointment, housing secretary Angela Rayner asked Pearson to lead a "rapid independent investigation" into the claims.

She said the investigation should focus on Birmingham, given consistent reports that the area was at the "epicentre of concerns" about poor-quality supported accommodation, while considering the extent to which any findings can be applied to the rest of the country.

"Good-quality supported housing can turn lives around and provide people with the support they need to live as independently as possible," Rayner wrote.

"There are increasing reports, however, that this system is being abused, with vulnerable people exploited at the expense of the taxpayer."

SEA is designed for people in the UK with additional needs, including people recovering from addiction and women fleeing domestic abuse.

In many cases it works well for people, but BBC investigations over the past five years have uncovered stories of vulnerable people, including care leavers and people with mental health problems, being let down by the system designed to support them.

Some residents said they had been left living alongside drug dealers and criminals, and fearing for their lives, despite some providers reportedly claiming more than £200 a week at the time for every person they house.

Supported housing expenditure had risen faster in Birmingham than the national average in recent years, a government spokesperson said.

Pat McFadden, Work and Pensions Secretary, said there were "real concerns" about how the system was operating.

"Sir David's investigation will get to the bottom of what's going on, and where we find wrongdoing, we will act to make sure money is spent on supporting people who need it," he said.

The council paid out £404.4m for SEA in the 2024-25 financial year, with a further £211.8m paid between April and July 2026.

More than 34,000 people in the city currently live in SEA, compared to about 22,000 living in London, despite its population being more than seven times larger.

The BBC has previously heard evidence of claims that some housing providers were willing to make benefit claims for people who did not live in their properties.

The council introduced controls, requiring SEA providers to submit evidence they were delivering more than minimal care to their tenants.

But a recent internal audit showed the authority could not show the review had been completed for 72% of the claims tested.

At the time the results were published, 12,700 live cases were waiting review, of which around 7,100 had exceeded the six-month limit.

Bosses said a plan was in place to reduce the backlog to zero by the end of the year.

Preet Gill, the Labour MP for Birmingham Edgbaston, said she welcomed the independent review.

"I have campaigned on exempt accommodation for nearly a decade and worked with residents, the council and police to shut down Saif Lodge, the first exempt accommodation property in the country to be closed in 2021," she said.

"Neighbours have had enough of the antisocial behaviour, and vulnerable people are being let down while some providers profit."

It is not the first time politicians have investigated the issue.

An inquiry by the Levelling Up, Housing and Communities Committee in 2022 reported that some vulnerable people had faced rape and exploitation by landlord "gangsters" in England's "complete mess" of an exempt housing system.

That was two years after Birmingham was named as one of five pilot projects designed to improve quality, enforcement, oversight and value for money in the sector.

Tuesday's announcement follows a recent letter to the prime minister from councillors Robert Alden and Ken Wood, demanding urgent intervention.

Campaigners have called for action for years, under both Conservative and Labour governments.

Alden, the councillor for Erdington and leader of the Birmingham Conservative group, said it was right that the government examines "why Birmingham has become the epicentre of this crisis and what must change".

"Residents deserve answers about how this was allowed to happen.

"Vulnerable people placed in badly run accommodation deserve proper support, and neighbourhoods suffering the consequences deserve action."

Charities, residents and politicians told Panorama last month that parts of the system were being exploited.

The programme found property agents drawing people into the taxpayer-funded system using social media videos offering free rooms, PlayStation consoles and holidays.

Patricia Coleman-Taylor, who runs Birmingham anti-poverty charity Narthex, said many vulnerable people were being used as "cash cows to generate income" that goes from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) into "the back pocket of the landlords".

Alysha told Panorama that she had moved into SEA 18 months ago, a survivor of domestic abuse.

She had nowhere to go and no family living nearby, so she was made homeless and relying on universal credit.

"I never thought I'd be homeless and I never thought my marriage would break down, but it did," she said.

"I felt extremely alone. I needed help getting myself back on to my feet, and that's how I got myself into supported accommodation."

She has since lived in three different SEA properties but admitted her experience was far from the fresh start she needed.

Alysha was forced to leave her first placement after just six months.

"There was one day at about 05:30 in the morning, where I was woken up to screaming and growling and banging.

"They'd been fighting really badly. The house was covered in blood, police were called, and the house was no longer safe."

Her second SEA initially looked "amazing" with brand new kitchen appliances and mattresses but Alysha quickly learnt it was not as it appeared.

Managed by a private provider, Alysha said she was promised weekly counselling sessions, access to food banks, and help with GPs.

"But it's not the case, it's not the case at all," she said.

"They're not interested, they come and they just want you to sign that paper to say Alysha's done support this week and that's it."

She added that the home had been left without heating at one point in the winter.

Jane and Melvin, residents living in Selly Oak, said the house next door to them was converted into SEA.

The couple admit at times they felt unsafe in their own home with the tenants of the property having involvement with guns, knives, and drugs.

"There were people overdosing," Jane recalled, adding: "Twice the front door was kicked in by people who didn't live there."

Jane said she and her husband never objected to the property being used to support people in need.

But she felt as though those living in the SEA were left to run "amuck".

"I think they were lacking the support that they needed, really," she explained.

Yoro red card overturned, but refs' chief Webb backs decision

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:00:32 GMT

Leny Yoro was sent off for this tackle on Alexander Isak

Manchester United defender Leny Yoro has had the red card shown to him at Anfield overturned by the Football Association - even though referees' chief Howard Webb has backed the decision to send the defender off.

Yoro was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott for bringing down Liverpool forward Alexander Isak just eight minutes into Sunday's match.

Isak had run onto a ball that bounced over Matthijs de Ligt but took a heavy touch that meant the ball was likely to run through to United goalkeeper Senne Lammens even if Yoro had not brought down the Swede.

New United head coach Mauricio Pochettino was furious at a decision he felt had changed the course of the game, which Liverpool won 4-0.

"The ball wasn't in his control," he said. "Isak, when he saw the control wasn't good, it's normal to delay, and stop to the run. In that moment that Yoro came from the back, and you go down.

"But all that we play football; you know that wasn't intentional. That is never a foul."

The FA backed that view, meaning Yoro will be clear to face Brentford in the Premier League at Old Trafford on Saturday.

However, in the latest edition of Mic'd Up on Sky Sports, Webb said Barrott got it right.

"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball," he said.

'No-one's coming to save us' - but how can Man Utd save themselves?

How on earth can the head of referees say a decision was right, but the FA say it was wrong?

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable," Webb said. "Certainly not clearly wrong."

Not clearly and obviously wrong for a VAR intervention, but clearly and obviously wrong for the FA to rescind the red card.

You wonder how the general fan is supposed to understand it all.

The FA's appeals process is notoriously difficult to predict, especially on highly borderline situations like Yoro.

A commission features three people, usually former players though sometimes there is a retired official is on the panel.

A simple majority is needed, so a club just needs two people to agree with them.

It's why clubs might appeal against red cards when it seems impossible to win, you just never know.

Such was the split of opinion on Yoro, United always stood a chance of at least getting those key two votes.

And this is the crux of appeals process. An FA commission is just the subjective opinion of three people.

Do the appeal again tomorrow with three different panel members, and United might lose.

This is why Pro Ref don't use the outcome of FA appeals to determine how games are officiated.

Two years ago, Brentford's Christian Norgaard won an appeal against a red card at Everton. That was a split 2:1 vote, but enough to say a decision was wrong.

Pro Ref told its referees not to alter their interpretation based on this vote.

Let's throw in another one. The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

Earlier this season, Brighton appealed against Pascal Struijk's VAR red card at Sunderland.

An FA commission upheld the appeal, but in contradiction the KMI Panel voted the VAR intervention was correct.

Make it make sense, supporters might ask.

This will forever be the problem with officiating, and indeed any hope of true consistency with VAR.

Was Yoro's red card right or wrong? On which side of the fence will the KMI Panel fall?

Football is just a floating mass of subjectivity. Of referees, of VARs, of panel members and of fans. It just depends whose opinion you ask.

Sporting coach Paulo Fonseca speaks to the media ahead of the Champions League clash with Manchester United

United have travelled to Lisbon for their next Champions League match on Wednesday (20:00 GMT).

The early dismissal of Yoro at Anfield meant Sporting had no chance to assess any changes Pochettino might have made after he replaced Michael Carrick during the international break.

But despite United sitting 19th in the Premier League, Sporting boss refuses to accept United are "fragile".

"I don't following the reasoning," said Fonseca, who was only appointed on 4 November after the Portuguese club bought him out of his contract at Lyon.

"Manchester is a great team," he said. "I don't believe a lot that great teams are fragile. The last game they played in the Champions League, they were trailing 2-0, then won 3-2 against a very difficult opponent in Roma.

"Moreover, when they have a new head coach, with such world-class players, it's extremely unpredictable to see if they will have a good day or bad day."

United have not won in the Premier League since August and have conceded 19 goals in their past six games in all competitions.

Yet, such was the nature of the Liverpool game, Fonseca has had to watch analysis of Pochettino's time in charge of the United States to get an idea of what to expect.

"Eight minutes, red card. It's impossible to make an analysis," he said.

"I tried to see Pochettino with the United States and what kind of solutions he used. There is some information but it is very difficult to predict."

French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:49:07 GMT

Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

The pair deny any wrongdoing.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.

Two arrested on suspicion of burglary at Prince and Princess of Wales's Norfolk home

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:19:29 GMT

Two men have been arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass at the Prince and Princess of Wales's country home on the Sandringham estate, police say.

Norfolk Police said it received a call just before 18:00 GMT on Monday following a report of suspicious activity at Anmer Hall.

Police deployed dogs, drones and a helicopter to search the area and arrested two men on the estate, who remain in custody.

The property was unoccupied at the time, police added. Kensington Palace said it did not comment on security matters.

William and Catherine do not live at Anmer Hall full-time, but use the estate as a country retreat during the holidays.

Val Blackmur, an 83-year-old resident who lives on the road leading up to the house, told the BBC it was "amazing" if anybody had been "stupid" enough to try breaking in.

The country retreat, which has 10 bedrooms, was a gift to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II following their wedding in 2011.

The red brick Georgian mansion is on the private Sandringham estate in Norfolk and is about two miles (3km) east from Sandringham House, one of the King's private residences.

The Prince and Princess's main home is on the Windsor Castle estate in Berkshire.

The Sandringham estate spans approximately 31 sq miles (80 sq km).

Members of the public can visit it, although the house and its gardens are currently closed.

The Royal Parkland, which is the woodland to the west of the main house, is open to the public all year round.

Many other members of the Royal Family also live on the estate, including Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, who moved on to Marsh Farm in February.

Despite tight security around members of the Royal Family, there have been several intrusions on their property in recent decades.

One of the more recent incidents was in 2024, when Thames Valley Police said burglars had broken into a farm on the Windsor Castle estate and stolen two vehicles.

Blackmur said: "We never seem to have any trouble so when something out of the ordinary happens that sort of makes you prick your ears up and think, what was all that about?"

The 83-year-old said it was not unusual to hear police cars or helicopters in the area.

"We've lived here 50 years now... we've never heard nothing like that," she said.

"Up at Anmer Hall it's so secluded and out of the way, not in full view - I should think people would be shocked."

Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:11:29 GMT

Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.

She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".

She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.

"Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."

In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10.

"I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said.

"It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."

Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".

Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content.

"It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."

They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".

Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.

A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.

One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.

A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

Southport survivors' parents 'disgusted' by school recovery funding

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 15:50:44 GMT

Parents of children injured in the Southport knife attack have criticised "huge discrepancies" in support money given to schools in the area after the stabbing.

Schools attended by 10 of the survivors received more than a million pounds in recovery funding between them, while schools attended by 13 other survivors received no direct funding, the families' lawyers have said.

Council documents published this afternoon reveal that £1,013,920 has been allocated to seven schools in the Sefton local authority area following the attack in July 2024.

The council says it was up to schools to tell it of the help and funding they needed, as seven local schools have done.

​​The largest recipient was Churchtown Primary School, which was given £546,815. It was attended by two of the girls who were killed, as well as children who survived.

The council also allocated £52,360 to Presfield High School and Specialist College, which was attended by the attacker, Axel Rudakubana.

Three girls - Bebe King, Elsie Dot Stancombe and Alice da Silva Aguiar - were murdered in what was described as the worst mass stabbing in modern British history.

Twenty-three girls survived the attack, which happened at a Taylor Swift-themed dance and yoga workshop for children.

Earlier this year, a BBC News special report heard from the parents of five girls who were seriously injured. The girls have not been publicly identified due to an anonymity order imposed by the courts.

Some parents said their daughters had missed out on support from local authorities after officials told them they did not know who their children were.

All said they felt their daughters were being forgotten, as their experiences had been erased from the public's understanding of the attack.

The mother of a girl the BBC has been calling Daisy, who was seven when she was stabbed 33 times in the attack, said she was "horrified" by the differences in funding.

"We have had to fight for every penny to support our daughter, and none of it has come from this fund," she said.

"To know that we have had such a private, anonymous, invisible battle to get our daughter the most basic support and care she needs at school, and that it has been provided by other local authorities, while Sefton Council was handing out over half a million pounds to a single school just makes me feel incredibly angry and sad."

She said that the council should have approached every school attended by children who were present at the attack and ensured that they had fair access to support.

The mother of two other surviving girls said that she was "absolutely disgusted".

"The council never spoke to us or asked us what we needed, meanwhile our daughters have been passed from pillar to post, moving schools to try and get the help they needed in class after everything they had been through," she said.

The elder daughter, whom we are calling Sarah, spoke to BBC Panorama last year. Aged 14 at the time of the attack, she was seriously wounded but managed to lead several other children, including her young sister, to safety.

The girls' father added: "Nobody is suggesting schools shouldn't have received funding. Nor should anyone question the importance of remembering the children whose lives were lost.

"But what about those who survived; the children who were physically injured; those who witnessed the unimaginable; those who are still struggling with their education, their mental health and everyday life."

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly, of Fletchers Solicitors, which represents 22 of the 23 surviving children, said the disparity in funding is "shameful and outrageous".

"Eye-watering sums have been handed out to single schools, while six schools attended by 13 surviving girls we represent received absolutely nothing from this pot," she said.

She accused Sefton Council of having "completely failed in its due diligence" to establish where money and support were most needed.

A spokesperson for Sefton Council said: "The children, families and school communities affected by the events of July 2024 remain at the heart of Southport's recovery and support of course continues."

The council said that it had initially made support available across Southport schools, with additional funding for those facing specific pressures arising from the attack.

It added that "schools who came to the council with additional needs were asked to provide specific information about what they required" and that "allocations varied based on the type of help required by those schools."

The council also said that the individual school grants were only one part of a wider response, which included increasing capacity in children and family services across the local authority.

Sooryavanshi, 15, breaks sixes record by scoring 204 off 53 balls

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 14:52:50 GMT

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made his T20 international debut for India in July but is yet to play a one-day international

India's 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hit the most sixes ever recorded in a senior men's innings in blazing 204 from 53 balls for India A against the United Arab Emirates.

While almost halving the record for the fastest double-century in List A cricket, Sooryavanshi hit 28 sixes and seven fours in the Asia Cup Rising Stars competition - easily breaking Chad Bowes' previous record of 103 balls from 2024.

The teenage opener also broke the record for the fastest century and 150, the latter of which he already held, before being caught at long-off with his side five runs from victory.

India A ultimately passed their target of 250, played against a UAE side that featured a number of internationals but was not their current first-choice side, in 14.2 overs in Doha.

Sooryavanshi now holds the following records in List A cricket, the categorisation given to senior one-day matches:

Fastest fifty: 11 balls v Sri Lanka A, 21 June (previously Kaushalya Weeraratne, 12 balls, 1 November 2005)

Fastest hundred: 28 balls, today (previously Jake Fraser-McGurk, 29 balls, 8 October 2023)

Fastest 150: 40 balls, today (previously himself, 59 balls, 24 December 2025)

Fastest 200: 52 balls, today (previously Chad Bowes, 103 balls, 22 October 2024)

The previous record for the most sixes in senior matches was 26, struck by Tanmay Agarwal in an innings of 366 for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in India's first-class Ranji Trophy competition in January 2024.

The record in List A cricket was 23 sixes, struck by D'Arcy Short for Queensland in his 257 against Tasmania on 28 September 2018.

Sooryavanshi also holds the records of being the youngest century-maker in both List A and T20 cricket and the youngest captain in T20s.

This video can not be played

More records for Sooryavanshi

"The first thing that's required in this format is being fearless, he's got plenty of that," former India batter Deep Dasgupta told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Technically he's quite unique. There is a tendency of being over-coached in this generation, there's so many coaches and when you start playing franchise cricket.

"The best part is he has been fast-tracked so he hasn't had a lot of coaches, he's kind of untouched. What you see of him is predominantly what his natural game is.

"That bat swing, the hand speed, which is very, very natural and one of the quickest you'll come across. Technically he's very gifted, he's very special and he's definitely the real deal."

Sooryavanshi has rapidly become a sensation in T20 cricket since making his debut in the Indian Premier League in 2025 at the age of 14.

He has hit two hundreds and six fifties in his first two seasons in the competition and has earned 10 caps for India in the shortest format since making his debut against England in July.

The left-hander, who was batting in only his 16th List A innings in Doha and made his second century in the format, is yet to play for India in 50-over cricket.

He put on partnerships of 68 with opening partner Abhishek Sharma, who scored 12, 40 with Prabhsimran Singh, who added just three, and 137 with Rinku Singh, who scored an unbeaten 27.

The India A side, which featured a number of internationals, restricted the UAE to 249-8 in 50 overs, external after their opposition had chosen to bat and swiftly reached 254-3 to win by seven wickets and guarantee their place in the semi-finals.

The Rising Stars competition features A sides from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan alongside squads from the UAE, Nepal and Hong Kong.

India A, who now top Group B, beat Nepal and lost to Pakistan A in their previous two matches in the competition, with Sooryavanshi making scores of 26 and 11.

Pakistan A will retake the top spot if they beat Nepal on Tuesday, with semi-finals on Thursday and Friday to follow before Sunday's final.

Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 13:46:07 GMT

A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence".

The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales.

The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled.

Here's what you need to know.

This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign.

While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review.

First the short term.

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Then the long term.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.

The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.

The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.

Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

Alan Milburn's report - which proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK - recommended that Pip be removed from people under 25 as part of a package of measures to tackle youth unemployment.

Today's review does not make the same recommendation. It will be up to the government to decide how they marry the two reports. They have said they are committed to reforming the Pip assessment process, but what that means in practice probably won't be known until the New Year when they publish their considered response.

From dancing on the Tube to being sectioned: Sabrina Bahsoon on her psychosis misdiagnosis

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 09:47:20 GMT

Sabrina Bahsoon became known globally as Tube Girl after self-shot videos of her dancing and lip-syncing on the London Underground blew up online.

The 26-year-old content creator had the world at her feet when she went viral in 2023, going on to build a social media following of more than 900,000 people.

She signed major brand endorsement deals and was pursuing a music career.

But then her "whole life turned upside down" when she had what appeared to be a psychotic episode.

Her symptoms made her violent and erratic, leading to her being sectioned in a mental health hospital - where doctors treated her with anti-psychotic medication.

But Bahsoon's family, helped by her father's neurologist friend, pushed for further tests.

And two months into her hospital treatment, doctors got to the truth.

She actually had a rare, but treatable, autoimmune disease which is known to sometimes present as psychiatric symptoms, as well as seizures, confusion and memory loss.

In her first interview since the experience, she tells BBC News she wants hospitals to offer a series of tests as standard practice if patients have these symptoms.

"In a way I do feel let down by the care I received. I feel like the urgency to discover what was actually wrong with me wasn't there," she says.

"And I also feel as a woman being written off completely as a psychotic patient without further investigation was a mistake."

A spokesperson for the hospital she attended has apologised for Bahsoon's experience and says an investigation has been launched into her care.

Bahsoon first had "psychotic symptoms" in March this year after filming a video on the Tube with girl group Flo.

She says that evening she began to scream, cry and her conversations became "very erratic".

The next day she broke up with her boyfriend, which prompted her sisters to check on her, as it was so unexpected.

Bahsoon says her condition got worse, becoming violent towards herself and posting videos which didn't make sense, before her sisters called 999 for an ambulance.

"I'm normally a very relaxed person, maybe anxious at times, but the way I was speaking about harming myself and the way I was screaming and being violent was super out of character for me," she says.

A&E doctors initially thought her symptoms could have been provoked by stress and a lack of sleep, discharging her with sleeping tablets.

She then began destroying things at home and spoke about having hallucinations, which led to police bringing her to hospital in handcuffs.

Bahsoon was sectioned and moved to a psychiatric ward where she was treated with antipsychotic medication, which she says made her "docile".

"I went from being a total firecracker to being completely catatonic," she says.

"I stopped eating, drinking. I could not speak properly."

Bahsoon has "very faint memories" of this period, she says, but her family has since shown her clips of her having breakdowns which she finds "heartbreaking".

After two months on the psychiatric ward, Bahsoon was diagnosed with an autoimmune disease called anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

It was caused by tumours in her ovaries, known as teratomas, producing antibodies which attacked her body.

She had surgery to remove the tumours in June, which she says brought on a "drastic" change in her behaviour from "freaking out" to having more understanding of what was happening around her.

Bahsoon has since been recovering back in her home country of Malaysia and is having therapy to "deal with all the trauma".

But she says she feels "very lucky" as doctors have told her she is part of a small percentage of people who they expect to make a full recovery.

The content creator first revealed what happened in a TikTok video in October, and says she is sharing her story as she wants to raise awareness of the disease.

She also wants to "push people to advocate for themselves" if they feel they're not getting the "treatment they deserve".

"I do want reform in the way that hospitals deal with psychotic patients or patients that present with psychotic symptoms," she says.

"I hope I'm sharing my story so that nobody else has to go through this."

She plans to return to her content creation in the new year and is looking forward to "enjoying life with a whole new perspective and appreciation for what I do and what I now can help people with".

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is more typical in women and mainly affects young people, with about 40% of cases aged under 18, according to the charity Encephalitis International (EI).

Dr Ava Easton MBE, chief executive of EI, says a "frightening" aspect is how quickly someone's behaviour and personality can appear to change.

"A person may suddenly seem confused, distressed or [to be] experiencing psychosis when the underlying problem is actually inflammation of their brain," she says.

She says there's a "real risk" of it going undiagnosed and encourages people to look out for the warning signs.

According to the NHS, cases of all types of encephalitis are rare, and EI says the condition affects about 6,000 people in the UK each year.

A spokesperson for Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, which was the first to treat Bahsoon, said they were "very sorry" for what she experienced.

They said an internal review found some aspects of her initial assessment "were not followed up as they should have been" and an investigation had been started.

Dr Ed Beveridge, divisional medical director at Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust, also confirmed they'd be part of that review.

He said anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was a "rare autoimmune condition" that is not "routinely screened for nationally".

"We are pleased that her condition has now been identified and treated."

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump

BBC News Tue, 24 Nov 2026 07:26:27 GMT

Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.

But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.

That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".

Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.

Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.

Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.

But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.

Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.

China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.

And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.

What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.

Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.

What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.

Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.

Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

Two AI companies reveal ‘Earth-shattering’ solutions to major maths problem

New Scientist November 24, 2026

Two AI companies have released “Earth-shattering” solutions to a problem related to P versus NP, considered one of the most difficult puzzles in mathematics. Coming a few days after a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the achievement is a further sign that the pace of progress being made by AI in maths is unlike anything ever seen before.

P versus NP relates to how difficult some problems are to solve using a computer. P problems are relatively simple to solve, but NP problems quickly become drastically more difficult as their size increases. If P could be proved to be the same as NP, then we would have a radically faster way to solve a host of computationally intensive problems, and there would be a dramatic effect on society: computer encryption would break, logistical and engineering problems could be highly optimised, and new drugs could be discovered more easily.

A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out

It is one of the seven Millennium Prize problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, which promise a $1 million award to anyone who can solve them. One of those, the Poincaré conjecture, fell in 2010. Two others have fallen to AI: the Navier-Stokes puzzle in September and the Riemann hypothesis last week.

Advertisement

The new AI results concern VP versus VNP, a problem posed after mathematicians and computer scientists realised the importance of P versus NP, but made little progress towards a solution. The idea was to replace the binary logic of computers with arithmetic, which imposes a more structured problem set. It is supposed to be a stepping stone along the way to P vs NP – not necessarily something that would lead directly to a solution, but something that would widen our understanding and help clear a path to more on P vs NP.

Yesterday, Anthropic quietly published its VP versus VNP finding on its GitHub page with no wider announcement. The work proves that VNP isn’t contained within VP and that some classes of problems are simply difficult to solve no matter what. The company said the discovery was made by an internal research version of its Claude model, which also wrote the paper and a formalisation, a conversion of the proof to computer code that allows it to be methodically and logically picked apart and proved correct. “No human mathematician has checked the proof,” the company said.

On the same day, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI released a paper on GitHub setting out its own solution to the same problem, also including a formalisation. The two solutions are similar in some ways but diverge on key points. Neither company responded to a request for comment, but the timestamps of the uploads suggest Anthropic beat OpenAI to the prize by about 6 hours.

Free newsletter

Tom Gur at the University of Cambridge was surprised by the news and says he thought many other discoveries would be made before VP versus VNP was solved.

“If you’d have asked me in what now feels like ancient history, which would be, I don’t know, August, I would have told you that I don’t think I will live to see it,” says Gur. “We are seeing here decades of progress in days. It’s an exciting time to be alive.”

Mathematicians argue about the relative difficulty of the two problems, and how far a solution to VP versus VNP gets us to a solution to P versus NP. “But one thing you can say for sure is that this is Earth-shattering progress,” says Gur. “It’s just so far beyond the range of techniques that we had before.”

The difficulty facing mathematicians working on either puzzle – VP versus VNP or P versus NP – is that proving that a problem previously thought to be very hard is actually easy is straightforward: simply show an algorithm that solves it easily. But proving that a problem or set of problems is actually very hard, and will always remain so, requires evidence that there is no algorithm that can be written which can solve it easily.

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

“The reality is that we have a very, very, very limited arsenal of tools to prove this limitation [that some algorithms are intrinsically hard],” says Gur. The proof of VP versus VNP is an extremely powerful tool, but the question is how generalisable it is, he says. “I think we need, as a community, more time to study these results to understand.”

Varun Kanade at the University of Oxford thinks the new proofs will help with – but not directly lead to – a solution for P versus NP. “It does get us closer in the sense that it makes progress on a problem related to the main one, but my sense is that we will require new techniques for the P v NP question,” he says. “At this point, I have to say that I’m not surprised that AI has made progress on this question, having seen the recent announcement of the proof of the Riemann hypothesis.”

But Ben Livshits at Imperial College London says not everyone will be buoyed by the discoveries and the way they were achieved.

“AI is now doing research-level mathematics and theoretical computer science, and I don’t think we’ve properly thought through the longer-term effects,” says Livshits. “For theoretical computer scientists, many of whom have spent years or whole careers on these problems, it’s a very mixed blessing, and several have already said so.”
