The mystery of sub-Neptunes – the planets we thought shouldn’t exist

New Scientist November 24, 2026

For almost a decade, the Kepler Space Telescope trailed Earth’s orbit, watching out for flickers in the light of distant stars. In 2011, two years after its launch, the NASA mission found what it was looking for: the signature of a roughly Earth-sized planet dimming out a tiny sliver of light as it transited across the face of its star.

The identification of Kepler-10b, a planet almost 1.5 times the size of Earth that orbits a star around 600 light years away, was the first time we had spotted a rocky exoplanet – a world beyond our solar system. Since then, our rapidly expanding exoplanet catalogue has revealed plenty of surprises, but one above all: most planets in our galaxy aren’t like Earth. In fact, they are like nothing in our solar system at all.

Out of the now 6451 confirmed exoplanets, by far the most common type are the “sub-Neptunes”, planets between Earth and Neptune in size that old theories of planet formation based on our solar system didn’t predict. And there are lots of them – over 3000 at the last count. “You know how evolution, like, really likes making crabs? Planet formation seems to really like making sub-Neptunes,” says astrophysicist Matthew Nixon at Arizona State University.

Advertisement

Is our solar system a cosmic oddity? Evidence from exoplanets says yes

But there is no sub-Neptune in our solar system, and that leaves researchers with a puzzle: what exactly are these mysterious planets? Now, aided by NASA’s orbiting high-tech thermal camera, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), they are coming into sharper focus. New discoveries are answering some questions, but raising many more about what sub-Neptunes look like, how they form – and whether they might even host life.

Exoplanetary science is still young. Astronomers spotted the first planet beyond our solar system, a gas giant circling a pulsar, in 1992. In 1995 came the first exoplanet around a sun-like star, a giant, close-orbiting “hot Jupiter” called 51 Pegasi b. But the hunt didn’t hit its high season until Kepler launched in 2009. It flew with just one instrument: a photometer that could precisely measure stars’ brightness and catch the telltale flickers of passing planets. By the time the mission ran out of fuel in 2018, it had discovered over half of all exoplanets we know today.

Back in those early days, our ideas of how planets formed were guided by a sample of one: our solar system. It is widely agreed that our sun formed from the gravitational collapse of the solar nebula, a giant, spinning cloud of hydrogen and helium gas, plus a sprinkling of heavier elements. Once the young sun ignited, a disc of material continued circling it that would give rise to the planets.

Looking at our solar system, scientists broadly concluded that what planets look like came down to where they formed within this nebular Frisbee. Closer to the sun, it is too hot for anything but rock and metals to solidify and clump together, meaning less material to sweep up into planets. So, the planets of the inner solar system – Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars – ended up small and rocky. Meanwhile, in longer orbits beyond the “snow line”, where compounds such as water, ammonia and methane freeze out and form ices, baby planetary cores could get bigger. These bigger cores had the gravitational heft to gobble up hydrogen and helium gas from the solar nebula. They formed the outer solar system’s two gas giants, Jupiter and Saturn, and its more distant “ice giants”, Uranus and Neptune.

Earth is the solar system’s largest rocky planet; Neptune, at around four times Earth’s diameter, is its smallest giant planet. The gap in size between the two seemed natural. Given how we thought planets form, worlds much bigger than Earth should be incredibly rare within the snow line. That, it turns out, isn’t true.

Exoplanet astronomers have found everything from alien gas titans that would dwarf Jupiter to planetary pebbles comparable to Mercury. But among confirmed exoplanets with a known radius, about half are sub-Neptunes, many of them hewing in warm orbits very close to their stars. “They’re really the ultimate mystery,” says exoplanet astronomer Eliza Kempton at the University of Chicago.

Kempton has been studying sub-Neptunes since before they were called sub-Neptunes. In 2010, even before Kepler found that first Earth-sized planet, she and her colleagues used the ground-based Very Large Telescope facility in Chile to observe the hazy atmosphere of a planet called GJ 1214 b some 48 light years away from Earth. With a radius 2.7 times that of Earth, but orbiting far closer to its star than Mercury does to the sun, that planet is now something of a poster child for the sub-Neptunes. But back then, it was a “super-Earth”.

“We just called everything a super-Earth,” says Kempton. “This was before we even knew that small planets bifurcate into, like, the ‘smaller’ class and the ‘bigger’ class.” That divide refers to a striking discovery made in 2017 that deepened the mystery of sub-Neptunes further still. When astronomers used Kepler data to chart the number of exoplanets of different sizes, it revealed two bumps. One was centred on planets with radii about 1.4 times Earth’s, and another on those of about 2.4 Earth radii. In between, there was a gap with relatively few planets. The sub-Neptunes appeared to be not just one population of planets, but two.

The discovery of this “radius valley” lent support to an idea that harsh radiation emitted from young stars, plus leftover heat from planet formation, blasts away the baby blankets of hydrogen and helium gas enveloping smaller planets. That leaves bare, rocky worlds that form the super-Earth peak. Bigger planets with more gravity, meanwhile, hold onto at least some hydrogen and helium. They end up as puffier, gas-cloaked worlds in the sub-Neptune peak.

In this picture, terrestrial planets like Earth might be the naked cores of erstwhile sub-Neptunes. “If you’re ultimately interested in more Earth-like worlds, sub-Neptunes represent a kind of arrested stage of development. These are the things that stop short of becoming something like Earth,” says planetary scientist Raymond Pierrehumbert at the University of Oxford. “I think of them almost like fossilised atmospheres.”Unlike the ice giants of our solar system, sub-Neptunes close to their stars might form pretty dry – as “gas dwarfs” with no ice, just a rocky interior and a thick gas envelope made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. But there are other possibilities. The discovery of hot Jupiters – gas giant planets in close orbits where they couldn’t possibly have formed – helped scientists realise that planets can migrate, something we now know probably happened in our solar system, too. Sub-Neptunes could be ice worlds that form beyond their planetary system’s snow line and wander inwards. In some simulations, this migration produces a radius valley: one that divides small, rocky planets from big, watery ones. Since JWST’s launch in 2021, astronomers have been able to start differentiating between such scenarios. Its great infrared eye sees in wavelengths of light at which molecules such as water, ammonia, carbon dioxide and methane leave distinctive fingerprints on starlight passing through exoplanets’ upper atmospheres.

10 stunning James Webb Space Telescope images show the beauty of space

In at least one case, that of the hot sub-Neptune TOI-421 b, which orbits its sun-like star far closer than Mercury does our sun, JWST observations largely match what you would expect for a gas dwarf. But observations are revealing that sub-Neptunes are a diverse group (see “Five ways to make a sub-Neptune”, below). If some of them are worlds with abundant water, it would be a big deal for the search for life. “Where you can find water, you can find habitable conditions,” says astrophysicist Caroline Piaulet-Ghorayeb also at the University of Chicago. Finding sub-Neptune water worlds “would kind of change our thinking about habitability”, she says. Earth-sized planets are very hard to observe in detail with JWST, so bigger water worlds could be our best immediate hope for finding signs of life on an exoplanet.

The mere presence of water doesn’t make a habitable planet. Sub-Neptunes could be balls of exotic, high-pressure ice and “supercritical” fluids that are neither liquid nor gas – mini ice giants, not ocean worlds. And because hydrogen is a strong greenhouse gas, sub-Neptunes with hydrogen atmospheres can end up as boiling “steam worlds” with atmospheres rich in water vapour. JWST observations suggest that a watery sub-Neptune called GJ 9827 d is such a planet.

However, in the lead-up to JWST’s launch, astrophysicist Nikku Madhusudhan at the University of Cambridge and his colleagues showed that water worlds with thin hydrogen atmospheres could have liquid water on their surfaces (too thick an atmosphere, and the water boils). Madhusudhan later dubbed these planets “Hycean” worlds, a portmanteau of “hydrogen” and “ocean”. JWST observations have hinted that a sub-Neptune called K2-18 b orbiting a star some 125 light years from Earth might belong to this group. It sits in its star’s habitable zone, where it is theoretically cool enough for surface liquid water.

This plot thickened in 2023, when Madhusudhan’s team spotted what it interpreted as tentative evidence for dimethyl sulphide (DMS) in K2-18 b’s atmosphere. On Earth, DMS is made only by life – primarily plankton in the ocean. The team doubled down after follow-up JWST observations, but the result remains fiercely disputed. Nixon objects that the data isn’t enough to uniquely identify a molecule as complex as DMS. “A lot of other molecules, if you were to test them, you would also get a comparable result,” he says. Madhusudhan stands by the detection. He argues that researchers have historically accepted detections of more mundane gases like CO2 based on comparable evidence.

If there is DMS on K2-18 b, it is possible that an unknown chemical process might produce it, rather than alien microbes. Madhusudhan says he would “absolutely” be happy either way. “The discovery of a new chemical process in a planetary atmosphere? I mean, that’s a huge deal,” he says. “To me, that is as good as finding life.”

But even the identification of K2-18 b as a Hycean world is disputed. What scientists see in sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres depends in large part on what happens out of view, deep in the planets’ hot, high-pressure interiors. The mix of molecules JWST has spotted in K2-18 b’s atmosphere matches a planet with water oceans – but might also fit a gaseous mini-Neptune without a real surface, or a gas dwarf with a magma ocean simmering below its hydrogen envelope.

Earth once had a magma ocean, too. Rocky worlds go through an initial molten phase with a global magma ocean before they cool down and solidify. Some sub-Neptunes might trap enough primordial heat below blankets of gas and icy material that their magma oceans never freeze – with significant consequences. “Magma oceans are a chemical factory,” says Pierrehumbert. “Chemicals can get in there and react and do all sorts of stuff.” One reason to think K2-18 b is a watery world is the lack of ammonia in its atmosphere: ammonia dissolves in water. But it also dissolves in liquid rock. So ultimately, researchers need to learn more about K2-18 b’s atmosphere to pin down its composition.

Magma oceans do more than conceal compounds such as ammonia – they “fundamentally change the composition of the atmosphere”, says Kempton. Reactions between hydrogen and magma could even produce abundant water on planets that were born dry, without any water, she adds. This process might have produced some of Earth’s water back when it had a magma ocean.

Magma isn’t the only thing that might be smouldering deep within sub-Neptunes. A study led by Kempton’s University of Chicago colleague Jeehyun Yang recently found that sub-Neptunes could be a bit like combustion engines, burning carbon-rich compounds to produce soot. A layer of these planets might be, rather literally, on fire, says Yang. Clouds of black soot belched up from below would block out some molecular signals, perhaps explaining a pattern of muted molecular fingerprints in JWST data from several sub-Neptunes.

Some worlds might make soot; others might actually be made of it. Just as there is a snow line beyond which water is solid, there is a “soot line” around young stars where organic carbon molecules can start to form grains of black, tarry material. Sub-Neptunes are reviving an old idea that this could create “soot worlds”, says planetary scientist Zifan Lin at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri. Lin and his colleague Sara Seager at the University of Toronto recently showed that soot worlds with cores of rock and metal, overlain by layers of diamond and graphite and with hydrogen-rich atmospheres, could match JWST observations of three sub-Neptunes, including K2-18 b.

So, gas dwarfs, water worlds, soot planets – what’s the answer? The boundaries might be fuzzier than they sound. Recent work by Piaulet-Ghorayeb and her colleagues has shown that some sub-Neptunes that appear dry could hide water deep in their interiors, where it is invisible to telescopes. And there could be sooty water worlds, sooty gas dwarfs and everything in between.

An abridged inventory of everything there is in the universe – from rogue planets and exomoons to supernovae, supermassive black holes and the cosmic web.

One lesson sub-Neptunes have already taught scientists is that planetary evolution, not just formation, determines what worlds are made of. Losing an atmosphere or reacting one with a magma ocean, say, shapes a planet just as profoundly as forming beyond or within the snow line. Nixon says he is working on finding ways to distinguish between water worlds that wandered inwards and sub-Neptunes that formed dry and later made their own water. To this end, he is observing a hot sub-Neptune called HD 86226 that is virtually guaranteed to have a magma ocean, eliminating some guesswork.

Ideally, scientists would eventually like to understand whether sub-Neptunes are all basically variations on the same planetary theme, or are many sub-groups with different histories. Observations so far have pinpointed only a few molecules in a handful of sub-Neptunes’ atmospheres. Surveys of more sub-Neptunes are under way, and these could help pick out different groups if they exist.

The more we learn about sub-Neptunes, the more they surprise us, making them one of the most exciting active frontiers in exoplanetary science. We still don’t know why our solar system lacks one of these abundant worlds, but they are the closest thing to a world like Earth that we can observe easily at present. Through them, we learn not only about the broader universe, but also about the forces that sculpt worlds like our own. “The sub-Neptunes give us that next stepping stone,” says Kempton. “We’re kind of marching our way towards the study of Earth-like worlds in the future.”

18 brilliant and surprising gifts for science lovers this Christmas

New Scientist November 24, 2026

The New Scientist Christmas gift guide is assembled by our crack team of science editors and experts. If you’re struggling for gift ideas, you will find unexpected and ingenious suggestions for amateur astronomers and animal and nature lovers, as well as those fond of food, beauty and puzzles. And surely that covers all of us?

If you’re looking for a quick and easy jigsaw to breeze through while watching holiday movies, Nervous System puzzles probably aren’t for you. But if you want something that’s part puzzle, part work of art, and that will keep you transfixed for hours, they’ll definitely do the trick. Nervous System makes laser-cut wooden puzzles with uniquely shaped pieces and science themes, and they are absolutely beautiful. I’m particularly a fan of their geode puzzles, featuring concentric wiggles of bright colour, including wiggly sides that defy every puzzler’s instinct to start with the edge pieces. For even more of a challenge, they make infinity puzzles that can be assembled and reassembled many different ways – those have no edge pieces at all, and some don’t even have a picture on them! Nervous System also sells absolutely stunning jewellery, lamps and sculptures, but to me the puzzles are the real show-stoppers.

Nervous System puzzles, from $45 (£32)

Advertisement

Leah Crane

The eccentric filmmaker Werner Herzog famously declared that he travels with only a second set of underwear, a map, a toothbrush and a set of binoculars. I don’t travel quite so lightly, but on my next trip, I definitely want to add a pair of nice binos to my baggage. I tested out three sets at varying price levels, taking them down to my favourite spot on my local river and out to my backyard during a clear night with a half-moon overhead. The Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 binoculars are extremely well balanced and were the most comfortable in my hands. They were particularly well-suited for twilight and brighter. The other Nikon set I tried was the Stabilised 12×25 S, which is much more compact. For my small hands that was fine, and the stabilisation was marvellous at reducing any shaking, both while looking at something fixed like the moon or moving quickly to track an eagle fishing for dinner. The stabilisation requires batteries, so these are probably best –suited to the more prepared adventurer. The stand–out pair was the CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik. I’ve never seen anything look better than they did through these lenses. They let in an enormous amount of light, making the world look like the brightness has been turned up. And the moon’s craters looked stunningly crisp. For the birdwatcher, wildlife lover or stargazer in your life, these would be a worthwhile, although pretty major, splurge.

Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42, £159

Nikon Stabilised 12×25 S, £729

CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik, from £1070

Chelsea Whyte

Thomas Nagel’s famous 1974 essay, “What is it like to be a bat?”, argued that we can never fully know the experience of being a bat (or any other animal). I have been testing that argument with my fantastic bat detector. The device picks up on the ultrasound frequencies emitted by bats as they fly overhead and converts them into clicks that we can hear. It also displays the frequency of the squeak, and that allows us to identify the species. In my London back garden I get mostly pipistrelles, our smallest bat at just 4 grams. Nagel is right – I don’t know what it is like to fly and catch moths by echolocation. But it is quite thrilling to hear the clicks as a bat swoops past in the dark, and that experience has got me a little closer to appreciating what it is like to be a bat. There are several options available, but I used the Magenta 5 bat detector from Wildcare.

Magenta 5 bat detector, £105

Rowan Hooper

If you have a jetsetter in your life, they are probably by definition the kind of person who is tricky to find a gift for. So why not gift them something money can’t buy (well, almost): an end to jet lag? Many moons ago, I was on a journalism fellowship about sleep at Harvard Medical School, when I visited the lab of sleep scientist Steven Lockley. I was fascinated by his experiments, including work he was doing with NASA astronauts, which looked at circadian rhythms, sleep and what happens when our bodies are out of sync with the natural rhythms of the day. Aside from astronauts, many of us who remain earthbound can still feel these effects – especially those who do regular shift work or long-distance travel. What’s more, a body clock that’s out of whack can have serious health consequences.

I followed Lockley’s research closely over the years, and he was generous enough, whenever I travelled back to Boston, to make me a tailored jet-lag plan – when to sleep or nap in the days before and during my flight, as well as when to wear sunglasses and drink caffeine, all based on what time my flight was and the time difference. Fast forward about a decade, and this service is no longer a personal one – Lockley has created an app called Timeshifter, which allows users to plug in their flight details and instantly receive a step-by-step plan to minimise jet lag. There’s a version of the app for shift workers, too.

I recently tried it on a trip to New York, purchasing a one-off plan rather than the subscription, and I can honestly say that I barely felt any jet lag at all – while my husband was falling asleep in his sushi at dinner.

Timeshifter app, $6.99/month or $69.99/year (£5.30/month or £53/year)

Catherine de Lange

Forget spin classes and aerobics – fitness these days is all about strength over heart rate. If a loved one has started talking about “Lifting PBs” and “protein-maxxing”, you could do much worse than getting them some proper footwear for their gym trips. There’s emerging evidence to suggest barefoot trainers strengthen foot muscles compared with regular trainers, including the small, stabilising muscles that improve balance. Vivobarefoot’s Motus Strength are specifically designed for weightlifting sessions – I’ve been wearing them to the gym for the last few weeks and am a total convert. You can also get barefoot shoes for hiking and trail running, for those who prefer the great outdoors to the weights floor.

Vivobarefoot Motus Strength, £150

Madeleine Cuff

If, like me, you grew up collecting Pokémon cards but now shudder at the prices and scalpers, there’s a brilliant alternative, and it’s science-themed. Life TCG lets players collect, trade and play using cards based on real-world creatures, with gameplay reminiscent of Top Trumps. But the artwork is the real highlight, a charming mix of realistic paintings, quirky cartoons and special-edition photography. One of my first packs even revealed a stunning South Chinese tiger card (one of my favourite animals). The gameplay itself is fairly simple, but the cards are beautiful enough to work as collectible art pieces in their own right. Better still, first-edition holographic cards are genuinely rare. Each is printed in numbers matching that animal’s estimated population in the wild. Life TCG also donates a portion of its profits to WWF. Collecting cards that look great, teach you something and support wildlife conservation? That’s a rare win.

Life TCG cards, from £15

Emily Bates

For more than 8000 years (in between struggling to survive), humans have been harvesting and fermenting grapes to make the delicious liquid we call wine. Over that time, we’ve amassed more knowledge about this plant-based product than any other – except the secrets of what gives a wine its distinctive quality. Noble Nine is a state-of-the-art guide to that quest and many other things vinous by researcher Andrew Wood – perhaps the only academic anywhere lucky enough to do a PhD in the biology of wine quality. Our first metaphorical glass comes from the merlot wine grape, and we cheerfully drink our way through the other eight in Wood’s selection, including chenin blanc, pinot noir, shiraz, and ending up with sauvignon blanc. Cheers, everyone!

Noble Nine: The story and science of the world’s favourite wines by Andrew Wood, £20

Liz Else

I’ve got a little herb garden outside on my patio, and there’s no better feeling during the warmer months than popping out to fetch some fresh coriander or basil midway through dinner prep. But in the winter, I usually rely on plastic packets of supermarket herbs, which inevitably wilt in the fridge before I use them all. The solution? An indoor herb garden that lets you grow fresh herbs all year round. I’ve tested a few models, and the Auk Mini 2 is the winner for easy setup, stylish design and bountiful harvest. It fits on a shelf in my kitchen and costs about 50p per week to run.

Auk Mini 2, £209

Madeleine Cuff

For my son’s 10th birthday, his grandmother wanted to gift him a very extravagant present – a 3D printer. I wasn’t convinced at first, worried it would be too big for the house, too technical, dangerous (who wants to let their kids play with melting plastic?) and generally a bad idea. A few months in, I’m happy to be recommending this as a great present for a very special young person in your life. We went for the Bambu Labs A1 mini, which is small enough to be stored out of sight and brought out for supervised use. So far, it’s been very easy to “plug and play”, and my son has printed a range of plastic tat that nobody needed, and a couple of “gifts” for me, including a stand for my phone while I cook (how thoughtful!). Now that we’ve grasped the basics, the next step is for him to learn to design his own projects, which is where things become more educational. I’m also hoping we can use it to print spare parts when appliances break at home. Unlike toys that get played with a few times and forgotten, a 3D printer is a gift that can evolve with your child’s abilities and get used for years to come.

Bambu Labs A1 mini 3D printer, £139

Catherine de Lange

Feeling yourself immersed in the deep vibrations of a singing bowl isn’t just a pleasant acoustic experience. Sound baths – when you listen, usually while lying down, to acoustic instruments –are deeply, deeply relaxing. Studies have found the experience helps reduce feelings of anxiety and tension, and there’s also evidence they can improve both sleep and cognitive function. Sound baths are a meditative practice and that, for me, is where the true benefits lie. Silent meditation is difficult, and it’s hard not to grow frustrated with myself for my wandering thoughts and inability to focus on my breath. The beautiful music of sound baths provides an external, soothing distraction. They provide a space to pause and allow to-do lists to gently fade away. There are both private and group-class sound baths, either of which would make a thoughtful gift as a shared activity or simply a new year’s reset.

Sound bath vouchers, from £25 (A few options in London, Brighton & Manchester)

Olivia Goldhill

A regular topic of conversation when I get together with my wider family is how we would survive in the event of an apocalypse, and who would contribute what skills. With my husband an engineer, my brother-in-law a doctor and my mum a brilliant gardener, we think we’d do pretty well, but I’ve decided the key thing I’d contribute is my copy of The Book. Subtitled “the ultimate guide to rebuilding civilization”, it covers everything from making fire and beer to leathercraft and traps. Running to 400 pages, it was written with the scientific and technical advice of Lewis Dartnell at the University of Westminster, UK, and would be a fun and practical gift for anyone in your life who is eyeing the future with trepidation.

The Book, £99

Alison Flood

It is widely accepted that growing your own fruit and vegetables is not only mentally rewarding, but that the food tastes especially good when the gap between picking it and eating it is minimised. But, I thought, what about mushrooms? To find out, I grew my own mushrooms with foolproof growing kits from Merryhill Mushrooms. Choose the species of mushroom, and the company delivers the kit to your door. I tried regular chestnut mushrooms and the impressive lion’s mane mushroom. You really don’t have to do much other than keep their box humid; within a couple of weeks, the mushrooms had emerged from the mycelial mass, and I had picked and eaten them. Mushroom steaks and “pulled shroom” curry. Delicious!

Mushroom growing kit from Merryhill Mushrooms, from £18.95

Rowan Hooper

Last year, I stumbled upon the Space store in the Oxford covered market, drawn in by the floating, spinning globes in the window display. The thing that particularly caught my eye was a true 3D-printed model of the moon, suspended by a magnet – it looked like it defied gravity. I subsequently splashed out and bought it! It’s now a great addition to my desk and has become something I really love. The model is raised so that the surface is textured, and you can interact with it a bit. The globe also has three light tones (warm, cool and neutral), which is great for setting a mood. You can get it slightly cheaper elsewhere but if you can, I would highly suggest supporting the Space store. And if this one can’t be justified, they have many other cool products and globe lights that don’t float.

Smart moon lamp, £159

Phoebe Watts

Vegetable oils are in almost everything, from beauty products and sandwiches to even pet food. But producing them requires a huge amount of land, energy and water. Clean Food Group is an exciting British company working to change that, using precision fermentation to produce oils from yeast in vats. It estimates its CleanOil product offers a 90 per cent cut to carbon emissions compared with using palm oil. Scottish beauty company Raven Beauty became the first company to use CleanOil in consumer products this year, releasing a facial cleanser in September, which I road-tested for a New Scientist video. Now Raven has released a range of body oils also featuring CleanOil, which would make a great gift for someone who deserves a bit of pampering. Plus, I think this small company deserves a cheer for being one of the first in line for pioneering green technology.

Body oil, £38

Madeleine Cuff

We may be used to talking about how many times around the sun we have travelled each birthday. But for the inquisitive-minded, there’s more detail to be had. Have you stopped to consider, for instance, how many volcanoes have erupted since the day you were born, or how many times your heart has beaten? How many dinosaurs were named in that time, or elements discovered?

This is the premise behind Days of You, a beautiful and personalised hardback book, packed full of data specifically tailored to a specific person. All you have to do is provide the name, date of birth and place of birth of your special someone, and the team behind Days of You (which, incidentally, is the brainchild of former New Scientist staffer Matt Walker) pulls together stats and data ranging from the shape of the moon on the birthday in question to what the price of tea and the best-selling album were that year. This is essentially a beautifully visualised piece of data journalism, where the subject is your lucky recipient.

It may sound simple, but much of the data is hard to come by – especially from some of the weather stations – and must be tailored to the birth location in question. For that reason, the book is only available for those born in the US and the UK.

Books usually take 5-6 working days from order to door, the team says, but to be sure, they recommend ordering by 10 December. They also make personalised calendars, mugs, and prints for new babies.

The Days of You, £49

Catherine de Lange

Teenagers usually come in for the most scrutiny over phone use, but the truth is we could all do with cutting back on our screen time, no matter our age. Have a chat with your nearest and dearest about their New Year’s resolutions and see if reducing their phone use comes up. If it does, a Brick might be the perfect gift this Christmas. It’s a small magnetic tile, and when you tap your phone against it, a pre-selected group of apps is blocked from use until you tap again. I use mine to curb scrolling during work hours and reduce my phone use around my children at the weekend. I’ve found the extra effort it takes to go and find the Brick to tap and unlock your apps has been enough to rewire my behaviour pretty significantly. Brick has also just launched Brick Night, which blocks selected apps from being used when you enter your bedroom – perfect for preventing doomscrolling before bed.

Brick, £49, Brick Night, £119

Madeleine Cuff

Severe eczema healed by novel immune-calming pill in clinical trial

New Scientist November 24, 2026

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says Gayle Ross at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

Advertisement

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is effective, it has had limited uptake in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

In the clinical trial, 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average 72 per cent reduction in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said Terence Rooney, the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a webcast on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a trial of KT-621 in people with asthma, since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

Toddlers form complex memories but may then lose access to them

New Scientist November 24, 2026

We can form complicated memories in our earliest years, even though most of us ultimately lose the ability to recall them, a study of almost 400 toddlers suggests.

The research throws new light on infantile amnesia, which leaves most adults unable to remember events that occurred when they were under the age of 3 or 4. It builds on a 2025 study showing that infants do, in fact, have the capacity to form specific memories before infantile amnesia kicks in. Tristan Yates at Columbia University in New York, who worked on that study, says the new experiment shows that early infant memory includes the ability to recall complex information, linking the location of an object to its surroundings.

Markus Werkle-Bergner at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin and his colleagues tested 388 toddlers, aged 18 to 24 months at the time the research began, using a game of hide-and-seek. The children entered a room with four boxes, its walls transformed by projected images into either a jungle or an underwater world.

Advertisement

Reading for pleasure boosts memory, empathy and mental health

Their task was to find Corky, a toy puppet whose hiding place changed with the setting. The children then returned a day later – and again after delays of one, three or six months – and were asked each time to remember where Corky was hiding.

Some of the children retained a full memory of the hide-and-seek game a day after they played. They remembered that Corky’s location changed depending on the surrounding scene – either underwater or jungle – and went to the hiding place that matched the scene in question.

Other children had a partial memory. They muddled up the two hiding places, approaching Corky’s underwater hiding place in the jungle scene, or vice versa. Some children seemed to retain no memory of the game at all, and simply chose a box in which Corky had never appeared.

Free newsletter

Among children who remembered both hiding places in their correct settings a day after playing the game, the researchers discovered that 32 per cent then went on to retain complete memories of the game months later. However, 45 per cent showed no reliable memory of the game after the months-long interval.

Age and language development did little to explain the differences, according to the researchers. “What remains unclear is why the toddlers differed so greatly,” says Werkle-Bergner.

A possible explanation is that memory is tied to how well children learned the game in the first place. For example, the children who couldn’t remember anything about Corky’s location a day after playing may not have understood the rules of the game in the first place. But among the children who could remember the toy’s location a day later, and so did understand the game, this understanding didn’t predict which of them would remember Corky’s location months later.

Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss

To further investigate, the researchers used non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) to measure electrical activity in some of the children’s brains. Among children who correctly recalled Corky’s location, a distinctive pattern of activity appeared in their brains just before they did so. This pattern became even clearer in the brains of children who could successfully recall Corky’s location after a delay of several months.

The researchers say this suggests that later forgetting might reflect difficulty retrieving a memory rather than simply a failure to store it in the first place.

Paul Frankland at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto says this idea fits with findings he and his colleagues made about a decade ago during experiments in mice, in which apparently forgotten memories could sometimes be restored by activating neurons involved in their formation.

Lapses in memory are a normal part of ageing but can also be signs of dementia. Here’s how to distinguish between typical brain ageing and cognitive decline

However, the EEG readings in the current work cannot establish beyond doubt that infant memories remain intact in the brain even after they can no longer be recalled, Frankland cautions.

The experiment also cannot show whether memories formed in infancy survive in an inaccessible form into adulthood, says Robyn Fivush at Emory University, Georgia. Language, social development and a growing sense of self all influence what people remember, she says.

Frankland thinks a more direct test might reveal more. “Ideally, we would want to identify the neural representation of a memory when it is first formed and then determine whether that same representation can be reactivated after the memory has been forgotten,” he says.

bioRxiv DOI: 10.64898/2026.10.19.755340

Super El Niño is making the global omega-3 shortage much worse

New Scientist November 24, 2026

Long-chain omega-3s are important for our heart and brain health, but most of us aren’t eating anything like the recommended amount. In fact, we couldn’t all eat enough even if we tried – the global supply of long-chain omega-3s is too low. Now, the super El Niño is making the problem even worse.

Humans evolved to be surprisingly fat – no wonder we struggle with dieting

The issue is that, whether you get your long-chain omega-3s from supplements or by eating farmed fish, those almost all derive from wild fish harvested from the oceans. The mega-El Niño that developed this year is hitting key fish stocks by reducing the upwelling of nutrient-rich waters off South America. This not only reduces catches, it also lessens the amount of omega-3s in the fish that are caught. In October, Peru banned any further anchovy catches this year – and Peru alone supplies around a fifth of the omega-3-rich fishmeal and fish oil used worldwide. This will lead to a huge shortfall and soaring prices.

While this El Niño will end, the long-term outlook is dire. The world’s population is still growing, but the fish oil supply cannot be increased. What’s more, the long-chain omega-3s in marine fish ultimately derive from algae, and the amount of omega-3s that algae produce seems to depend on water temperatures. As the world’s oceans warm, the supply of omega-3s may decline. Now for the good news: we have already developed solutions. We’ve just got to use them.

Advertisement

At this point, some of you will be thinking: “What are you talking about? I get all the omega-3s I need from eating foods such as walnuts, flaxseeds and chia seeds. Who needs fish oil?”

Well, you do. You’ll have noticed I have been talking about long-chain omega-3s. Some plants are rich in short-chain omega-3s such as ALA, but they don’t contain the two key long-chain omega-3s EPA and DHA. Our bodies can convert a little ALA into EPA and DHA, but we need to eat foods containing EPA and DHA to get enough.

We know that EPA and DHA are important for the heart and immune system, among other things, and for brain and eye development during pregnancy and childhood. But there is still a lot of uncertainty about just how much we need. That said, many organisations recommend adults get at least 250 milligrams of EPA and DHA combined per day through their diet.

For instance, the UK’s National Health Service recommends people eat two portions of fish a week, including at least one oily fish. But most people around the world get less than 250 mg of EPA and DHA in their diets, a 2014 study found. The situation more than a decade later is almost certainly worse, because over half of the fish we now eat comes from fish farms, and levels of long-chain omega-3s in farmed fish have plummeted. For instance, a 2016 study found that levels of EPA and DHA in farmed salmon from Scotland halved from 2006 to 2015.

“People are buying salmon because it’s got a health benefit,” says Johnathan Napier at Rothamsted Research in the UK. “There was no label saying ‘50 per cent less EPA and DHA’, so I think the consumer was badly misled in that respect.”

We now need to eat three portions of fish per week to get enough, he says. The reason why is that farmed salmon used to be fed entirely on fishmeal and fish oil, but, as prices have risen because of the limited supply, a growing portion of their feed has come from crop plants instead (and sometimes even chickens).

This reduces the nutritional value of our food, and it is also probably bad for the fish. “Because omega-3s are important for the immune response, they’re probably more susceptible to disease,” says Napier.

Eating more fish is also problematic. Pollutants such as dioxins and PCBs can accumulate in fish oil and then in the people eating it. The NHS advises girls and women not to eat more than two portions of oily fish a week because of the risk of these pollutants affecting fetuses.

The overlooked longevity nutrients that may add years to your life

There are two alternatives to fish oil as a source of long-chain omega-3s. One is to grow the marine algae that make it in the first place. This is already being done by a number of companies to produce vegan supplements, as well as additives for fish feeds. Algal EPA and DHA could replace a quarter of that obtained from fish oil within five years if production keeps expanding, according to a European Commission report out this year.

But Napier doubts that large-scale production will take off. “The thing that kills you in the end is the cost,” he says.

Algae don’t produce high levels of omega-3s. What they do make isn’t in an easily extractable form, and growing them requires expensive equipment, feedstocks and processing, he says. “It just costs too much money.”

The second alternative is to genetically modify (GM) plants to produce long-chain omega-3s by adding genes from algae. A GM canola (rapeseed) whose oil is around 10 per cent DHA is already being grown in the US to produce DHA for supplements and fish feed. The fish feed, produced by a Melbourne-based multinational called Nufarm, is being used in Canada and Chile as well as the US, and has also been approved in Norway.

The problem is that the GM canola produces very little EPA. Another company did manage to modify canola to produce EPA, but that produced no DHA, says Napier. His team, however, has created a GM camelina whose oil contains more than 10 per cent EPA and 10 per cent DHA. Last year, Nufarm acquired the rights to this technology.

“We can make the same level of EPA and DHA as you would find in a fish oil in our GM camelina,” says Napier, who is working with Nufarm to help get the camelina on the market.

His team has also modified the camelina to produce a pigment called astaxanthin, which gives salmon its colour. Like long-chain omega-3s, the astaxanthin in salmon ultimately derives from marine algae, so, as fish feeds have changed, producers have had to start feeding them synthetic astaxanthin made from petrochemicals, because consumers won’t buy grey salmon. In other words, the GM camelina could provide at least three of the key compounds found in fish meal.

Will this approach take off? Crop production can be scaled up more easily than algal production. In places such as Europe, there are a lot of regulatory barriers to growing and selling GM crops directly, but GM crops are already imported for animal feed.

So we will have to wait and see, but certainly in technological terms, we already have two solutions to the shortage of fish-oil-derived long-chain omega-3s. And getting them from algae or GM crops instead of fish will avoid the issues with dioxins and PCBs.

There is also the question of sustainability, but it’s hard to compare the different approaches. Catching wild fish, growing crops and cultivating algae can all be very destructive, but often in different ways. There are also many environmental issues with farming fish.

Would the best solution sustainability-wise be to cut out fish altogether and get our long-chain omega-3s directly from GM plants instead? Napier says eating fish does have benefits besides providing omega-3s. However, together with Cathie Martin at the John Innes Centre in the UK, he has created a tomato that is rich in EPA. The team is now working to boost the DHA levels.

Omega-3-rich GM tomatoes won’t reach supermarket shelves in Europe any time soon, but could do so in countries such as the US, where getting GM crops approved is much easier. I, for one, think they are a brilliant idea, and can’t wait to try them.

The technology that could make government internet blackouts impossible

New Scientist November 24, 2026

An emerging satellite communication technology could curtail the ability of authoritarian regimes to cut off internet access to citizens.

Internet blackouts are a common fixture in countries like Myanmar, Pakistan, Ethiopia and Iran during periods of civil unrest, making organising any type of dissenting activity very difficult.

Iran’s regime, however, is worried that direct-to-cell (D2C) satellite internet will make it easier for citizens to escape restrictions. The country’s deputy communications minister, Mohammad Hafez Hakami, said on 30 September it may make blackouts impossible in the future by rendering current measures like device registration and user-identity verification ineffective, perhaps one day forcing the government to resort to more extreme measures like electricity blackouts.

Advertisement

How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses

Satellite internet, notably SpaceX’s Starlink, has already allowed some protesters and organisers in countries like Iran to weather internet blackouts by circumventing local carriers entirely.

However, the cost of a Starlink terminal needed to use the service can reportedly reach up to $4000 on the black-market Telegram chats where they are sold. Plus, the threat of potential jail time – up to two years in prison for possession in Iran – is a powerful deterrent.

D2C could change the game by letting standard, unmodified mobile phones connect to satellites in low Earth orbit, without any specialised hardware like a Starlink terminal or a satellite phone.

The satellites carry onboard mobile base stations, which act as cell towers in space, and currently broadcast on mobile operators’ ordinary ground spectrum. Companies like SpaceX and AST SpaceMobile are investing billions in getting the technology off the ground, with the promise of largely eliminating internet “dead zones” in rural areas where connectivity is unavailable or places where it has been cut off by natural disasters or power cuts.

Free newsletter

A basic version is already commercially available in the US through T-Mobile, mainly for texting and some low-bandwidth apps. SpaceX plans to start launching a next-generation constellation capable of broadband-style speeds during 2027, with commercial roll-out targeted for the first half of 2028.

Mahsa Alimardani, a researcher at the Oxford Internet Institute and founder of the D2C Coalition, sees the technology as a way to make services like Starlink more available to the wider population in countries like Iran. “You had to be privileged enough to afford Starlink, and it was really confined to the major cities like Tehran. It wasn’t an egalitarian tool,” she says. D2C technology could also be harder for the government to trace, as there is no large dish to hunt down.

But there are many technical issues that could stop D2C acting as a panacea for countries like Iran. The service as it is currently provided by Starlink and T-Mobile has a low bandwidth. Speeds average around 4 megabits per second per beam, which must be shared by users within the area, meaning limited capacity except for basic use cases like SMS messaging. The antenna on a mobile phone is much smaller than a Starlink terminal, limiting its ability to receive large amounts of data.

‘Most of it is good’: Tim Berners-Lee on the state of the web now

The other primary issue is overcoming the lack of permission and cooperation from a hostile host country. The satellite has to transmit in part of the radio spectrum that mobile phones can receive. If mobile operators in the country are already using that part of the spectrum, then the terrestrial signal would be much stronger than the satellite signal – so existing cell phone towers would effectively function as jammers.

“If there’s a tower down the road, it will overpower the satellite signal that’s going from hundreds of miles up in space,” says Tim Farrar at telecoms consultancy TMF Associates. “The link is already fragile.”

That could change in the future. Starlink’s next-generation D2C service will run on new frequency bands, the AWS-4 and H-block spectrum that SpaceX agreed to buy licences for in 2025. SpaceX is predicting speeds of 150 megabits per second under ideal conditions for its next-generation D2C Starlink service, roughly 38 times faster than current speeds. As the service will run on a different spectrum, existing cell towers in densely populated areas like Tehran will be unable to act as jammers.

SpaceX says it is working with chip-makers to get the necessary modems into next-generation smartphones. The firm’s CEO Elon Musk has predicted that it will take around two years for the mobile industry to start shipping compatible modems in their phones, but it could be a long time before those phones are available to ordinary Iranians.

Worried about an AI apocalypse? Here’s how to think about the risk of doom

The final issue is international law. Under the International Telecommunication Union’s radio regulations, transmitters operating on a country’s territory need that country’s authorisation. This has led the United Nations body to side with Iran in its complaints against Starlink. Digital rights groups, such as Witness, Access Now and Article 19, have been lobbying governments, regulators and satellite providers to allow US communications companies to switch on their D2C service over Iran since January 2026.

D2C technology could be a valuable tool for millions of people living under authoritarian regimes even with current technology, but the legal and technical hurdles mean its impact on internet blackouts will be limited for the foreseeable future.

“I suspect Iranian leadership’s concern is less about what direct-to-cell can actually do at the moment and more about where it’s going and what it might come to symbolise,” says Alimardani.

A satellite operator working without a licence and independently of the state, she argues, undermines Iran’s entire model of centralised internet governance, which helps explain the authorities’ efforts to seize the relatively small number of Starlink terminals already in the country.

“That is the fundamental thing that the regime has always sought to do: control communications. Control the narrative. Control the ability to mobilise and to organise. A channel that they can’t switch off is a direct challenge to that fundamental aspect of their system,” says Alimardani.

Submarine finds world’s deepest explosive volcanic activity in Mariana trench

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Scientists exploring the Mariana trench with a remotely operated submarine rover have discovered the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic activity to date. Experts say that the nature of the activity is also unusual and ripe for further exploration.

Robert Stern, formerly at the University of Texas at Dallas, and his colleagues were collecting rock samples at the Mariana trench – the deepest valley in the world’s oceans, and home to the deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep – to understand the geology of the unique spot.

The Mariana trench began to form about 52 million years ago when one tectonic plate – the Pacific plate – slid or “subducted” under another called the Philippine Sea plate. At Challenger Deep, the trench is almost 11,000 metres below sea level.

Advertisement

‘Shazam for whales’ uses AI to track sounds heard in Mariana Trench

Focusing on an area about 6100 metres deep, in the vicinity of Challenger Deep, the team found deposits containing volcanic ash and rock – evidence of the deepest volcanic eruptions ever reported. The location was also unusual, occurring in an area where the mantle is generally not thought to be hot enough to melt. The team made the discovery using a remotely operated submersible named Jason.

While the team hasn’t yet identified exactly where the eruptions occurred, only finding evidence of volcanic activity in samples, they believe that it can’t have occurred far above the collection site on the trench wall. This is because the volcanic ash and rock in the samples had welded onto rocks at the sample site, showing it was hot when it was deposited. If the volcanic activity had occurred at a much shallower depth, the volcanic ash would have cooled by the time it reached the site 6000 metres below sea level.

Peter Kokelaar at the University of Liverpool, UK, says that the site sits closer to the meeting point of tectonic plates than would usually be expected. “It’s probably the deepest product of an active volcanic system that’s been recorded,” says Kokelaar. “It’s particularly interesting because it’s a peculiar place for active volcanism, so close to the trench.”

Free newsletter

Peter Rowley at the University of Bristol, UK, says that the site seems to show evidence that the Pacific plate is subducting deeper under the Philippine plate than expected, creating a stretching effect on the upper section of the Philippine Sea plate and thinning it out. This thinning might make it easier for mantle material to punch through the crust to trigger volcanic activity.

“Material that was originally quite deep down, stuff from the upper mantle, is actually quite accessible. So what they’re sampling is material which has some mantle origin to it. And getting to access mantle material is something we’ve been trying to do in various locations for a very long time,” says Rowley. “It’s an unusual tectonic setup.”

“So, certainly, [this is] explosive volcanic activity at greater depths than we’ve seen before,” says Rowley. “Possibly this is the deepest volcanism we’ve seen. Submarine volcanism is something we’ve got quite big knowledge gaps in. It’s that famous thing that we know less about the seafloor than we do about the moon.”

Frontiers in Earth Science DOI: 10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

The overlooked longevity nutrients that may add years to your life

New Scientist November 23, 2026

Bruce Ames was remarkable in many ways. A renowned biochemist who continued working into his nineties, he is best known for developing a low-cost screening test for cancer-causing substances. But he devoted the latter stages of his long career to an intriguing idea: that a hitherto-unrecognised class of nutrients plays a key role in promoting healthy ageing. “Many as-yet-unknown longevity vitamins and proteins likely remain to be discovered,” he wrote in one of his last papers, in 2022, just a couple of years before he passed away, aged 95.

But could such nutrients have been hiding in plain sight all along? A number of promising candidates are under investigation, including some found in mushrooms and seaweed. Proving the long-term health impacts of dietary factors in rigorous trials is a huge challenge, and the field of anti-ageing supplements has been plagued by ideas that failed to live up to their promise, but we could still be on the cusp of finding out if Ames was right. If so, what might we one day be dosing up with for the benefit of our future selves?

Rapid bursts of ageing are causing a total rethink of how we grow old

A healthy diet requires various vitamins and minerals for basic metabolic reactions in the human body – that is, to keep us alive in the immediate future. There are around 30 of these essential micronutrients, including the vitamins from A to K, and minerals such as calcium and iron. A deficiency in these can cause conditions such as scurvy, rickets and beriberi.

Advertisement

But Ames had a compelling idea that inadequate intake of micronutrients also causes insidious, long-term damage. Building on his many years of research investigating metabolism and ageing, in 2006 he proposed that when vitamins and minerals are in short supply, our bodies operate a triage system, allocating them to systems involved in immediate survival and sacrificing other functions that are more important for long-term health, such as DNA repair and maintenance of mitochondria. This could explain why moderate deficiencies in vitamin D, for instance, are associated with certain cancers and cardiovascular disease.

His subsequent studies, working with Joyce McCann at the Children’s Hospital Oakland Research Institute in California, demonstrated that when selenium and vitamin K are scarce, they are indeed preferentially allocated to the biological systems that are most important for short-term survival.

This led Ames to the idea that some dietary compounds are particularly adept at supporting long-term health, and that there may be an entire other class of unrecognised nutrients that might be capable of activating various protective pathways in our bodies. If we consume enough of them, he suggested, they can fine-tune our metabolism and help shield us from insidious, long-term damage.

In that 2022 paper, Ames produced a list of around 40 nutrients – key ingredients for thousands of chemical reactions throughout the body – which he believed to be critical for preventing chronic conditions and promoting longevity.

“I propose that many of the known vitamins and minerals have, besides a ‘survival’ function, aging-delaying (‘longevity’) functions as well. I also propose that other dietary biochemicals, not officially recognized as vitamins or as having age-delaying functions, have a positive age-delaying effect,” he wrote.

Perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that some lesser-known substances in our diet may have this impact. There are myriad biochemicals in our food, and we know surprising little about this “nutritional dark matter” or its impacts on the body. But proving the efficacy of any purported longevity nutrients – substances whose effects gradually accumulate over the long term – was always going to be difficult, not least because they would sail under the radar of standard tests for deficiencies.

Free newsletter

A recent academic book, Supplements and Drugs for Healthy Longevity, describes more than 250 chemicals that are listed in various databases as potentially being able to alter the ageing process. However, it notes that the evidence mainly comes from experiments on organisms such as yeasts, worms or other animals. “[Strong evidence] on the human species is absolutely missing,” says Suresh Rattan, a biogerontologist at Aarhus University in Denmark, who co-edited the book.

This could change, however, as the results of robust clinical trials begin to roll in, and with new research efforts under way to identify nutrients that may slow the clock.

One of these is a 2025 analysis of 777 generally healthy and active people aged over 70 who took part in the DO-HEALTH randomised controlled trial to investigate whether vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids and a simple home exercise programme could prevent disease in older age and thereby prolong healthy life expectancy. This measured the biological age of the participants after three years of the trial and found that omega-3 alone moderately slowed the rate of biological ageing, with extra benefits from the addition of vitamin D or exercise.

Although we don’t yet have data about the ultimate impact this has on healthspan – the number of years that we live in good health – the study’s authors noted that “even small changes in biological aging, if sustained, may have relevant effects on population health”.

Another large-scale clinical trial that reported results earlier this year analysed the anti-ageing effect of a daily supplement of cocoa extract (containing high concentrations of substances called flavanols, thought to assist healthy ageing) and a daily multivitamin in 958 people in the US aged over 60. This found that the cocoa extract had no impact, but the multivitamin resulted in a small but significant reduction in the rate of biological ageing, which might be linked to our micronutrient requirements increasing with age.

The negative flavanol finding is interesting, because Ames, too, thought that certain substances in food that aren’t classed as vitamins could have a positive long-term impact on our health. But rather than flavanols, the candidates he proposed were pigments called carotenoids, as well as certain antioxidants produced by bacteria and fungi. Now, initiatives to investigate some of these are under way, with researchers in Singapore at the forefront of these efforts.

It is projected that, by 2050, a third of Singapore’s population will be over 65, with spiralling rates of conditions such as cancer and dementia too. The urgency of the situation has led to large-scale investment in clinical trials exploring new ways to elongate healthspan – and among the nutrients in the crosshairs of researchers there is one highlighted by Ames called ergothioneine. Produced mainly by fungi and bacteria, the best dietary source of it is mushrooms, particularly oyster and shiitake varieties.

A number of studies from the past few years have already shown that eating mushrooms is associated with a lower risk of various chronic conditions and longer life expectancy. Humans have also evolved adaptations that allow our bodies to absorb and retain ergothioneine. A specific transporter molecule for this nutrient in our intestines and other tissues means that when we eat foods such as mushrooms, it is distributed around the body – suggesting that it is important for us. But why?

New insight into how we age suggests it may be driven by a failure to switch off the forces that build our bodies. If true, it could lead to a deeper understanding of ageing – and the possibility of slowing it

Research from three decades ago revealed that ergothioneine is a particularly powerful antioxidant, a substance that helps negate damage to cells caused by unstable molecules called free radicals, one of the underlying drivers of ageing. It is up to 30 times better at neutralising free radicals than glutathione, one of the body’s innate antioxidants.

Barry Halliwell, a biochemist recruited by the National University of Singapore to lead anti-ageing trials, suspects that an ergothioneine deficiency could be linked to numerous neurodegenerative conditions. “Age-related diseases of the brain, Parkinson’s, vascular dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, cognitive impairment, are all associated with low ergothioneine levels,” says Halliwell. And research on human brain cells and miniature lab-grown organs known as organoids suggests that consuming sufficient ergothioneine might actively protect the brain.

This evidence has convinced Halliwell that maintaining a minimal level of ergothioneine in the bloodstream may be essential for a healthy brain. “Our hypothesis is that it’s actually a vitamin and you need it,” he says. “But it’s different to, say, vitamin C, where you’ll start to have symptoms within a few months if you don’t get enough. We think that the consequences of ergothioneine deficiency take a long time to manifest.”

In an attempt to find out if that is true, he and his colleagues launched a pilot study a few years ago where people aged over 60 with mild cognitive impairment took ergothioneine supplements for a year. Because the study was interrupted by the covid-19 pandemic, they were only able to recruit 19 people, as opposed to the planned 150, but there were still signs that it improved memory and learning abilities and slowed neuron damage. “We just got funding to redo the whole trial,” says Halliwell. “We need to do a full double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial, which we are planning.”

Meanwhile, in the UK, a trial is measuring the impact of ergothioneine, as well as another antioxidant called taxifolin (found in onions and fruits such as apples), on people aged 50 to 65 as a possible way of keeping the immune system more resilient through midlife, when it starts to decline. The aim is to see whether this reduces the prevalence of so-called senescent immune cells, white blood cells that have ceased to function normally and instead contribute to chronic levels of inflammation, and hence the ageing process. The results are due soon.

From dampening inflammation to boosting mental health, the many types of dietary fibre have a surprisingly large impact throughout the body. Here's how to get your fill

But ergothioneine is just one of the possible longevity nutrients in the spotlight. Other candidates have been pinpointed through studies of the foods common in the diets of people who live well for a long time, such as fucoidan, a chemical found in the cell walls of brown seaweed.

A number of large-scale population studies have highlighted an association between consuming more seaweed and lower levels of both cognitive and physical frailty. Fucoidan, which can activate a gene called SIRT6 that promotes DNA repair, is one possible explanation.

Andrea Maier, director of the National University of Singapore’s Academy for Healthy Longevity and the mastermind behind the country’s various approaches to slowing ageing, is now leading a trial giving 2.4 grams of fucoidan per day to 60 Singaporeans aged 50 to 80 with signs of pre-frailty. The aim is to see if it can slow ageing based on inflammatory and immune signals in their blood, as well as their DNA.

In addition, the team will examine body composition, muscle and sleep quality, cognition and skin health. “In roughly four or five months, we will know if you should eat more brown seaweed,” says Maier.

Elsewhere, other researchers are working to identify overlooked compounds in food that might be important to our health. In 2024, for instance, a team led by Sastia Putri at Osaka University in Japan analysed the chemical footprint of tempeh, a food made from fermented soya beans that is reputed to protect against heart disease. This enabled the researchers to pinpoint a substance called meglutol, a cholesterol-lowering chemical found in soya beans that increases in concentration following fermentation. “It works in a similar way to statins,” says Putri.

This is an important step forward in understanding unrecognised nutrients in our food, but there is still a long way to go to discover any impacts that tempeh and meglutol might have on long-term health. And it is important to remember that there have been plenty of red herrings in relation to longevity nutrients.

For instance, Ames enthused about taurine, an amino acid thought to support the brain, muscle and heart. Studies showed that concentrations of taurine in our blood decline with age, suggesting that deficiencies might be a driver of ageing. However, a major analysis last year by a team at the US National Institute on Aging instead found huge variation in the amount of circulating taurine between adults, and no clear association between taurine levels and health status.

Researchers in Singapore faced their own setback when studying another proposed longevity nutrient called alpha-ketoglutarate, or AKG, which plays critical roles within the body in everything from energy production to kidney function. Animal studies have shown that AKG can have a potent impact on lifespan, and AKG supplements are also used by athletes to aid muscle repair and recovery. However, when Maier and her colleagues trialled a daily supplement of AKG in people aged 40 to 60 who were deemed to be ageing rapidly, based on a biological test assessing changes to their DNA, it failed to offer noticeable health improvements.

Maier suspects that AKG could make more difference in a more vulnerable population, and a new trial taking place in Singapore is examining whether it can help prevent the development of post-operative frailty in older adults after heart surgery.

These findings also raise the question of how longevity nutrients might best be utilised. Rather than standalone supplements, Putri, Rattan and many others think they are more likely to offer health benefits when present in whole foods. In light of this, Putri is now developing ways of increasing the meglutol concentration within tempeh by tweaking the fermentation process. “What I find really interesting about food is that there’s rarely just one interesting compound,” she says. “Tempeh contains many that may have useful effects, and some may work together synergistically.”

A new understanding of our relationship with our "friendly" gut microbes shows they actually have a dark side and help cause ageing. Here's how to fight back

More broadly, Rattan isn’t convinced of Ames’s ideas about longevity nutrients, pointing out how the field of ageing has long been dogged by unrealistic claims. He highlights the bursts of hyperbole surrounding the purported benefits of different supplements including NAD+, a substance produced by human cells that helps convert the energy within food into a form that our bodies can use.

Some researchers have described the steady decline of NAD+ levels in our cells through the decades as “the driving force in ageing”, giving rise to a burgeoning industry of companies selling various formulations of NAD+ or nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), its precursor molecule.

But while Rattan suggests that boosting NAD+ may be useful for people with certain conditions, he says there is little evidence that it alters the ageing process, describing the supplements as “gimmicks”. “In people with cardiological or even some eye problems, these things can be useful,” he says. “But when we take them as geroprotectors, it’s mostly hype.”

However, while Rattan still isn’t convinced that a single nutrient can slow ageing and extend life, he does expect the research efforts in Singapore to shed new light on the role that different nutritional deficiencies can play in the loss of physical or mental function with age.

Addressing these shortfalls could allow people to retain their independence for longer, and may eventually enable more of us to maintain our vitality into a ripe old age – just like Ames.
