COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus

New Scientist November 23, 2026

A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet?

The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.

Advertisement

But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.

Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.

Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”

Free newsletter

The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.

Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”

Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.

But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?

The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.

With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.

The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come

But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.

The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.

There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.

UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

Christchurch Hospital’s emergency department has the highest patient volumes in the country, with demand growing faster than the city’s population, Health New Zealand says.

The health agency is exploring options to expand after-hours and urgent care services across Greater Christchurch, identifying the eastern suburbs as an area it believes is “underserved”.

In a request for information (RFI) published on the Government Electronic Tenders Service on November 12, Health NZ acknowledged a significant proportion of the growth in ED presentations had been among patients with less urgent conditions.

“The area currently appears to be underserved for alternatives to attending ED for care,” the document reads.

Health NZ believes additional after-hours and urgent care services could meet the needs of some patients attending ED.

It is seeking suggestions from healthcare providers for services operating during periods of higher demand, particularly evenings, weekends and public holidays.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

The move comes amid ongoing pressure on Christchurch Hospital’s ED, where nearly 2000 patients spent more than 12 hours in the first six months of this year, a nearly 70% increase on the same period in 2025.

Figures released to the Herald under the Official Information Act show the number of patients spending more than six hours in ED also rose 24%, from 13,585 to 16,847.

That increase came despite overall presentations falling slightly year-on-year, from 72,092 to 71,134.

Measures introduced to manage demand included additional evening and weekend urgent care clinics at three Christchurch general practices and 750 extra urgent care telehealth vouchers.

Under the latest initiative, Health NZ wants a significant proportion of additional care to be delivered face-to-face, ruling out services that operate predominantly online.

It is also not seeking another 24-hour face-to-face service, as one is already in place.

Instead, additional services would complement existing urgent care facilities and operate as part of a wider network.

Healthcare providers are being asked to outline what services they could offer, where and when they would operate, which communities they would serve and how they would recruit the necessary workforce.

Health NZ is also seeking suggestions on potential funding models.

“At this stage we are not requesting detailed costed proposals which would be part of procurement to follow this RFI, but we are interested in a high-level funding model to meet workforce requirements.”

A question-and-answer session for potential providers is scheduled for November 27, with responses due by December 11.

Marlborough wilding conifer teams race to spray 650ha before El Niño

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

Wilding conifer control volunteers in the Awatere Wilding Conifer Management Unit at Pudding Hill last week.

Wilding conifer control teams are racing to spray hundreds of hectares of invasive pines in Marlborough before windy El Niño conditions kick in.

The $1.6 million project to aerially spray 650 hectares in the Molesworth and Branch-Leatham areas was funded in May’s Budget by central government as part of a wider $109m package targeting New Zealand’s two million-hectare infestation.

Boffa Miskell biosecurity project manager Marcus Girvan, project director for the Molesworth and Branch-Leatham work, told Local Democracy Reporting on Monday that aerial boom spraying started on November 20 in calm conditions.

El Niño’s hot, dry and windy weather could arrive within weeks, which could cause aerial spraying to pause as the chemical spray would evaporate, Girvan said.

Girvan said he hoped to get at least half of the planned spraying done before El Niño conditions kicked in.

The project was due to end in February 2027.

El Niño’s impact on ground conifer control work was also “top of mind”, Girvan said.

Ground crews could face higher fire risk and potential limits on spark-generating equipment such as chainsaws, he said.

The crew of at least 20 would try to adapt by working earlier in the morning when humidity was higher, but “if it gets too hot and too dry, then [we’ll] need to stop work”, he said.

Any missed work would continue in autumn, he said.

While any season with higher temperatures and wind could accelerate conifer spread, Girvan said whether El Niño supercharged that growth would not be known for two to three years, when the first saplings would begin to appear.

Southern Marlborough Restoration Trust chairman John Oswald told LDR he was confident wind would not prevent them completing their full programme.

“The wind is a problem for us every year, but we’ll get the programme done; we always do,” he said.

Asked whether stronger winds could see more conifer seeds spreading further, Oswald said a “seed rain event”, where winds could carry seeds for up to 30km, required “perfect conditions”.

“The soil moisture has to be right, the germination cycle has to be right, the humidity has to be right, and the updrafts, which are caused by high winds, will all have to coincide,” Oswald said.

Those conditions did not happen often, “maybe once every five years”, and no one could predict whether El Niño would trigger one, he said.

At a November 12 council meeting, the council’s senior biosecurity projects officer Rob Simons welcomed the Government’s cash injection after three years of underfunding.

The Molesworth control unit received $5.7m in funding for the 2026-27 financial year, with $1m towards the control unit in the Branch-Leatham area north of Molesworth.

Simons said the bolstered budget would help the project team claw back neglected areas.

Consistent funding would be vital going forward or the trees would reclaim the land, “essentially losing the investments that you’ve made”, Simons said.

- LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

Vehicle importer wound back odometers by almost 50 million kms

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

The imported trucks had rolled-back odometers and forged documents. Photo / New Zealand Customs Service

By Milly Matthews, student journalist

An Auckland vehicle importer has been jailed for nearly two-and-a-half years for winding back odometers by almost 50 million kilometres.

The man was also ordered to pay $27,000 in reparation, while his company was ordered to pay a further $315,000.

A Customs investigation – in collaboration with the NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi – looked at 174 used vehicles imported from Japan and found the importer had been intentionally winding back odometers between August 2020 and January 2024 to make the vehicles appear more valuable.

In total, 48,674,800km in mileage was wiped from odometers.

Individual vehicles had between 60,000km and 840,000km wound back, and Customs estimated the profit was close to $5.6 million.

Customs acting investigations manager Nigel Barnes said the man’s actions were not an error.

“This was deliberate and calculated fraud. The man wound back odometers and forged export certificates to conceal the vehicles’ true histories and inflate their value.

“Accurate mileage helps people assess a vehicle’s value, safety, and maintenance needs. The deception denied buyers the information they needed to make informed decisions.”

Some forged certificates contained false information about their year of manufacture or carrying capacity.

NZTA head of vehicle regulation Geoff Williamson said all affected vehicle owners had been contacted, and those in use were “recalled, corrected and, when required, recertified”.

Classic Builders founders Peter Cooney and Matt Lagerberg mark 30 years in business

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

Classic Builders co-founders Peter Cooney and Matt Lagerberg are marking 30 years in business.

Classic Builders has come a long way since its co-founders ran the business out of a car boot in Tauranga 30 years ago.

The residential builder – now one of New Zealand’s leading construction companies with more than 9000 homes built nationwide – celebrates the milestone birthday today.

Co-founder and Classic Group director Peter Cooney told the Bay of Plenty Times he has to “pinch” himself when he reflects on the company’s journey.

In 1996, he founded the company with Matt Lagerberg and they delivered its first Tauranga home.

Cooney paired his property development experience with Lagerberg’s building expertise after noticing a market gap for good-quality affordable housing.

“I wasn’t a builder, but I knew about selling and marketing,” Cooney said.

“That’s where Matt came in. He had the construction expertise … It was a good combination.”

Lagerberg, now Classic Group managing director, described their partnership as “yin and yang”.

“We each had different strengths, and I think that’s why we’ve worked together for so long. We know our lanes, and we respect what the other brings to the business.”

Classic Builders has built more than 9000 homes nationwide since its inception, from affordable entry-level builds to high-end custom homes.

Bay of Plenty projects have included Ōmokoroa’s Kamai Views, Pyes Pa’s Kennedy Ridge, and Pāpāmoa’s East Quarter. The business recently opened a new office on Cameron Rd.

Classic Group was named New Zealand’s third busiest builder in the annual Hubexo Construction League report, published in April.

The only build-to-sell residential builder in the top 10, Classic started $569.7 million in projects last year, with an average project value of $28.4m.

Cooney said managing a company of such scale through construction downturns had been “one hell of a challenge”.

A disciplined approach grew the team from two to 300 employees, while the Classic brand expanded to include several other diversified businesses.

Also under the Classic Group banner are Classic Developments, Classic Life, Classic Capital, Classic Technology, Classic Collectives, and CBC Construction.

Classic Group has a $300 million partnership with the New Zealand Super Fund, the Kaha Ake initiative, and one of its many projects is Riverside Tauriko – a housing development with 3000 homes, schooling, local and neighbourhood commercial centres and community facilities in Tauriko West.

“It’s quite a feat to get from where we started, out of the boot of a car,” Cooney said.

He said becoming a leading building company was never the goal.

“We took the attitude that the low end of the market deserves to be as well built as the high end.”

He said many major construction companies had failed over the last 30 years.

“It’s a challenge to stay at the top of your game in this industry – it’s quite an achievement. You sort of have to look back and pinch yourself.”

Cooney said financial discipline was critical as cash flow could dry up overnight if the market turned.

“We are constantly monitoring the cash flows. There is so much at stake and so much can go wrong. You need to be sure that you’ve got plenty of contingency tucked away.”

Cooney said one of the “biggest turning points” was developing land.

“We realised that if we could develop land ourselves, rather than relying entirely on other developers, we could control more of our own future.”

Lagerberg said they had the right systems and processes.

“When you’re building one house, there are so many suppliers, subcontractors and different stages involved. When you’re building hundreds, you need to be incredibly organised.

“We’ve spent years developing and improving our systems, and that has allowed us to grow while maintaining consistency.”

Cooney said the construction industry was “very volatile” and the last three years had been the “toughest years we’ve ever been in”.

He said the Global Financial Crisis was a “real eye-opener” and showed how quickly the market could change.

“That period taught us a lot about financial discipline and being able to adapt quickly. You can’t assume the good times will last forever.”

Lagerberg said they had a responsibility to their people – some of whom had been with the business for more than 20 years.

“Some have retired, others have moved on to different opportunities, but they’ve all played a part in building Classic into what it is today.

“Without those people, we wouldn’t be where we are.”

Cooney said he loved seeing people get ahead.

“Seeing someone start on the tools and progress into a construction management or regional management role is fantastic.

“Neither Matt nor I started with much. We worked incredibly hard to get where we are, so I get a lot of satisfaction from seeing other people succeed.”

Looking forward, Lagerberg said the business would continue evolving.

“If we want the Classic brand to stand the test of time, we need to keep adapting.

“We’re looking at different opportunities and ways the business might develop, but the fundamental goal remains the same.”

Cooney said customers would remain the most important part of the business.

“People come to us because they want a home that meets their needs. Our job is to deliver that outcome.”

Bijou Johnson is a journalist based in the Bay of Plenty. She grew up in Tauranga and joined NZME in 2025 after studying communications at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

Hinemihi carvings that survived Tarawera eruption could be displayed at Rotorua Museum after UK return

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

Original carvings from historic meeting house Hinemihi o te Ao Tawhito are planned for display at the Rotorua Museum after their return to Aotearoa from England.

Hinemihi o te Ao Tawhito is a traditional Māori meeting house (wharenui) that sheltered survivors of the 1886 Mount Tarawera eruption, near Rotorua.

It was made in 1880 at Te Wairoa by revered carver Tene Waitere for Tūhourangi chief Āporo Wharekāniwha.

After the Tarawera eruption, the wharenui was left abandoned, with its walls buried and roof layered with debris.

William Hillier Onslow, the Governor-General from 1889 to 1892, bought Hinemihi for £50 as a memento of his time in New Zealand.

He effectively saved the ailing wharenui but also removed it from its homeland.

The structure was moved to England in 1892.

The meeting house has been at Clandon Park in Surrey. It has been used as a garden shed and children’s playhouse.

Local Māori have been working to return Hinemihi to New Zealand.

A statement this month from the British Council, the UK’s international organisation for cultural relations, said proposals were underway for the whakairo (carvings) of Hinemihi to return home to Aotearoa while new, original whakairo would be placed in a new working whare at Clandon.

A charitable trust – Ngā Kohinga Whakairo o Hinemihi – was established in 2019 to work on behalf of iwi, hapū and uri (descendants) for the return of the Hinemihi carvings.

Group chairman Rangitihi Pene, who has led four delegations to London since 2019, told the Rotorua Daily Post statutory permissions were needed before the exchange could happen.

The first was Guildford Borough Council granting resource consent to allow carvings to be permanently taken off the wharenui structure.

“If that’s successful, and all indications are it’ll be successful, then it goes to the Arts Council England to approve an export licence that’s due to take place in July 2027,” Pene said.

An official order would then need to be issued by the Charity Commission, he said.

The exchange would hopefully take place in March 2028, with the new whare opening in Clandon later that year, Pene said.

He said six carvers were working on about 29 new carvings for the “one for one” exchange.

Another group was working on 33 tukutuku (ornamental lattice-work) panels for the new whare, he said.

Pene said Hinemihi “saved the lives of our ancestors and here we are because of that”.

The plan was to place the original carvings in Rotorua Museum, due to reopen in 2028, he said.

Rotorua Museum and Heritage community experience manager Stewart Brown said the carvings’ return presented a special opportunity and it was excited about the possibility of the museum temporarily displaying and caring for them.

Discussions were still at an early stage and more work was needed before any decisions were made or arrangements confirmed, Brown said.

“We look forward to continuing those conversations and will share more when we are able.”

A delegation from the UK’s National Trust (a conservation charity) and Te Maru o Hinemihi (a UK-based community interest group) spent five days in Rotorua last week to share progress of the Hinemihi cultural exchange project.

Pene, also the Hinemihi Marae chairman, said the delegation visited the marae on Saturday.

“I believe that because of the make-up of this delegation, it’s the best possible sign we could have. It indicates that ... our journey is coming to an end.”

Kent Rawlinson, the National Trust creative and cultural director for Clandon Park, said the delegation was welcomed on to Hinemihi Marae and spoke about the exchange process.

“We have spent so much time back in the UK telling Hinemihi’s story and through that, she’s been helping us persuade everybody that she should return home.”

Speaking about it in Rotorua with whānau was a “magical, touching and empowering experience”, Rawlinson said.

The delegation also visited Hinemihi’s original site.

“We’ve seen so many pictures and heard her story so many times, but standing on that spot really connecting with that sort of whenua [land] was massively emotional for us.”

They visited the studio where new whakairo were being carved.

Progress was previously shared via Zoom. Meeting with the carvers who talked about their whakapapa links to Hinemihi and seeing the carvings in person was “breathtaking”.

National Trust London and Southeast region assistant director Natasha Woollard said a delegation had been going to the UK for a few years, “so this was a really important moment for us to make the journey and to meet our partners on their land”.

They discussed what they hoped to achieve in the next two years, she said.

Woollard saw progress on the tukutuku panels that would be enjoyed by future generations in the new whare.

She said “that was a really wonderful moment – the symbolism, the ancestry, the cultural significance of the designs”.

Woollard thanked the community for providing a rich and meaningful itinerary in Rotorua.

National Trust cultural heritage curator Rachael Chambers said the trust was grateful for the support of Heritage New Zealand and the British Council New Zealand and the Pacific.

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Terminal cancer: Whanganui family fundraises for devoted mum’s final wishes

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

Hinerua Wiari surrounded by her whānau at Hiruhārama Marae, Jerusalem, where she grew up. Photo / Holly Huriana Photography

A Whanganui family touched by terminal cancer is seeking donations “no matter how big or small” to bring their loved one’s final wishes to life.

Jerusalem’s Hinerua Wiari, 42, a single mother of five, was diagnosed with terminal pancreatic cancer about three months ago.

Determined to spend her remaining time creating memories with her children, Wiari, currently living in Palmerston North, handwrote a list of things she has always wanted to see and do.

Her whānau are fundraising to make that list a reality.

Wiari’s niece Shazjanaya “Shazae” Rata said it was “heartbreaking” when they learned about her diagnosis, particularly for her children.

“It’s just been hard on all of us watching someone we love go through something like this, especially at a young age,” Rata said.

Her aunt rarely asked for help and was often the person giving, she said.

“She was always there [for us], even with five kids of her own or barely nothing, she would always find a way to be there.”

The fundraiser was a way to do the same for her, Rata said.

“Just giving back to someone we love because she’d do the same for any of us.

“That’s just the kind of woman she is and it’s something our whānau will always love her for.”

Wiari’s niece and goddaughter Keela Rae Wiari said her auntie treated her like a daughter.

“That’s something I will always cherish and be grateful for,” Keela Rae said.

“She means so much to our family.”

Her aunt was a devoted mother with a “beautiful sense of humour”, she said.

“She’s one of those people who can walk into a room and make everybody laugh.”

Much of the list was things their family had planned to do for years.

“But now time’s short.”

It was now about creating something to “hold on to”.

“To create all of these memories and opportunities for her to experience while she is still with us, and for her children to experience them with her.”

Hinerua Wiari grew up along the Awa, spending her first nearly 18 years in Jerusalem.

She said her early life was difficult, navigating family upheaval after her father’s sudden death when she was 2 and untreated trauma symptoms.

“I had a pretty rough life in that sense.

“When I lost my dad, it was a traumatic time.”

She later struggled with mental health through her teens and substance abuse.

“And then I ended up with kids, and I had to start slowly waking up and getting my life back together.”

Throughout everything, her children had been her rock and motivation, she said.

“I didn’t want them to grow up the way that I grew up.

“And I’ve been wanting to change, break the cycle for all our rangatahi, especially my kids.”

Two years ago, on her 40th birthday, she did a charity boxing fight for suicide awareness.

“I wasn’t ... Muhammad Ali but I got in the ring.”

She said she felt like she had just started getting her life together.

“Then I get cancer. Cancer is the most ugliest thing that I’ve ever had to deal with, and I’ve dealt with some crappy things in my life.”

Her advice to others was to go to every check-up and “keep an eye on your body”.

“I would not wish this upon anybody in the world.”

When she learned her family wanted to make her list real, the love and support she felt, including from outside her family, had been “overwhelming”.

She said she struggled to put into words how grateful she was for her whānau.

“I’m always crying every day.

“If I didn’t have whānau holding me up and keeping me strong, I probably would’ve given up ages ago.

“I didn’t think I was that special.”

The item on her list she wanted most was a car that could fit all her children so they could go places on days when she had more energy.

“To be honest ... I don’t really care what I do.

“I just want to be able to make all the memories I can.”

Donations can be made by bank transfer to M Corby, account number 060793-0313735-27.

Erin Smith is a multimedia journalist based in Whanganui.

David Seymour gives new detail on Wellington College pupils caught wagging at cricket, claims classes weren’t missed

Act leader David Seymour has corrected the record for a second time after he claimed Wellington College students spotted at a cricket game were wagging and jeopardising their futures – after learning the boys involved weren’t missing any lessons.

On Monday the trio were caught on camera during school hours watching the final day of the Black Caps-India test match, held opposite their school at Basin Reserve.

The boys ducked down and tried unsuccessfully to hide their faces, but were easily identifiable on the live feed, earning school rubbish duty as a punishment.

Seymour – who has made school attendance a key plank of his role as Associate Education Minister – previously claimed the boys had been put on rubbish duty as punishment for wagging, warning rubbish collection might be the only career open to them in future if they didn’t get qualifications.

He then had to apologise to rubbish collectors after learning several qualifications were needed for that job, including a class 4 licence.

“So the situation for these boys may be worse than I first thought, that may not be an option open to them,” Seymour said.

But he told Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge TODAY one of the schoolboys, “Paddy”, had since set him straight via email, pointing out they weren’t wagging – they just weren’t meant to leave school grounds.

However, that didn’t explain why they were put on rubbish duty, Seymour said.

“It turns out they weren’t supposed to leave the school but he wasn’t missing any learning, so the plot thickens.”

He even had praise for the trio – agreeing with his fellow panellist, Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, that their uniforms looked very smart.

Seymour said, in the past three years, 175,000 more students had been regularly attending school, which “for the future of our country [is] one of the most important numbers we can have”.

New Christchurch fine dining restaurant Odelia: Sam and Emily Heaven bring a touch of Europe to the Garden City

New Zealand Herald November 24, 2026

Chef Emily Heaven in the cellar at Restaurant Odelia, which offers a unique fine dining experience to the growing Christchurch food scene. Photo / Anna Heath

There is nothing like Restaurant Odelia. A unique nine-table experience is about to flavour-bomb the Christchurch hospitality scene, offering a new direction in fine dining through excited new faces in exciting new spaces. Mike Thorpe reports.

From the moment diners walk through the Heavens’ front door (no need to knock), they are in the company of Sam and Emily. Heaven is their surname, as well as their standard for hosting diners.

The front door is next to the kitchen – and the kitchen is open plan.

“It’s so important for us to see them and them to see us, and to show that we’re here to cook for you - as a labour of love,” Sam says.

The husband-and-wife team are young – but they have already banked a wealth of experience at some of the best restaurants on the planet.

Sam served his apprenticeship in Auckland under Peter Gordon (at the Sugar Club) before joining Clare Smyth’s Oncore (three-hatted fine dining) in Sydney. After heading to the UK, he found his way to Heston Blumenthal’s world-renowned The Fat Duck (three Michelin stars).

“I would say that was my refining moment. They took what I learned at Oncore, and the level of push and drive and perfection I was looking for, and they just refined me into what I am now,” Sam says.

He describes his time at The Fat Duck as “eye-opening” and “a privilege”.

Emily, originally from Cape Town, South Africa, worked in the United States before coming to New Zealand and starting at The Grove (Auckland).

In the UK, she was head pastry chef at a “one-star” establishment in London before linking up with Sam (who was head chef) at Interlude, West Sussex. Emily was head pastry chef.

They were there for 18 months and proudly retained the restaurant’s Michelin star before returning to New Zealand with a dream of opening Odelia in the upmarket Christchurch suburb of Merivale.

Stars are a theme at the quirkily shaped restaurant. Not only are they visible through parts of the dining room ceiling, but they also aligned when the Heavens were searching the country for their perfect location. Gaining a Michelin star of their own is the plan, meaning they’d need to be in one of the four places that Michelin visits: Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch or Queenstown.

“We just couldn’t really afford Queenstown. Auckland, we’ve both worked there. When we came to Christchurch, we just really felt the vibe. We fell in love with the city,” Emily says.

“It just felt like something in the atmosphere, like it just had a bit of a buzz and then obviously when we saw this building we were like, ‘What?’ It was meant to be.

“Christchurch is the place, this building is the place.”

The pair met when they worked together at the opening of the Hyatt in Auckland and have been married for three years.

Odelia is an ode to everything the Heavens have picked up along the way, from their obvious culinary skills to their obsession with restoring antique kitchen apparatuses. They’re not just there for aesthetic value, either.

“We will bring out all the antiques that we have collected to make it a little bit more interactive. It’s like a chef’s table experience without having to sit at a chef’s table. So you get the best of both worlds,” Sam says.

Of course, you don’t have to immerse yourself in the full Odelia experience; the tables for two can be just that.

“If you want to be left alone, we can do that,” Sam adds.

Everything is deliberate at Odelia. Everything has a reason and a story. And you’re invited to see and experience all of it. The only thing kept in the dark here are the mushrooms. They’re being carefully cultivated inside the cellar – which you’re invited into, naturally.

In fact, the cellar hosts one of the courses. And, of course, it was a major selling point for the hosts.

“We walked inside the room and our jaws were just on the floor. It was everything we could have dreamed for and we just knew the cheese table in there would be phenomenal,” Emily says.

The beating heart of Odelia is the kitchen; small but perfectly formed, bringing husband and wife face to face as they meticulously craft each dish in a 10-course tasting menu.

In fairness, “tasting” doesn’t begin to do justice to this sensory journey. It is a carefully created and cleverly curated marriage of flavours, textures and cultures that reveals itself to your palate in layers. Course after course.

“Our style of dining is very European. Obviously we’ve been working for some amazing chefs all around the world, London, Sydney, Bray [The Fat Duck]. It’s our chance to bring that kind of dining to New Zealand, which is something a little bit different to what we have here at the moment,” Sam says.

“Some of them [the courses] are smaller, just one bite, one punchy bite of just absolute flavour. And then some of them will be larger plates. We don’t want people to get too full too fast, and then we don’t want people to leave hungry. That’s really important to us.”

The dining room itself is unique. A semi-conservatory-style extension of the main building, it’s positioned to welcome Christchurch’s vast spectrum of sunsets.

Regardless of the forecast, the Heavens will open on December 2, but not before a soft opening for their family and friends. Then, Sam and Emily will cook for the people who have helped inspire them – and in turn, Odelia.

“It’s just us, in a restaurant,” Sam says.

Restaurant Odelia can be found at 108 Papanui Rd, Merivale.

The extended tasting menu is $255 per person, and the standard tasting menu is $185 per person - available for both lunch and dinner.

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Footnotes, villains and a redacted donkey: Is this book about to save literature?

Sydney Morning Herald November 25, 2026

If there’s one place you should be safe from audience participation, it’s when reading a book. Not any more. Early on in Jasper Fforde’s Dark Reading Matter the author makes a request of his readers – no matter where you are, or what you are doing, if you see text appear in a certain font, could you please read it aloud.

The first time I see this I’m at home, and despite being the sort of person who strategically positions herself in comedy shows for minimal interaction, or who got through school choir by half-heartedly miming, I find myself gingerly speaking the words aloud: “Oh my goodness, they’ve trodden on the gibbon.”

Dark Reading Matter is the eighth and final book in the Thursday Next series. It started in 2001 with Fforde’s debut novel, The Eyre Affair, and tracks the titular Thursday Next, a detective, as she fights battles of varying surreality against corporations, corruption and, on occasion, Enid Blyton characters.

“I think that the real jumping-off point for this book was that I dedicated it to readers,” says Fforde. “If you’ve been reading my series for the last 25 years, this is for us … and we’re going to have some fun.”

The series has always been meta – the main character lives in an alternate version of our world, and within her world she discovers that books aren’t simply objects containing words; they’re the output of the BookWorld, where all the characters are real and performing books kind of like a play.

Beyond that they have their own society and lives and, yes, a police force, which is there to stop things going off the rails. In the final novel, however, Fforde takes the opportunity to shake off all shackles and see what truly is possible with the written word. Our world is suddenly a new layer on top of things, we the reader have a role to play – thus the speaking aloud – and Fforde himself turns up in the book – well, sort of. “He’s awful!” says Fforde with a laugh. “I mean, he’s a terrible human being.”

The techniques Fforde uses in all his books push at the boundaries of what we expect. His novels throw you in the deep end, with their seemingly chaotic blend of wordplay, adventure and hard truths – but it’s at 3am, when you realise you haven’t been able to put the book down, that you realise how intricately put together it all is. There’s a reason for the seemingly random illustration at the front. That isn’t just any donkey on the cover. And the gibbon is important.

Under all the fun and the wordplay his books all take on deeper themes; they’re about free will, they fight against unchecked authority and they advocate for what is fair and right. Here is no different – what on the surface may seem like silliness is actually a battle cry. Dark Reading Matter is first and foremost a joy to read and a love letter to the readers who have come on this decades-long journey with Fforde and his fictional detective Thursday Next – but at its core it’s a fight for the future of literature.

Dark Reading Matter comes at an existential moment for literature; at a time when physical stories are being literally cut up and fed into machines to teach AI how to write.

The key antagonist of the story, Roger Thatt, is trying to gain access to the “dark reading matter” – not the BookWorld but all the bits from around the edge. It’s the place where all ideas and potential ideas go; memories, thoughts, discarded drafts. Thatt wants to harvest it all, to monetise it, to control inspiration.

This novel manages to explore the threat of AI without being preachy or dull – a miraculous achievement in a saturated conversation – and manages to do it through both plot and structure.

“I was out to write a book that AI could not scrape. It could not scrape this. It could not understand it,” he says. It’s true – what would artificial intelligence make of conversations that happen purely in the footnotes, which in the book are used as a communication system? How would it navigate the narrative impact of font changes? Or, stepping back, would the character names – including Landen Parke-Laine, Acheron Hades and Jack Schitt – and the entire blend of pop culture, history and puns that go into creating them even be a possibility? “It can’t think up new stuff. It can only take old stuff and repackage it,” he says.

Before he was an author, Fforde was in the film industry, working as a focus puller. He started at age 19, and across a 20-year career worked on films including GoldenEye, Entrapment and The Mask of Zorro, but it was a volatile industry. “The jobs could dry up literally any moment.”

He started writing short stories at the age of 27, and across the next 12 years “I had five books written and [none published]. No one interested at all.” He found a strange freedom in the rejection, however, and started writing The Eyre Affair.

“I thought, well, it doesn’t matter what I write because I’m not going to be published. So I’m just writing for fun.” The manuscript was “fun and silly, and it just mixes everything together – literary theory and vampires and werewolves and everything else”. The resulting book deal was enough that Fforde could stop work. His final project was an ad featuring Leonardo DiCaprio – “and the following week I was an author”. The Eyre Affair was an instant hit and became a New York Times bestseller.

Though Fforde is still a keen photographer and still working in the creative industries, there is both a wistfulness and an edge of concern when he talks about the film industry. “I miss it a lot,” he says. The threat of AI is looming, though. “If I was in the film industry now, I would be thinking it’s all over for us,” he reflects. “If I was an actor or a filmmaker I would be terrified.” He pauses. “Or, alternatively, I would be thinking I need to start a theatre troupe. You know – this could be the greatest resurgence of theatre that the world may ever see.”

Fforde has been pushing boundaries, subverting expectations and challenging himself with every book he writes. The Constant Rabbit is a novel that takes on nationalism and Brexit specifically while also being about anthropomorphised rabbits. His first standalone novel Early Riser imagines a world where the human race hibernates for months each year. The Shades of Grey novels take on discrimination and class through a society that ranks people based on what colours they can perceive.

There is another, quieter thread that laces through the latter half of Dark Reading Matter, in a non-fiction detour where a version of Fforde himself is the protagonist. He reflects on articles he’s read, on his writing, and in one section recalls drives with his mother “during her latter years when the Alzheimer’s became momentarily not the debilitation that it was, but a gift that could keep on giving: I could take her on these drives each week and every time she would enjoy it as though the first”, he writes.

“All of us will be involved with dementia … either personally or someone close to us, and it was a very big part of my life,” Fforde says.

When he takes us further into the dark reading matter of the novel, we’re taken to a place populated by memories, with one character meeting their younger self, the balance of recollection uneven between them. “The concept that there is a place where every human experience has ended up, all our memories, all our moments that we feel have gone are all still there – I think that’s a way, way bigger idea than I could even write about … There’s a nod to a theory about black holes, that because information can’t be destroyed, information cannot vanish forever,” he reflects.

“I don’t know whether I put it in there but all the stories that my mum told me, about things that she’d done in the past, I retold back to her when we had our afternoons together, driving up on the Elan. She couldn’t remember them, of course, and they’d gone … we’d actually swapped memories, that I now had her memories in a weird way.”

He points to a prescient idea from Kurt Vonnegut’s The Sirens of Titan, about shared human knowledge that could be taken as a precursor to the internet, or the pool of knowledge drawn upon by AI. “I’ll paraphrase,” says Fforde. “There is a cloud of collective consciousness that floats over all of us – you draw from the cloud and you put into the cloud, and authors, I felt, taking this idea further, you promote your world-view, which you hope – you think – is positive … In our small way, as authors and as painters and as singer-songwriters, we’re trying to push that cloud into a direction that makes sense for a more pluralist and fair, free society. Away from the right-wingers, the billionaire tech oligarchs, into a place where we all mutually support one another.”

On Dark Reading Matter: “What does this do for literature? I’m not sure it does anything. I think it’s trying to just make people feel that there is a better place that we could be … I think there’s a way in which we can just try and shift things a little bit for the better.” He pauses, then, unable to let the comment go without some self-deprecation, adds: “But it does make me sound a little grand and pompous.”

The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

We did a blind taste test of 22 Christmas hams. Here’s the best to buy in 2026

Sydney Morning Herald November 25, 2026

For the first time, Good Food’s annual ham tasting has a tie for the top spot between a triple-smoked and an all-rounder. Plus the fanciest ham, the best value buy and a crowd-pleaser.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

No gift articles left

The festive season has arrived, and it brings ham. Brined, smoked and ready to battle it out in a high-stakes taste test spanning supermarkets to small-batch independent smokehouses.

This is the fourth and largest-ever blind taste test Good Food has conducted, featuring 22 bone-in leg hams sourced from across Victoria and NSW, sliced and served before a judging panel of 10 restaurant critics, chefs and butchers at Surry Hills restaurant Bessie’s.

On their mission to uncover Australia’s best Christmas ham, judges used a 20-point scoring system to assess the flavour (12 points), texture (four points), appearance (two points) and scent (two points) of each entrant, without ever knowing where it came from.

Two minutes of silent scoring time are allotted to each ham, with a further two minutes for discussion, but the process ultimately takes more than two hours. It produces sodium-induced headaches. It makes you realise how much a single slice of ham can differ between producers – there are slimy hams, so wet you could almost wring them out like a sponge; delicate hams, dancing between smoky and sweet; and hams so salty the panel likened them to potato chips. The latter was Coles’ triple-smoked leg ham, for the record.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

1:39

Good Food's Christmas ham taste test 2026

Featuring 22 hams, 10 judges and five winning categories.

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox.

What makes a good ham, you ask? Butcher-chef Darren O’Rourke, who spent more than a decade as head butcher for Victor Churchill, advises us to look for hams with an even pink colour, no cracks in the skin, and a texture that’s neither wet nor dry – just a little moist, with a bit of bite to it.

Our findings revealed two further key factors to consider when buying a Christmas ham in 2026: the first, is that experience delivers. The hams that performed best typically came from places where pigs have been brined and smoked every year for decades. The second, is that price isn’t a necessary determinant of quality. While happy pigs are consistently tasty pigs, free-range ethical farming can be found at various price-points.

And, as always, the triple-smoked ham is always a safe bet.

With a list so grand, we won’t present notes on every entrant this year. Rather, you’ll find our Top 10, ranked in ascending order, with a few new categories to spotlight those that scored highly in a particular area – the butchers’ favourite, or the best value option, for example. The full list of hams judged will be provided at the end, in alphabetical order.

But before we kick off, let us tell you about one ham our judges collectively passed on.

THE PASS

$10.99 per kilogram

Ah, how the mighty have fallen. In 2024, this affordable little number took home gold. This year, it received the lowest score of any supermarket ham.

It had the wet sheen of a forgotten slice of deli ham at the supermarket, and a flavour that failed to carry through its nice-enough aroma. And what was that flavour, anyway?

“Does it taste like fish?” asked Good Food’s head of food Sarah Norris. “Maybe like a smoked trout?”

Yucky.

$45.86 per kilogram

The winner of the 2025 Christmas ham taste test hustled to prepare this certified organic Wessex saddleback leg ham in time for tasting. Within just six days, the ham (already procured from its pasture at Le Bon Terroir D’Emj in Tenterfield) was cured and shipped to be carved up at Bessie’s — so take its drop in rank with a generous grain of salt, as a few days’ rest might’ve done it well.

Some found the texture a little wet, some a little dry, but it was just right for LP’s Quality Meats chef-founder Luke Powell. “This was my favourite so far,” he said.

“It was a bit sweet, not too salty, and the smoke was there but not overpowering. It just felt very balanced.”

$8 per kilogram

A mild-mannered ham, destined for a life among cheese slices and Tip Top bread.

“That’s a straight-up, inoffensive, streamlined ham,” said The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide co-editor David Matthews.

Even so, it left an impression. Though it was the first cab off the rank, Olympus Dining Redfern head chef Özge Kalvo was still thinking about its light flavour, with notes of apple, seven hams later: “I thought it was the best,” she said.

$15.50 per kilogram

She’s salty, she’s smoky, and she’s back with divisive intensity.

“This is quite a spectacular-looking ham,” said The Age Good Food Guide co-editor Frank Sweet.

Each year, Woolies’ triple-smoked leg ham beguiles our judges with its lush, meaty texture and heady scent of karri wood.

“This is a Christmas Day ham, a one-day-of-the-year ham,” said Good Food’s national food editor Erina Starkey. “But even the next day, it might be too much.”

The salt content feels higher this year, and harsher. “I ate one slice, but I don’t think I could eat three,” said Kalvo. Head of Good Food Sarah Norris agreed: “I don’t think I could eat piles of it.”

$56.67 per kilogram

Judges questioned how a ham could achieve such ferocity of flavour without artificial intervention. Could it be liquid smoke? MSG? Not quite. This Victorian-bred free-range ham is brined for 48 hours, then smoked over German beech wood until its flesh, still remarkably moist, smoulders with bushfire intensity.

Chef-restaurateur Nathan Sasi called it: “That reminded me of very traditional, [Central] European smoked meats,” he said. “Smoky in a way that’s a little bit overpowering … but I liked it.”

It also read premium to Matthews: “The fat tasted so clean and sweet, it was probably the best piece of fat I’ve had.”

THE CROWD PLEASER

$16.99 per kilogram

Exhausted by the mere thought of planning Christmas lunch? Buy this ham and call it a day. With the smallest spread of scores across all 10 judges and 22 hams, it’s the safest bet to satisfy those “foodie” relatives (as well as their fussy children).

“It didn’t blow my head off, but there was something about it, something on there, that stood out,” said butcher Darren O’Rourke. “Maybe cloves?”

It’s a traditional European recipe, passed down through the four generations of Deignan family butchers at the Black Forest Smokehouse in Marrickville. Their hams are pleasantly salty, blushed pink, with a subtle edge of ironbark smoke.

THE FANCIEST HAM

$24-$30 per kilogram

They say happy pigs are tasty pigs, and Otway Pork controls that process from paddock to plate. Each pig is ethically raised on sustainable Victorian pastures, spanning Geelong to the South Australian border, where they’re free to wander and wallow without any added hormones or growth promotants.

You can tell the difference: “The best thing about it was the texture,” said Ca Com (Richmond) chef Kimberly Tang, recently named Young Chef of the Year by The Age Good Food Guide. Each slice was firm, moist and rippled with silky rivulets of fat.

“It also had a nice festive flavour,” said Starkey. “You could tell they used some nice wood chips to give it a lovely flavour that felt Christmassy, but without being overpowering.”

Otway naturally smokes their hams over mountain ash woodchips, creating a refined flavour that led the company to win the gold medal for traditional leg ham and ham on the bone at the Australian Charcuterie Awards this year.

It’s not the only award-winner on this list, but it is the only one managing every step of the process.

$15.99 per kilogram

“A powerful ham,” said Sweet. “Rich, bitey, salty … and a good colour, I like that a lot.”

You might not have heard of Blue Ribbon before. Honestly, neither had we. It’s a small neighbourhood butcher in Leumeah, near Campbelltown, that quietly took home gold for its traditional leg ham at the Australian Meat Industry Council awards in May.

You can smell the smoke in each slice, but it’s stronger on the nose than the palate, noted Kalvo: “It had a rounded taste, with creamy fat,” she said.

“It ticks all of the boxes well: the smoke, the salt, the texture, the richness of flavour,” said Starkey. “It was such a lovely eating experience.”

$37.50 per kilogram

This is a ham for those who want a bit of depth and complexity. The people who swirl their glass of red wine a little too enthusiastically, perhaps. It has a flavour the judges couldn’t quite pinpoint – “Like fresh herbs,” said Kalvo; “Maybe onion?” said Sweet.

A quick check of the ingredients list reveals a spice mix of pepper, parsley and rosemary, as well as honey, carrot and celery powder. It’s wood-smoked in small batches by a Polish family smokehouse in Dandenong, Victoria. They’ve been doing it since the ’90s, and they’re big on using Australian free-range pork with no added nitrates.

“I liked the aromats, it was quite flavourful,” said Tang, who picked up notes of bay leaves and peppercorns. “The bite as well, it had like a roast-beef bite, but it was still tender and moist.”

“It’s very fresh meat, a very summer ham, with a long, clean aftertaste,” said Matthews.

THE BUTCHERS’ PICK

$16.99 per kilogram

Fair warning: This is a very popular ham, and though Black Forest has several stockists (including Harris Farm), it might be tricky to track down.

It’s little wonder, really – this is one of those hams that looks good right off the rack, and it was an immediate hit among the judges. “God damn!” said Sweet. “I think that might have been the ham of the day for me, love it, really premium-tasting.”

“It was my favourite one so far,” said O’Rourke, our resident butcher. “It was soft, sweet, with a clean finish.”

Together with Powell, our honorary butcher, this ham scored highest among judges with first-hand curing and smoking experience. It was wood-smoked over ironbark three times, but maintained such balance that you could still taste the spices, and the gentle sweetness and the salty brine shine through. “Lovely smoke,” said Powell. “Great flavour.”

THE BEST VALUE

$9.99 per kilogram

For a moment, it looked like Harris Farm’s Spring Grove ham might be a little, well, wet. Instead, these slices came right to the very cliff edge, like Thelma and Louise before the credits roll. It wavers in that anticipatory spot – silky, plump and a little sweet.

“It’s been my favourite so far,” said Powell, praising its gently salty flavour, Goldilocks mouthfeel, and its even colouring.

“I like that the smoke wasn’t in your face,” said Tang. “It lingered, [more like] an after-effect.”

Spring Grove is a food manufacturer operating out of Casino, NSW. Its pigs are sourced from the family owned Anderlea farm, in the South Burnett region of Queensland. Spring Grove CEO Phillip McCaughey said they’re chosen for their consistent quality with structured fat and balanced flavour. Each ham is cured for about 48 hours before being smoked with Beechwood.

There’s one catch. We bought this ham from Harris Farm, which has stores in NSW, QLD and the ACT, but does not have a presence in Victoria.

$11.99 per kilogram

It was the last one on the refrigerated shelf at Costco, and it immediately caught my attention. I was there for the Central Highlands leg ham, but this one had a dark even tone that suggested something special.

D’Orsogna is a small-goods manufacturer founded in Perth by an Italian family in 1949, and they’ve been stocked in major supermarkets (including Woolworths) since the ’70s. Their triple-smoked ham is rich, with a soft, sweet smokiness and even colouring.

“This one was the best for smokiness,” said Kalvo. “I felt like it was smoked from the fire, like real wood smoke.”

“It was decadent,” said Starkey. “Festive and Christmassy.”

Democrat Victoria Broderick unseats eight-term Republican incumbent in Tennessee to win election

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 20:20:24 GMT

Victory expands Democrats’ House majority, its largest advantage in three decades

Democrat Victoria Broderick has won Tennessee’s fourth congressional district, unseating eight-term Republican incumbent Scott DesJarlais in one of the biggest House upsets of the cycle. The victory expands Democrats’ historic House majority in the 120th Congress to 259 seats, the party’s largest advantage in three decades, and flips a seat that Donald Trump carried by more than 20 points in 2024.

Broderick, 34, a former technology and logistics professional who previously ran for Congress in 2024, told the Guardian in an interview before her race was called that she connected with constituents who had not voted in years and met Republicans concerned about affordability who appreciated the “integrity” she brought to the race.

“We’ve been neglected in this district,” she said earlier this month. “People want representatives who understand what they are going through, who understand the costs of going to the gas station or grocery store. I’m that representative.”

Tennessee’s congressional map was redrawn as part of the GOP’s mid-decade gerrymandering effort before this year’s midterm elections, and election forecasters had rated the district as “solidly Republican”. Yet Broderick prevailed by fewer than 400 votes, according to the Associated Press race call. DesJarlais, 62, who aligned himself closely with Trump during his time in office, conceded to Broderick last week after the razor-thin contest but the race was officially called on Tuesday.

“We all leave here with our heads held high, and we hope the Fourth District continues to receive the attention and care it so richly deserves,” DesJarlais wrote in a statement. “All of us hope that the new Member of Congress feels the same level of awe and gratitude for this tremendous undertaking that I felt every day I had the privilege of serving.”

DesJarlais’ stunning defeat comes despite significantly out-fundraising Broderick in the run-up to the election and with many national Democrats dismissing her campaign as a long shot. Broderick will now be the sole Democrat in Tennessee’s congressional delegation on Capitol Hill, underscoring the scale of an upset few in either party saw coming.

Broderick said that she managed to pull off the upset without support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the party’s House campaign arm. “The Democratic party wasn’t paying attention to this race,” she said. “I knew I was the underdog.”

A day after the election, on 4 November, Broderick had already declared victory. “We did not have the political machine behind us. We didn’t have corporate Pac money, we didn’t have powerful insiders. We had you, the people,” she wrote on social media. “That turns out that is all we needed.”

DesJarlais, a physician, was also dogged by controversy during his time in office, particularly after it was revealed that he urged his ex-wife to have two abortions before their marriage despite his anti-abortion stance. Divorce trial transcripts also showed that he admitted to sexual relationships with patients.

Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 20:04:00 GMT

Opening game ends in draw by repetition

Defending champion plays white in Game 2

Read our move-by-move report of Game 1

Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’

Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny.

After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger. “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.”

The players

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending his world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest world title match in chess history. The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, overlooking Lake Geneva, with both players aged 20 when the first move is played.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in December 2024, aged 18, shattering the previous record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the title, plummeting to No 26 in the world rankings from a career-high No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances, raising doubts over his chances of retaining the crown in his first title defense.

Sindarov, roughly six months older than Gukesh, stunned the chess establishment with a commanding performance at this year’s eight-man Candidates tournament in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws against a stacked field that included Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough year that included winning the 2025 Fide World Cup in Goa. He is the first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the world championship.

The format

The match consists of 14 classical games, with one point awarded for a win and a half-point for a draw. The first player to reach 7½ points wins the title. Each player has 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting at move 41. Players cannot agree to a draw before black’s 40th move.

If the match is tied 7-7 after 14 games, a series of faster tiebreaks will decide the champion: first four rapid games (15 minutes plus 10 seconds per move), then two rapid games (10 minutes plus five seconds), followed if necessary by two blitz games (three minutes plus two seconds). If still tied, single blitz games will be played, alternating colors, until one player wins.

The schedule

Sun 22 Nov Media day and opening ceremonyMon 23 Nov Media day and technical meetingTue 24 Nov Game 1 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Wed 25 Nov Game 2 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Thu 26 Nov Game 3 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Fri 27 Nov Rest daySat 28 Nov Game 4 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Sun 29 Nov Game 5 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Mon 30 Nov Game 6 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Tue 1 Dec Rest dayWed 2 Dec Game 7 (Sindarov–Gukesh)Thu 3 Dec Game 8 (Gukesh-Sindarov)Fri 4 Dec Game 9 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Sat 5 Dec Rest daySun 6 Dec Game 10 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Mon 7 Dec Game 11 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Tue 8 Dec Game 12 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Wed 9 Dec Rest dayThu 10 Dec Game 13 (Sindarov–Gukesh, if necessary)Fri 11 Dec Game 14 (Gukesh-Sindarov, if necessary)Sat 12 Dec Tiebreaks (if necessary) and closing ceremony

All games start at 3pm local time, 2pm GMT, 9am on the US east coast and 7.30pm in India.

Why isn't Magnus Carlsen playing?

Norway's Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash.

Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila.

Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, winning 7½–6½ to become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize.

Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation.

The prize money

The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games.

How to follow

The Guardian will provide live move-by-move commentary, expert analysis and reaction throughout the three-week match. Fans can also watch every game live on Fide’s official YouTube and Twitch channels.

Playing with the black pieces after Sunday’s drawing of lots, Gukesh opted for the Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez, the same opening Vladimir Kramnik famously used to frustrate Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title encounter. The queens came off on the eighth move and Sindarov soon steered play into a less familiar position with 13 Ne4.

The position remained even as the gap on the clocks widened. Gukesh spent nearly an hour combined on his 13th and 17th moves alone, using the second of those (17 … Bb4) to attack one of Sindarov’s rooks. By move 20, the champion was left with about 16 minutes left to take his next 20 turns, while Sindarov still had nearly an hour. Both players would gain an additional half-hour after completing move 40, with no time added before then.

Gukesh won a pawn, then brought his king forward to escape check (27 … Kf6) with less than nine minutes on his clock. Sindarov later said he had seen the move coming but underestimated how safe the king would be there. The challenger turned down a chance to trade rooks, denying Gukesh simplification while the champion had less time to think.

“Of course, I’m trying to push every moment because of the clock,” Sindarov said afterward. “In general I understand my position is very close to equal. … I’m trying to keep finding some interesting ideas, but he defended very well.”

Sindarov eventually won back the pawn, and before long his rook and Gukesh’s king were each moving back and forth between the same two squares. The challenger summoned the arbiter to claim a draw by threefold repetition, only to learn that the position had only occurred twice. The players shook hands over the peaceful result after 3hr 40min when the position duly recurred.

Both Gukesh and Sindarov are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title by some distance. Sindarov will turn 21 on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12.

Their careers have traced sharply divergent trajectories since Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion in December 2024. The Chennai native was only 18 when he defeated China’s Ding Liren to shatter the age record previously held by Garry Kasparov. He has struggled badly for form since reaching the summit, plummeting from a career-high No 3 ranking to No 26 after an extended string of disappointing performances, failing to win a single title over that span. That makes him the lowest-ranked reigning world champion since Elo ratings were introduced in 1971.

Sindarov, meanwhile, has surged from No 25 a year ago to a career-best No 4 after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup in Goa last November and an unbeaten tear through this year’s Candidates tournament in Cyprus, where he became the first player from Uzbekistan to earn a world title shot.

The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Sindarov went off Tuesday as the oddsmakers’ favorite, having won twice and drawn once in their three previous classical meetings.

The match resumes on Wednesday with Gukesh playing as white in Game 2. The first to reach 7½ points will be crowned the champion, with a series of shorter games scheduled if the contest finishes level after 14 games. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.

For Gukesh, who has spoken candidly about the psychological burden of holding the sport’s most prestigious title, the opportunity to finally sit down and play on Tuesday came as a relief. “Once you get to the game, it’s like your home,” he said. “It’s a game you’ve been playing for a lot of years. It feels safe.”

Gul swoops late for buoyant Galatasaray to condemn Aston Villa to Champions League loss

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 20:03:50 GMT

This was Aston Villa’s third trip to Istanbul in the calendar year but, this time, they departed with contrasting emotions. Unlike on the banks of the Bosphorus at Besiktas Park in May, scene of their unforgettable Europa League triumph, or at Fenerbahce in January, they came away with a bloody nose. Galatasaray’s matchwinner, Deniz Gul, came away with worse than that, needing treatment after taking a boot to the face from Nicolas Jackson as he scored from a corner on 77min, the game’s first effort on target.

Galatasaray maintained their commanding home form to extend Villa’s winless run to six in all competitions. A livid Unai Emery was booked for protesting to match officials as a low-quality game on a poor pitch ticked past five minutes of stoppage time.

History showed this was never going to be an easy hurdle for Villa. The Turkish champions have dropped points here once since the opening day of the season, a Champions League defeat against Barcelona last month. Galatasaray have now been beaten just once in 11 home meetings with Premier League opposition, with Arsenal, in 2014, the last English side to emerge victorious. Galatasaray beat Liverpool 1-0 here in last season’s round of 16 in March, before a comprehensive defeat at Anfield in the second leg. Eventually, in typically noisy, hostile surroundings, they overcame Villa by the same scoreline.

Villa had appeared generally comfortable despite the racket raining down from the stands. Taylor Harwood-Bellis looked strong on his first Champions League start. But Villa did not fashion their first opening – and first shot on goal – until a couple of minutes after going behind, the substitute Ibrahim Mbaye forcing Ugurcan Cakir into a save. While the assistant referee flagged the Senegal winger offside, replays suggested he may have been onside.
