NHS trusts to be investigated over ‘repeated failures’ to admit treatment errors

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:35:30 GMT

Failing in their legal duty of candour adds to the distress of patients and families and damages trust, says England’s public service ombudsman

Hospitals will be investigated for regularly breaching their legal duty to tell patients and their relatives when mistakes have happened.

The public service ombudsman for England is launching an investigation into “repeated failures” by NHS trusts to discharge their “duty of candour” to admit when treatment errors have led to patients dying or suffering harm.

Trusts’ lack of openness about mistakes is adding to the distress felt by those who have been harmed and undermining the “precarious trust between citizen and state”, Paula Sussex warned.

England’s 205 NHS care provider trusts were put under a statutory “duty of candour” in 2014 after the Mid Staffordshire care scandal to try to ensure that staff were honest about lapses in care.

However, critics say trusts’ widespread failure to discharge that obligation means patients and families are denied the truth, and that hospitals do not learn from their mistakes. Patient safety campaigners claim trusts’ breaches of the duty are part of a widespread NHS “cover-up culture”.

Sussex decided to investigate after looking into a number of cases in which patients had been harmed or died as a result of blunders that trusts did not disclose or report to the Care Quality Commission (CQC), as they are obliged to do.

“Patients and their families deserve to be met with honesty and transparency, especially when things go wrong. Too many families are left having to fight for answers and accountability,” she said.

In June, Sussex investigated a case in which a 70-year-old grandmother died avoidably after a series of failures in the care she experienced from Kettering general hospital NHS trust.

Staff were worried about her treatment, with one voicing unease that “her heart could stop at any point”. But neither the unnamed woman nor her family were ever told of these concerns and they were not recorded in her notes.

Her daughter told the ombudsman that “by raising concerns I gave them multiple opportunities to have a transparent conversation with us. But they never told us how serious it was or that she was dying.”

She said: “In the end we were given barely any time to prepare for her death and could not contact other relatives in time to come and say goodbye.

“It was a horrible experience and the lack of candour from the trust made the grief and trauma so much worse.”

Sussex will look into why the NHS is “inconsistent” in its adherence to the duty and make recommendations on how to improve in a report next year. Fear among staff of being blamed for making mistakes and their pressurised work environments may be factors, she said.

Duty of candour obliges trusts to be honest about any “notifiable safety incident” that has led to a patient dying or suffering severe or moderate or prolonged psychological harm.

“It’s unacceptable after over 10 years that trusts still do not always comply with the statutory duty of candour. The provisions in the regulations are clear but the reality is that implementation is sporadic at best,” said Guy Forster, the president of the Association of Personal Injury Lawyers.

“Without openness, lessons are not learned. Failures in care are repeated time and again, and more patients are needlessly harmed. Our members report that fear of repercussions from trust leadership often creates a culture in which staff are reluctant to speak out.”

Blackpool Teaching Hospitals NHS trust is facing a payout of over £3m to Hazel Gregory, its former head of safeguarding. The Health Service Journal reported last week that Gregory sued for unfair dismissal when she was sacked after raising concerns that it was concealing information about deaths, mistreatment of patients and sexual assaults. The judge at the employment tribunal that heard her case struck out the trust’s defence.

Sussex said an NHS campaign could alert both patients and staff to the existence of the duty of candour, to help overcome patients’ lack of knowledge of it, in the same way it has promoted awareness and take-up of Martha’s rule.

NHS England said that it is working to ensure that trusts do adhere to the duty of candour.

“We welcome this investigation by the ombudsman as we continue to transform our culture and improve patient safety across the NHS,” a spokesperson said.

“The NHS is strengthening its duty of candour, including through our Patient Safety Incident Response Framework, making compassionate engagement and involvement of patients and families a core principle after harm or safety incidents occur.”

The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:15:00 GMT

Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance

Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it. Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal?

Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK.

For the other 90% of claimants, the prospects are less certain. There is no repeat here of the Starmer government’s crass attempt to slash £5bn from the overall bill by raising thresholds across the board. Sir Stephen and his colleagues have accepted the message sent by Labour MPs last year, that they were not elected to strip benefits away from vulnerable people in the middle of a cost of living crisis. But while the recommendation is for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) to run its new impact assessments in a flexible, responsive and personalised way, the outcome, at least for some claimants, is likely to be reduced entitlements. Ministers should establish disabled people’s requirements before deciding what to spend. Sharing out too little money more fairly cannot be described as progress.

The proposal that disabled people should be involved in reform in an ongoing way sets a challenge for ministers. But the practical difficulties of participatory methods must not be allowed to obscure their advantages. This review gives an unusually vivid account of the DWP’s failings. Ministers should accept the principle of a “person‑centred” system despite its significant resource and workforce implications. They must find alternatives to processes that are frequently experienced as dehumanising.

This review is distinct from the recent Fonagy and Milburn reports, and should be treated as such. The Timms report’s focus on the costs of disability sits uneasily with the Milburn report’s emphasis on getting young people into work. Pip is not an unemployment benefit. For some, it is what makes working possible. Until ministers set out what new job support and training opportunities will look like, especially in the deprived areas where they are most needed, it is difficult to judge whether such measures are likely to succeed.

But the Timms review makes clear that a cash benefit such as Pip cannot simply be abolished. Labour should resist the scapegoating of disabled people: the working-age benefit bill is stable as a share of GDP. What has changed is its composition. How much of rising disability spending reflects worsening public health, failing public services and an inflexible labour market? Rising ill health among claimants is concerning, but cutting Pip would deepen generational inequality and hardship without addressing its causes.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:13:49 GMT

The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style

As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations.

In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

At the level of political optics, which this prime minister usually handles adeptly, it seems a strangely insensitive and high-handed approach. At last May’s Senedd elections, Welsh Labour suffered a historic political meltdown that saw voters defect in large numbers to the progressive nationalists of Mr ap Iorwerth’s Plaid Cymru. Responding this week to Mr Burnham’s letter, the first minister professed himself “gobsmacked” and said that Wales was not being viewed as “an equal nation” by Downing Street. An apparent refusal to engage at all with Plaid’s devolution agenda – which is also largely backed by Welsh Labour – risks becoming a gift for the nationalist cause.

Substantively, the government’s determination to maintain the status quo means persisting with anomalies that it is hard to justify, and which have fuelled an understandable sense of resentment towards Westminster. The unfairness (and stark inaccuracy) of defining HS2 as an “England and Wales project” rankles still. Scotland and Northern Ireland, where rail services and infrastructure are devolved, benefited from related Barnett formula money amounting to billions of pounds. Wales missed out, and its rail services and infrastructure have been historically underfunded from London.

Commissions such as that led by the former lord chief justice, Lord Thomas, have strongly recommended that justice be devolved in Wales as it is in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The case in favour, based on a recognition that priorities are best determined at close hand rather than remotely, resembles that made many times by Mr Burnham in his own advocacy for place-based politics. And if the crown estate and its revenues can be devolved in Scotland, it is hard to see why the same cannot apply to Wales.

Mr Burnham’s letter points to a potential loss of the benefits of cross-border cooperation in policing, and the intended role of Great British Railways in determining future investment in rail. But for a prime minister who understands how deeply political loyalties are rooted in place and belonging, the reluctance to engage with Wales’s sense of nationhood is striking. It also seems surprisingly shortsighted.

At the very least, a lengthier and more collaborative examination of the issues involved is in order. Mr ap Iorwerth has requested urgent talks with Downing Street. That wish should be swiftly granted, allowing a better, more constructive conversation to begin.

Chicken Shop Date host says she ended YouTube show … to find a real date

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 19:02:15 GMT

Amelia Dimoldenberg described two panic attacks and said she wanted to end the hit series ‘before I start resenting it’

Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of Chicken Shop Date, has said she decided to end the popular YouTube series which had increasingly left her feeling “isolated” and made her search for real relationships more challenging.

The comedian, 32, also revealed she had questioned the future of the interview series after suffering two panic attacks, saying she wanted to end it “before I start resenting it”.

Dimoldenberg announced in September that Chicken Shop Date was concluding, with the final episode due to be released on YouTube on Friday.

The presenter began the series aged 17 as a magazine column before transitioning to YouTube in 2014, interviewing celebrities in local chicken shops with her unconventional questions and deadpan silences.

Dimoldenberg wrote in The Cut magazine: “When you are a child who desires fame, you are really a child who yearns for connection.

“I thought the more famous I became, the more likely it was [that] someone would fall in love with me.

“If anything, playing a decade-long role of the serial dater has made my real dating life challenging.

“People often meet you with a preconceived idea of who you are, their curiosity misplaced. I am so proud of my success, but it has isolated me in some ways.”

Dimoldenberg said when she first started the show in 2014, initially interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene, part of her believed she could fall in love with someone on-camera, which she believes “grew into a delusion”.

She wrote: “Why wouldn’t a hot celebrity want to be with me? I wondered. I started this show when I was a teenager, so of course I’ve had crushes on guests.

“I have gone through every emotion a twentysomething woman might experience: fear that they might not like me back, overthinking if and how I should reach out to them again, wondering if they will be at the same glamorous awards show.”

She added: “To actually date a guest would have been transgressive and implausible in this constructed reality.

“Nevertheless, this belief has been what kept me going and I think kept the audience believing too. Now that the prophecy has gone unfulfilled, a new one must take shape.”

The presenter’s interviewees have included Ed Sheeran and Jennifer Lawrence. Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter.

The comedian also spoke of the panic attacks she has experienced.

She wrote: “I knew my perspective on Chicken Shop Date was changing around 18 months ago, when I had my first and then second panic attack ever in the space of a week.”

Dimoldenberg continued: “I had stopped drinking at the time because I was trying to pinpoint exactly why I felt so unlike myself.

“All of my emotions felt so much more visceral; I figured that’s what happens when you cut out a sedative.”

Dimoldenberg told the Edinburgh TV festival earlier this year she is writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them.

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:47:48 GMT

Tories accuse PM of ‘degrading’ Downing Street as Max Balegde takes down clip of himself miming explicit lyrics

Andy Burnham is facing a backlash for inviting social media influencers to Downing Street after one of a group attending an event posted a clip of himself miming to a viral song with explicit lyrics outside No 10.

Downing Street said it was right that Max Balegde had taken down a TikTok post of him mouthing the words “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” after attending an event at the prime minister’s residence.

Balegde was given the invitation as part of Burnham’s efforts to engage with online celebrities. Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth.

After criticism from Kemi Badenoch, Nigel Farage and others, the prime minister’s spokesperson said the post was not acceptable.

He said it was right that the PM listened to social media content creators who “reach millions of people who don’t get their news from traditional media”.

Content creators were invited to a No 10 reception on 9 November and videos from the evening have subsequently emerged online.

Another showed Luke Hamnett recreating Hugh Grant’s prime ministerial dance from the film Love Actually inside No 10.

The Conservatives have accused Burnham of turning No 10 into a joke and said he should not have allowed Downing Street to be “degraded”.

Badenoch said: “I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using No 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.” She said the videos would be seen by Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, meaning the UK’s adversaries would “see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country”.

In a reference to Balegde’s video, she said: “I think it is a disgrace that No 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that’s where we receive people like President Zelenskyy, showing them that they have the support of people in this country – is being degraded in this way.”

Ex-boss of Pride in London given suspended sentence for ‘harvesting’ documents

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:39:52 GMT

Christopher Joell-Deshields accessed internal records after organisation sacked him in ‘flagrant flouting’ of court order

The sacked boss of the Pride in London LGBTQ+ parade has been given a suspended prison sentence for his “flagrant” contempt of court when accessing the organisation’s records in breach of a judicial order.

Christopher Joell-Deshields, who was suspended as chief executive in summer 2025 and sacked in April, failed to give up access to Pride’s IT systems as ordered by the high court and instead “harvested” documents for his own use.

Between 50 and 60 internal documents were downloaded in September last year and used by Joell-Deshields to establish a rival LGBTQ+ event and to make a 208-page employment tribunal claim against Pride in London, in which he is claiming wrongful dismissal and discrimination.

London’s annual Pride parade is the largest LGBTQ+ event in the UK and attracts about 30,000 participants. It is funded by sponsors and a £125,000-a-year grant from the mayor of London.

Mr Justice Cotter said Joell-Deshields’ actions had been a “serious, wilful, flagrant flouting” of the high court. The judge said the defendant had avoided immediate imprisonment owing to his poor mental health and role as sole carer to his 15-year-old twin daughters.

Joell-Deshields, who was paid £87,500 a year as chief executive of London LGBT Community Pride, the body that trades as Pride in London, claimed in his witness statement to be “exhausted, overwhelmed and broken”. The judge said the court would not be as lenient if further evidence emerged of a breach of the courts order.

Joell-Deshields, who had been chief executive of Pride in London since 2021, was put under internal investigation in August 2025 and suspended the following month in response to whistleblowers’ claims of misconduct.

The allegations included bullying and the misuse of vouchers provided by an unnamed sponsor for volunteers at the Pride march, which he denies. Joell-Deshields was subsequently sacked.

In September, London LGBT Community Pride successfully applied to the high court for an injunction that would force Joell-Deshields to hand over company property and passwords for online accounts, including banks, Facebook and HM Revenue and Customs.

Joell-Deshields failed to comply with the order, under which he was also required to provide a statement confirming that he had given up or destroyed property belonging to the community interest company.

Rather than hand over the passwords and documents, Joell-Deshields used his access to Pride’s records to download documents, including privileged information he subsequently used in his employment claim.

Joell-Deshields claimed to the court that he had merely taken notes and that he could not recall downloading the information.

Cotter said this version of events was “unbelievable” and ruled that he had “harvested” the documents on 15 September last year, three days after being issued with a court order.

“I don’t accept that he does not recollect undertaking this exercise,” the judge said. “The court will not tolerate deliberate disobedience of such orders.”

Joell-Deshields, who it was claimed owned two houses in London, was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment for contempt in failing to hand over property and passwords and a concurrent jail sentence of four months for failing to submit his statement detailing the records he had held. The sentences are suspended for 18 months. He will also pay costs.

Jannik Sinner faces further time off the court after undergoing knee surgery. The former world No 1 has been sidelined with pain in his right knee since winning his second consecutive Wimbledon title in July.

Sinner said in a statement: “Over the past few months, together with my team, we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery. After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we had all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band. I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team.”

The iliotibial band is a thick band of fibrous connective tissue running down the outside of the thigh, and injuries associated with it are typically caused by overuse.

Sinner set a record by winning the first five Masters 1000 tournaments of the year, becoming only the second man after Novak Djokovic to complete the career Golden Masters. But he appeared exhausted in suffering a shock early loss at the French Open before rebounding strongly at Wimbledon. His absence has allowed Alexander Zverev to overtake him at the top of the rankings, while Carlos Alcaraz is now close behind in third after a hugely impressive comeback from his own injury issues.

The operation was carried out by Professor Lasse Lempainen, a Finnish specialist in orthopaedic surgery.

The teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off 53 balls for India A on Tuesday to break a host of records, including for the fastest century and double-century in List A cricket.

The 15-year-old Sooryavanshi struck a staggering 28 sixes, the most in a senior men’s innings, as India passed their target of 250 against the United Arab Emirates in just 14.2 overs.

Sooryavanshi reached his hundred off 28 balls to take Australian Jake Fraser-McGurk’s record by one delivery. He raised his 200 off 52 deliveries, smashing the 103-ball mark previously held by Chad Bowes. Sooryavanshi also broke his own record for fastest 150, reaching that milestone from 40 balls.

“No words to say for him. I would only say it’s like absolute carnage,” the India A captain, Tilak Varma, said after the Asia Cup Rising Stars match. “The way he played, I think first five overs the match was done, five overs we are 100 and the way he carried on after that, it was tremendous to watch. Honestly, everyone knows how he can hit the sixes.”

In July, Sooryavanshi became India’s youngest men’s international when he made his T20I debut against England in Manchester, eclipsing Sachin Tendulkar’s longstanding record. He amassed 776 runs for Rajasthan Royals to finish as the tournament’s leading run-scorer in this year’s IPL, at a remarkable strike rate of 237.30.

The Frenchman will no longer be required to serve a one-match suspension after a ruling by an independent panel. He fouled Alexander Isak when the Liverpool forward was through on goal in the early stages at Anfield but Mauricio Pochettino, United’s new head coach, insisted the striker would not have reached the ball, and therefore was not a sending-off offence. The referee Sam Barrott made a different assessment, for which the video assistant referee did not seek a review, a judgment supported by Pro Ref’s chief refereeing officer, Webb.

“The reason we’re talking about it is the fourth consideration [in Dogso decisions], that’s control or likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball,” Webb told Mic’d Up, which was recorded before the confirmation of the card being annulled.

“Isak’s got control of the ball, he’s got possession, he’s got the touch, he knocks it past Yoro. He’s moving at pace at that moment, and a foul comes in and knocks him down. There’s a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get on to that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would. The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. [It’s] certainly not clearly wrong.”

Pochettino expressed his opinion on Sunday: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”

Dominik Szoboszlai scored the resulting free-kick, setting Liverpool on their way to victory, to make it a difficult first match in charge for Pochettino. Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday in the Premier League.

Luke Cowan-Dickie is adamant England will not let complacency creep in after their record win over the All Blacks, insisting they will not repeat the mistakes of the 2019 World Cup.

Cowan-Dickie is one of three players, with Jamie George and Maro Itoje, who would claim a fourth career win for England against New Zealand on Saturday if Steve Borthwick’s side back up last weekend’s 37-12 victory at Twickenham. The Sale hooker was part of the squad who defeated the All Blacks in the 2019 World Cup semi-final in emphatic fashion and went into the final against South Africa as favourites. Eddie Jones’s side were comfortably outplayed by the Springboks, however, with Cowan-Dickie acknowledging that England failed to hit their emotional peak that day.

Last weekend England flew out of the blocks, inspired by having Lewis Moody at the point of their V-formation response to the haka, and Cowan-Dickie is convinced there will be no complacency against the wounded All Blacks. Borthwick gave the players Monday off before resuming training on Tuesday.

Cowan-Dickie said: “Back then was the semi-final of the World Cup, maybe we left too much emotion out there and didn’t take enough into the final? Could we learn anything from that? Maybe little parts, complacency? Maybe that’s a big one. But the way we trained today, I don’t see any complacency. The boys are as up for it as they were last week.

“It’s a difficult one, I don’t know if we were complacent, it’s just the amount of emotion that went into that semi-final game, did we build the emotions back up for that final? The team we’ve got now is completely different. There are a lot of younger boys involved and they’re frothing at the bit. Obviously Lewis last week added that little bit but, for me, it’s a Test match. If we were playing tomorrow I’d be ready to go.”

Meanwhile, England’s wing sensation Will Joseph has revealed he has been receiving advice from his elder brother, Jonathan – who won 54 caps for his country – after proving Borthwick’s find of the autumn. Joseph won his first cap in 2022 but had to wait four years for a second, in which he scored a record-equalling five tries, earlier this month.

Shop small, save big: 21 brilliant Black Friday bargains from UK independents

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 18:00:52 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From farm-to-table hot sauce to handwoven blankets, here are our favourite discounts from bricks-and-mortar shops and indie retailers

The best Black Friday deals

Listen: we love a discounted air fryer as much as the next person, but there’s no doubt shopping for Black Friday deals can feel a bit … icky. From handing even more of your cash to global corporations to the suspicion you’re adding to a mass of plastic floating somewhere in the Antarctic, it’s no wonder a third of Britons say they hate Black Friday.

But there is a way of having your discounted jacket and wearing it too. And that’s by shopping with local and independent retailers. Many wonderful bricks-and-mortar shops and small online retailers around the UK take part in Black Friday, often in creative and fun ways.

We’ve scoured the country for the best and most interesting deals across a range of regions and products. From preloved Gucci handbags to limited-edition rock’n’roll collectibles, handmade jewellery and farm-to-table hot sauces, these UK indie deals will give you more of that warm and fuzzy Christmas feeling this Black Friday, whether you’re buying a gift for a loved one or – even better – yourself.

Robinson’s, Belfast

This well-known Belfast shoe shop started life as a simple repair shop in 1954 before evolving to sell loafers, derbys, boat shoes and even its own line in Irish brogues. In a world of adult men in trainers, be the grownup in the room with 40% off selected brands from 16-30 November.

25-27 Queen’s Arcade, Belfast BT1 5FE

Loop Vintage, Manchester

Forget spending hours on Vinted searching for the same holy grail as everyone else … if you want an authentic, vintage or pre-owned designer bag, check out Loop in Manchester, where treasures from Hermès to Gucci to Balenciaga have been checked by experts. From 9–30 November it’s offering 5% off everything (and deeper discounts on bags) – naturally, the best stuff will go quickest.

4–10 London Road, Piccadilly, Manchester M1 3AN

Eye Room, Leeds

Husband-and-wife team Tomas and Hafiya Oppedal have been running this independent optician in Leeds for almost 10 years now, fitting customers with equally independent optical brands from around the world. Their beautiful store is a joy to visit – and if you do so during Black Friday week you can get 25% off your next pair of glasses.

9 Mill Hill, Leeds LS1 5DQ

The Broken Binding, Stratford-upon-Avon

How do you get 15,000 people queueing online to buy books they haven’t even seen? Ask the Broken Binding, the independent science fiction and fantasy specialist whose subscription boxes have become cult objects among genre obsessives. Founded during lockdown, it’s now publishing its own books, too. This Black Friday, selected titles are half price.

11 Red Lion Court, Bridge Street, Stratford-upon-Avon, CV37 6AB

Stripe & Stare, Plymouth

“Nothing great was ever achieved in uncomfortable knickers,” claims Stripe & Stare, a female-founded independent underwear and nightwear brand with unusually strong environmental credentials, including B Corp certification. Its underwear has been described as “the softest” by none other than Vogue – and it’s offering Black Friday discounts of up to 50% on selected items.

Hallby Gifts, Lichfield

For the person who deserves a proper treat but is impossible to buy for, Hallby Gifts might be your salvation. Former school teacher Amy Hall started making personalised care packages during lockdown, and now lets you assemble your own boxes of little luxuries, with donations supporting charities including Mind and FareShare. There’s 20% off sitewide from 17–30 November.

Bending Sound, Bangor

This family-run record shop was born out of frustration with Northern Ireland’s dwindling vinyl scene and has been thriving ever since – not just a treasure trove of high-quality pre-owned records but a mini music venue visited by the likes of Snow Patrol, Dermot Kennedy and Villagers. It’s offering customers the chance to submit a wishlist of Record Store Day Black Friday titles that will be sold on a first-come, first-served basis.

2 Bank Lane, Bangor, County Down BT20 5EG Northern Ireland

Lisa Angel, Norfolk

Lisa Angel started making charm bracelets on her living-room floor while on maternity leave in 2004, eventually selling her car to buy more stock. Two decades later, her Norwich-born business has grown into a small jewellery empire, specialising in the sort of personalised gifts that make you look like a considerably more thoughtful person than you are. There’s already 20% off all jewellery.

3 Lower Goat Lane, Norwich NR2 1EL

Resident Music, Brighton

This extremely cool record shop (with an Instagram following to match) specialises in alternative vinyl releases as well as reissues and back catalogues. It’s also a venue in its own right, hosting events both in-store and elsewhere, with guests this year ranging from Stewart Lee to Skepta. This Black Friday it’s offering first access to some special editions ranging from Bruce Springsteen to Florence + the Machine.

27-28 Kensington Gardens, North Laine, Brighton BN1 4AL

Night Owl Books, East Lothian

If you really want to offset your Amazon splurge this Black Friday, Night Owl Books – which also stocks gifts created by other local indies, all inspired by the natural world – is encouraging you not to buy but to swap your books in its beautiful shop. It’s all to raise money for East Lothian food bank.

1 Bridge Street, East Linton EH40 3AG

London Undercover, Bloomsbury

It’s hard to think of anything more British than a luxury umbrella shop. London Undercover is where fashion brands and fashionistas alike go to buy brollies handmade using traditional techniques, with personalised engraving and foil embossing on leather fasteners all part of the service. Situated on probably the most stylish street in London, the store is offering a nice and dry 20% off everything from 27-29 November.

28 Lamb’s Conduit Street, London WC1N 3LE

Genesis Publications, Surrey

If there’s space on your coffee table for a decadent, limited-edition music or photography book, this is the indie publisher for you. Founded in 1974, Genesis publishes leather-bound tributes to rock gods such as the Beatles, Jimi Hendrix and the Stones, earning an endorsement from Ronnie Wood in the process. It’s offering discounts of 20-30% on eligible editions, depending on the size of your splurge, from now until 30 November.

Angela Reed, Essex

This furniture and homeware shop has strong local roots: a fifth-generation business, established more than 140 years ago. Yet its design sensibility is deeply modern, with many tables, chairs and accessories that wouldn’t look out of place in a Thames-side loft apartment. For the whole of Black Friday week, it’s offering 10% off most products, with up to 40% online now.

5-7 Market Hill, Saffron Walden, Essex CB10 1HQ

Jobsons of Alnwick, Northumberland

Northumberland winters are not for the faint-hearted, and Jobsons of Alnwick has been dressing locals for them for more than a century. This traditional outfitter stocks the sort of sturdy knitwear, coats and scarves that might actually see you through a few winters, rather than one fashion season. There’s 20% off selected stock over Black Friday week, online and in-store.

Tower Showrooms, Bondgate Within, Alnwick, Northumberland NE66 1SX

Smoothie London, Islington

Colourful, playful and affordable, Smoothie is an unpretentious British jewellery brand that has grown from making huggie hoops and ear stacks into a place for any earring you can think of. It’s having its first-ever Christmas pop-up in north London this year, but you can grab a bargain before then. For four hours on Sunday 29 November you can get an impressive 40% off everything as well as some bonus deals.

Maison Noël, 264 Upper Street, Islington (from 5-13 December)

Dobell, Eastbourne

’Tis the season to buy a tuxedo – which, generally speaking, is a royal pain in the backside. You’re forced to either spend a fortune on something you’ll wear once a year at most, or rent something that never quite fits. British brand Dobell offers a third option with a range of affordable tuxes popular with Olympians, rappers and actors who haven’t yet hit Burberry ambassador status. It’s offering 25% off for Black Friday.

Mod Shoes, Cambridgeshire

Ever since its mid-60s heyday, the mod look has been an enduring presence on British streets. If a buttoned-up knitted polo, a pair of oxblood brogue boots and a spotted silk scarf are your kind of look, then hop on your virtual moped to family-run specialist clothes website Mod Shoes. It will be running select deals from 27 November.

Wolf & Badger, London

Situated on one of the best streets in Soho, Wolf & Badger offers up a cornucopia of ethical, independent clothing, jewellery and homeware brands – more than 2,000 of them, from across the world. You’ll get up to 40% off many of its products, but move quickly: its sale has already started.

102 Berwick Street, Soho, London W1F 0QB

Living Roots, Richmond

A blanket is one of those Christmas presents that sound boring until you receive a really good one. Living Roots specialises in hand-woven cotton throws, blankets and towels, with personalised options for people who like their gifts to look especially considered. Its Black Friday sale offers up to 50% off – an excellent excuse to make the sofa considerably more inviting.

Paper High, Lewes

Paper High started life as a Camden Market stall selling handmade journals and photo albums inspired by its owners’ travels in Kathmandu. More than 20 years later it’s grown into a company selling a range of fair trade stationery and gifts. It’s running its own Green Friday campaign from now until 1 December, during which you can get up to 50% off more than 80 bestselling products, while also helping fund the planting of 1,000 trees.

Wiltshire chilli farm, Wiltshire

Ranging from “tickle your tongue” to “run around screaming for a glass of milk” levels on the Scoville scale, these bestselling hot sauces cater for every palate. Made in the English countryside, they’re a great way to liven up your kitchen cabinet – especially with the farm offering 20% off sitewide from now until midnight on 30 November.

Farage preaches the Brexit gospel according to St Nige

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:42:10 GMT

Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be

This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. It’s hardly a secret that he prefers his own company. His fellow Reform MPs are a necessary inconvenience at best. Muppets at worst. He can barely hide his misogyny for Sarah Pochin, having written her off as a pisshead. Nor does he have a much higher opinion of Richard Tice, Zia Yusuf and the others. But even Nige has worked out that when it comes to having a Potemkin alternative cabinet, he can’t realistically do everything himself.

Only when it comes to Brexit, it seems, is Farage at his best as a one-man band. This is his battle. During Monday’s Commons statement, Andy Burnham said he didn’t want to keep “banging on about Europe”. But Nige most definitely does. Not least because the more he can talk about Brexit, the less people will criticise him for having no real plans for government. Most of his domestic policies collapse on contact with reality. As for foreign policy, he doesn’t have one. Unless you count having as little to do with the EU as possible.

Brexit is Nige’s lifeline. Without it, he would be nothing. Just another gobshite lurking on the fringes of politics. Now he has a sense of purpose again. Burnham has all but said he will make the next general election a referendum on Europe and that suits Nige just fine.

He’s never wanted to be the kind of politician that gets to grip with the day-to-day minutiae of governing the country. He’s a single-issue campaigner. Living his best life when he feels he’s the outsider looking in. Standing up for the Little Man against the Establishment. And he’s been given carte blanche to forget about the economy and the NHS. From now on it’s route one to Brexit.

So it was Nige and Nige alone who fronted Reform’s press conference. The man who was trying to paint himself as the authentic voice of Brexit. Distancing himself from the dozen or so Tories in the shadow cabinet who had campaigned for Remain before selling their souls to the Brexit cause. Why listen to the Tories who had brought you a bad Brexit deal when you could hear straight from the man without whom the UK would never have left the EU?

There was a problem with this, of course. Having spent much of the last few years rubbishing the Brexit deal, Nige now finds himself forced to defend it. It’s what the country voted for. How dare Burnham try to improve a deal that he himself recently described as a terrible. Now he had come to think of it, the deal was about as good as anyone could have expected. Give or take a very few minor wrinkles. The world sees hypocrisy, Nige sees expediency. That’s the joy of being back on the campaign trail. The truth can be whatever you want it to be.

This was to be the gospel according to Saint Nige. It hadn’t been a pleasure to be back in Brussels on the previous Thursday and Friday, he said. A total lie. He had loved every second. In the last few weeks, Reform had been sliding in the polls, mired in scandal. Now Nige had his mojo back. He had a purpose in life again. And he could invent any reality he chose. Like Burnham having effectively rejoined the single market and the political union with his EU reset. This was clearly nonsense. But Farage was just getting started.

The country had voted for a political earthquake in 2016 and there could be no going back. Vote Leave had always been about the hardest possible Brexit. Except just before the referendum Nige had appeared quite chilled about the prospect of the UK following the Norway option. Only that was yet another inconvenient truth to be airbrushed out of history. It had just been trash-talk. Nige had never really meant it. What he had really been trying to say was that leaving the single market and the customs union wasn’t nearly hard enough. For that we would also have to leave the ECHR.

Nige was completely unbothered that most people felt the Brexit deal had been bad for Britain and wanted a reset with the EU. This was all false consciousness and everyone would be bound to see sense if presented with a second referendum. What we all needed to remember was just how well the UK had been doing since we left the EU. The economy had been booming at unprecedented rates. Farmers had never had it so good. This may well come as news to farmers. Burnham was looking backwards, Farage was looking forwards. The End.

The media weren’t so easily convinced. Their recall of the last 10 years was more in tune with the public’s than Farage’s. But Nige was unbothered. This was him unplugged. Flying solo. The country should never trust the Tories again. They had secured the failed Brexit deal that he was now defending. Here was Nige mainlining himself. Unworried by his own contradictions. We shouldn’t worry that the man Farage had also described as his shadow chancellor had also been a remainer. Robert Jenrick was just an outlier. Nige gave the impression that if he never saw Honest Bob again it wouldn’t be a moment too soon.

Suella Braverman also got it in the neck for her ethnonationalist tendencies. Though not for handcuffing herself to Katie Price for a TV show. Nothing must deflect from the one true Brexit. He might have a cup of tea with Rupert Lowe though so long as he distanced himself from his racist followers. Er … There’s a reason racists are attracted to Lowe.

That just left time for Nige to reflect on the Jensen Huang saga. Farage guessed this proved that many of the highest performing organisations were run by one Superman. You reckoned that Nige was really thinking of someone a little closer to home.

Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:26:48 GMT

Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again

When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity.

Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday. But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes.

I have witnessed and felt this dynamic play out in my personal and professional life. I frequently self-censor and push down a whole host of emotions for fear of how I will be perceived. Of course, people-pleasing tendencies are not specific to Black women, but I am considerably more conscious of how I present myself when interacting with white people. And, as a mixed-race woman with white heritage, I am conscious that I experience a watered-down version of this phenomenon. In an old job, I comforted a dark-skinned Black woman after her manager said her quietness in meetings came across as “hostile”.

What happened with Odudu and Frostrup was similarly overt. Odudu’s conduct was clearly not aggressive. Watching, it felt like a baffling characterisation of her behaviour, which had the effect of derailing the argument and painting Odudu in a negative light, while casting Frostrup as the victim.

It came across as a textbook example of the “angry Black woman” trope. Throughout history, Black women have been repeatedly and unfairly painted as combative and antagonistic. It stems, in part, from the slavery era in the US, where Black women were dehumanised through racist caricatures – often depicting them as irrationally irate – to help justify their exploitation. You only have to look at recent depictions of women such as Serena Williams and Michelle Obama to understand how enduring this perception is.

What might look like a mild disagreement on a reality TV show is something more complicated. This is about an insidious societal double standard that judges Black women more harshly than white women, holding them to higher standards of behaviour while simultaneously denying them the same understanding and latitude. It also creates a trap in which Black women can’t stand up for themselves without having their argument – no matter how valid – undermined, diminished and wilfully misconstrued. It’s something that is instantly recognisable to those who have felt it, just as women will often innately feel when they are experiencing sexism, even if it is hard to pinpoint. It’s about antennae and, of course, its calibration.

And there are real-life consequences: Black women are often cast as bullies, and being perceived as irrational can stifle careers and limit progression. In schools, Black Caribbean girls and mixed white and Black Caribbean girls are permanently excluded at more than double the rate of white girls.

It wasn’t long before Nigel Farage waded into the debate. Frostrup’s “sharp comment” should not be conflated with racism, said the man whose party seems a magnet for racists.

Frostrup’s comment is not the most egregious offence, but, for all of us, the microaggressions pile up. The visceral response many women of colour will have felt – such as Frostrup’s Loose Women colleague Judi Love, who said she was triggered, comes from many small things accumulating over time. What could have been a learning moment for Frostrup and the viewers became more damaging because of her failure to acknowledge the impact without making the person who was hurt responsible for managing the fallout. Frostrup cried when she was pulled aside by other camp mates, who explained why her words were inappropriate, which itself compounded the pressure on Odudu to shrug off the hurt and to sympathise with her.

This isn’t a great place to be. It’s exhausting having to explain, over and over, why microaggressions are bad (particularly when the debate plays out via reality TV and social media – two cultural deserts of nuance and sensitivity). And via a programme that will leverage the outrage for controversy, figures and relevance.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It’s demoralising that we are still debating the existence and manifestations of racism, six years after we were assured that Black Lives Matter and are worthy of respect and reflection. Black women can well explain their experience of this difficult dynamic. AJ Odudu sought to do so. The question is: who listens?

Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain

Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:15:19 GMT

The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting?

That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028.

Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

The flimsy part is that Compass cannot claim its share price labours at a discount to competitors’, which tends to be a standard excuse on these occasions. “For most of the last decade Compass has traded at a valuation premium to its closest US peer Aramark, and also to Sodexo in Europe,” calculates a Morgan Stanley analyst.

Instead, Compass merely says the relisting would be a “natural evolution”, by which it means it generates two-thirds of its revenues, and three-quarters of its profits, in North America these days.

Compass’s stateside expansion over the past couple of decades has indeed been remarkable. But does the group really need to move its listing to “strengthen its competitive position and support its next phase of growth”, as the board says?

At best, the argument is marginal. The group operates sub-brands in local markets; the flag-waving owners of US sports stadiums do not appear bothered that the firm serving the Budweisers in the corporate boxes has a London-listed parent.

In the old days, success in the US would have been a reason for a UK company to champion its roots. Older readers will recall Hanson Trust’s classic TV advert in the 1980s with the slogan: “A company from over here that’s also doing rather well over there.”

Sadly, though, Compass’s drearier globalised view reflects a growing mood in UK boardrooms. Some – such as betting firm Flutter, equipment rental group Ashtead and building materials group CRH – have already played the geography card.

But Compass itself wasn’t previously viewed as a flight risk because it had downplayed the idea. One can wonder if megabucks pay at US companies has entered the thinking, but the dangerous part in its new vision is that it advances one step further the notion that, if a company makes the biggest chunk of its money in the US, that’s where the primary listing should be.

Scan the top end of the Footsie and there is a scary-sounding list of multinational operators that could take the same line. Try: Shell, BP, British American Tobacco, Diageo, Relx, Experian, Smith & Nephew, even LSEG (the owner of the London Stock Exchange). AstraZeneca has adopted an unconventional “harmonised” global listing via which, one suspects, trading in its shares will gravitate to New York.

They won’t all go, but this is a moment when the government – if it is bothered about the exodus – needs to offer more than ineffectual words.

It is traditional to beat up the LSE itself, but its chief executive, Dame Julia Hoggett, made some fair points in a recent BBC interview. Listing rules have been reformed (allowing, among other things, companies such as Compass to have a dollar-denominated share price while remaining in the index); the research side has had a shake-up; corporate governance requirements have been made more flexible.

But, she continued, the LSE does not set tax incentives to encourage domestic investment by pension funds and it cannot change stamp duty. The latter is the 0.5% levy on share purchases that is hopelessly uncompetitive by international standards, as argued in this column many times, and mostly hits retail investors and UK pension funds. Hoggett had a good line on capital export: “We talk about growth in every postcode, but too much of our capital is currently funding growth in every ZIP code.”

Fair point. One can deplore bland corporate thinking, but it is also true that the government (like the last few) has done very little to encourage companies to stay listed in London when they have the option to move. There has been an obsession with prodding pension money into private markets and infrastructure, but little love shown to public markets.

The survival of stamp duty at 0.5% is the most visible sign of Treasury orthodoxy. Even as listing rejigs such as AstraZeneca’s are set to take chunks out of the £3bn-a-year of receipts, the chancellor, John Healey, offered only yet another “under review” message in his budget. Come on, events are moving fast. Compass, an unexpected departee, is sending a worrying signal.

Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 17:00:50 GMT

A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place

As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point.

With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom.

In an attempt to conjure up that long-gone magic, Hexed is a film absolutely stuffed with it, a tale of witches, spells, cauldrons and curses that is at the very least neatly timed. Interest in all things Harry Potter remains sky-high (next month’s HBO adaptation is set to be the year’s most-watched TV show) as streaming hits like Carrie and The Body and a growing YA fantasy audience have shown that witchcraft, and all similarly categorised high school powers, have started to overtake the flagging superhero genre. But then why does something like Hexed still feel so dusty?

Like Wish, it’s a film clearly crafted by people who have deep affection for the Disney back catalogue but who can’t quite turn reverence for what came before into any real idea of where to take things going forward. Again, there’s something too calculated and businesslike, with nods to previous films and regurgitated life lessons, and while Disney adventures have always emerged from a Goliath-sized mega-corporation, the best ones can make you briefly forget that. Sure Disney might have, shamefully, tried to trademark Day of the Dead before the release of Coco (!) but the film itself was charming, sweet and genuinely moving. While the company might have turned Ratatouille into everything from a theme park ride to a branded set of cheese knives, thoughts of merchandise were not in one’s head while watching a rat’s thrilling journey from gourmand to head chef. But Hexed is too soulless and synthetically corporate to distract us from its ultimate Q4 marketing aims.

It takes place in a universe where witches have been Salem trialled away to another magic-filled realm (hello new Disney World section), where they live under the tyrannical control of Queen Celeste (voiced by Jodie Foster). A powerful young witch called Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) doesn’t yet know she’s a powerful young witch after her mother (Rashida Jones) decided to keep her talents hidden via a magic-suppressing bracelet (perfect merch op) forced on her wrist at a young age, a way to keep her safe in a world that does not take kindly to people like her. But as a rebellious teen, Billie discovers her true self and after a portal opens, she travels to the world of witches to team up with a three-eyed cat called Beef Roger Crummchuk (Walton Goggins, also a stuffed toy to be) to try to save her fellow witches from their evil queen.

It’s a story of mothers and daughters and how both can try to foster empathy for the other but even a lower-tier Disney film like Brave managed to teach this same lesson with far more skill and infinitely more heart. There’s no real joy or fizz in Billie’s discovery of her powers or ingenuity to how she then uses them and the film quickly starts to resemble not just a by-the-numbers, save-the-kingdom Disney tale but also a Marvel-like superhero adventure, especially in the numbingly effects-laden showdown finale. Foster has real command as a voice actor but her villain isn’t really villainous or distinctive enough, despite attempts to paint her as a recognisably authoritarian-like ruler. Goggins is a similarly effective vocal presence but, again, his sidekick isn’t written in a way that’s all that memorable with his dialogue, together with that of another anonymously underwritten owl sidekick, depressingly devoid of any spark or inventive humour. There’s also something a little cheap and inelegant about how he’s animated and coloured, similar to some purple-eyed henchwitches, who all look like they belong in a cheap Saturday morning cartoon not a big-budget Disney epic (the choice to score a giant action sequence with Demi Lovato’s Confident also feels notably unrefined). There’s an overly hectic style to too many scenes and a lack of grace to the set-pieces, more likely to induce a headache over a sense of awe, taking us further and further away from what used to elevate the studio far above its competitors.

There would be few greater big screen pleasures at this moment than a true return to form for Disney, an original, invigorating crowd-pleaser to rival what so many of us grew up watching and loving but Hexed is another hollow and glumly disappointing also-ran. Don’t tell Mickey but it’s perhaps telling that this month’s best new animated film about a rule-breaking goth girl dealing with spells and familial strife is actually on Netflix. Forget magic, the kingdom is in need of a miracle.

Hexed is out in US cinemas on 25 November, in Australian cinemas on 26 November and in the UK on 27 November

Oceans, fossil fuels and keeping 1.5 alive: the missed opportunities at Cop31

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:53:32 GMT

The collapse of the ‘Antalya pact’ took away the chance of a unifying effort to deal with a number of issues

The “Antalya pact” was supposed to be the keystone document agreed at the UN’s Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, but in the final days and hours countries became entrenched, leaving the pact dead in the water.

But what did it say, and what opportunities were missed when it died?

We take a look.

The 31st UN climate summit was the first to acknowledge the inevitable breach of the hard-won 2015 Paris climate goal to keep global heating to 1.5C, confirmed by scientists just months before. Nations most vulnerable to the climate crisis want to “keep 1.5 alive” with a pact that would promise that the world would keep trying. The final version of the pact said:

Reaffirms its resolve to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5C to limit both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot, recognizes the need for deep, rapid and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions in line with 1.5C pathways and resolves to close adaptation gaps and enhance action and support to enable countries and communities to better avert, prepare for, adapt to, respond to and recover from adverse climate impacts;

While many low-lying nations, in particular in the Pacific, thought this language was not strong enough, it would have become an important touchstone and a signal they had not been abandoned.

Co-hosts Turkey and Australia wanted to bring a voluntary goal to increase electrification around the world into a universally agreed pact.

Examples of electrification are swapping petrol- and diesel-powered vehicles to EVs, or changing gas cooking and water heaters to electric versions with heat pumps and induction hobs. They are all better for people’s health and a more efficient way to use energy.

Increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, alongside efforts to, inter alia, increase clean energy, improve energy efficiency, and enhance deployment of other low-emission technologies, alongside enhancing storage, system flexibility and modern and resilient grids, and improving energy access;

The Australian climate minister, Chris Bowen, insisted this shift was inevitable anyway, and said more than 90 countries had signed the voluntary “35 by 35” pledge.

Days before the final texts were presented to countries to ultimately negotiate in the plenary rooms, the draft Antalya pact had made a strong reference several times of a need to get off fossil fuels.

…… urges Parties to accelerate its implementation, including transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly and equitable manner; emphasizes the importance of phasing out inefficient fossil fuel subsidies that do not address energy poverty or just transitions, as soon as possible, building on the first global stocktake;

Calls for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.

While the global shift away from fossil fuels is happening, although uneven around the planet, the pact would have sent a strong message. But in the end, petro states including Saudi Arabia would not allow the words “fossil fuels” to be mentioned.

Carbon capture, utilisation and storage was pushed, in particular by Saudi Arabia, as a crucial set of technologies that had to be deployed at scale to help bring temperatures back down from the now inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C Paris temperature target.

But CCUS has mostly been deployed by fossil fuel companies so far, with one analyst saying it would have been a “a Trojan horse for fossil fuel interests”.

Increasing carbon capture, utilization and storage deployment with an aim to achieve gigatonne scale globally by 2035 as a collective global aspiration, and encouraging all actors, including industry, to scale up research and development recognizing the role of carbon capture, utilization and storage, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors;

For context, the Global CCS Institute says projects around the world have the capacity (if working properly, and they rarely do) to store 68m tonnes a year of CO2. This is less than 0.2% of the 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 emitted from burning fossil fuels in 2026.

“A teaspoon of carbon capture cannot excuse an ocean of fossil fuel expansion,” said Denise Cauchi from Climate Action Network Australia. “We dodged a bullet that would have put a gaping loophole in global climate agreements.”

But there are other carbon drawdown techniques that would also have been given a lift from the pact. Carbon dioxide removal technologies that pull CO2 from the atmosphere, such as “direct air-capture” projects and reforestation, would have been given approval. Done carefully and scaled up, they could help lower temperatures.

Cop co-president Australia wanted to make Antalya the summit where the ocean’s critical role in the climate crisis was acknowledged in a global pact. The ocean has absorbed more than 90% of the extra heat caused by human activity, and absorbs about a third of the extra CO2.

Expresses deep concern about the impacts of climate change on the ocean, livelihoods, food security, and biodiversity, including as a result of ocean warming and sea level rise, and recognizes the important contribution of sustainable ocean-based climate action to strengthening adaptation and resilience and advancing mitigation efforts while delivering benefits for communities and biodiversity;

References to the ocean were littered through the final-but-fated draft of the pact, in terms of its importance, and raised concerns about threats to scientific monitoring.

Some of these sections of the pact may have been saved by a late effort from Fiji, which asked for them to be considered separately by the conference. This was not passed, but it was moved into the convention process to be discussed by its subsidiary bodies.

Outside the Cop process, there is a voluntary global pledge to reduce methane emissions by 30% by 2030. The Antalya pact would have given a focus to these efforts.

Also recognizes that reductions in anthropogenic methane and other non-carbon dioxide emissions contribute to limiting the magnitude of peak warming, taking into consideration the fundamental priorities of safeguarding food security, livelihoods and respecting different cultural practices and national circumstances;

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas over time frames much shorter than CO2, and so reducing their levels in the atmosphere will mean quicker temperature reductions.

For all the missed opportunities highlighted here, the death of the pact does not mean those chances have gone. But a unifying pact would have helped drive campaigns, policy development, capital raising and climate action around the world.

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:39:00 GMT

After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia, which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along anyone human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang, and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Payton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

You Can See Everything’s chaotic battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:37:54 GMT

In Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, the protagonists and film-makers battle over who is the hero and who is the villain. It’s a fascinating insight into modern celebrity promotion

Don’t get the Close Up delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Thank you for signing up to the Close Up newsletter. This is our first-ever edition! And, just like on the show, I’ll be zooming in on the big culture questions and recommending things I’m obsessed with. I’ll also give you a sneak peek of what’s coming up on the show and what the team have been talking about behind the scenes.

OK, I’ll admit it: I wanted to hate You Can See Everything, the A24 documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, which finally arrived in UK cinemas last week. The marketing was slick, the hype was unparalleled. I didn’t believe a three-hour documentary about a disgraced tech CEO could be that good. But, like our colleague Adrian and basically every film critic who’s seen it, I left the cinema thinking: that was amazing and what on earth did I just watch?

In my 20s, I worked in corporate PR. Big companies employed our agency to promote their chief executives, tell the company’s story to the media and politicians, and protect everyone’s reputations. Our job, my job, was to create and control the narrative – to tell stories that made our clients the good guys. If you find the right angle, anyone can become the hero of a story. A betting company becomes one of the biggest employers on the UK high street, with bricks-and-mortar shops that provide much-needed jobs. An arms company is “one of the world’s leading manufacturers” – a national asset to be proud of. My colleagues were bright, young and talented. Most of them now work for big tech companies.

You Can See Everything is a chaotic and confusing battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes. Her husband Billy Evans’s version of the story is that a smart but overly trusting young woman who was manipulated by others (and is madly in love with her brilliant spouse). Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim encourage you to question Billy and Elizabeth’s relationship, presenting him as potentially controlling, narcissistic and money-hungry. Holmes, meanwhile, paints herself as misunderstood, innocent and unassuming, afraid of the limelight and at times Madonna-like. The appearance of Amanda Seyfried (who played Holmes in The Dropout, a 2022 TV drama about the CEO) is a much-needed pressure valve, in that she voices what most of the audience has been thinking for the first half of the film: what the hell is going on?. But even she attempts to shape the narrative around her portrayal of Holmes and the duty actors have to tell the truth about real-life subjects. At times, different versions of all these stories win out.

If I were advising Elizabeth Holmes on her image, I would have recommended she make a documentary. From Beyoncé to the Beckhams, biographical documentaries that let high-profile people construct a plausible-but-rose-tinted version of their lives have become part of the PR playbook. And a famous director is increasingly part of that package. Oscar-winning film-maker Fisher Stevens directed the David Beckham documentary, largely sidestepping the more uncomfortable aspects of Beckham’s public life, including allegations surrounding Rebecca Loos, along with any other controversies that might have harmed the family brand. Rick Rubin made an eight-part (!) docu-series about Jay-Z. Jon M Chu, who was behind Crazy Rich Asians and Wicked, directed two Justin Bieber documentaries.

I’m not sure I would have suggested Holmes invite Nathan Fielder to move into her home. That level of round the clock access makes it harder to control the image you present. But while You Can See Everything may not have been the film Holmes and Evans wanted, it has already changed the conversation around the former Theranos CEO.

A peek into what we’re obsessing about in our team WhatsApp group

In the Close Up group chat, we’re already planning our spring around two very specific things: hockey and yearning. 🏒💕

Season two of Heated Rivalry – the queer Canadian ice hockey romance that became one of this year’s biggest breakout shows – is dropping in April. That means more of hockey hotties Shane and Ilya, and more unhinged fan edits. And the same month, the second season of Amazon’s Off Campus (another sexy hockey series) is also out.

We’ve also been obsessed with the phrase “low-budget vagina, Amanda!” If you don’t know what I’m referring to, you need to watch this clip from the Real Housewives of London reunion that went viral last week. The internet did what it does best and there are already multiple club remixes, which we’ve been sharing nonstop. This is my favourite.
