On this Sunday’s culture swap, Lanre and I are watching classic films we’ve never seen. You’ll get to hear why I avoided the Terminator movies for so long, and Lanre’s very strong opinions about Richard Gere’s wardrobe and performance in Pretty Woman. My love for Julia Roberts runs deep – she is one of the ultimate film stars and such a joy to watch, even when the film itself falls short (see After the Hunt, Ticket to Paradise). So here are my top five movies starring the woman with the megawatt smile.

Pretty Woman | A plot that’s also a critique of financial capitalism, and chemistry so good that she and Gere reprised it for the unofficial sequel Runaway Bride. I stand by this film as Roberts’s best work.

Erin Brockovich | Based on a heartbreaking and inspiring true story of a woman’s fight to get justice for a community affected by groundwater contamination, this film rightly secured Roberts the Oscar for best actress.

Notting Hill | United with Richard Curtis and Hugh Grant for one of the ultimate 90s romcoms. And a supporting cast to die for (Rhys Ifans! Emma Chambers! Gina McKee!)

Mystic Pizza | An underrated cult classic about three young waitresses coming of age in coastal Connecticut. Inspired by a real restaurant that still exists.

Mona Lisa Smile | Art, education and womanhood – a lovely comfort watch.

What’s your favourite Julia movie? Are you a fellow Mystic Pizza obsessive? Will Steel Magnolias always have your heart? Let me know your thoughts by replying to this email, or contacting me via thecloseup@theguardian. com, and we may include them in a future newsletter.

Who needs perfume? The incredible link between body odour and relationships that last

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:32:08 GMT

The longer you have been with your partner, the more likely you are to find their natural scent arousing, according to a study from Radboud University in the Netherlands

Name: Body odour.

Age: Everyone has always smelled of something.

Function: Phwoar.

This cannot possibly be right. I just sat next to a guy on a bus, and his scent was definitely not phwoar. Let me ask you a question: are you in a long-term romantic relationship with this man?

No, of course not. Well, there’s your answer, then. If you were, you would have scientifically found his smell irresistible.

I’m not sure about that. Do not question science, especially not the paper just published by the Behavioural Science Institute at Radboud University in the Netherlands, which claims that the longer a couple have been together, the more likely they are to find each other’s body odour sexually arousing.

This doesn’t sound right. Trust me. Researchers got their subjects to fish out a T-shirt worn by their partner and sniff deeply from it, rating the smell by its pleasantness, intensity, and its soothing and sexually arousing aspects.

And what did they discover? Well, although you might assume that the smell of someone you’ve been going out with for a while would primarily feel safe and familiar, it actually just makes you quite horny.

So it isn’t like getting used to a bad smell? Absolutely not. The study found that odour-evoked sexual arousal grew throughout the duration of a relationship. People who had been together for 400 months were almost four times more likely to be aroused by smell than people who had just got together.

This is astounding. I just have to get someone used to my smell and they’ll fall in love with me. Hang on, it isn’t quite that simple.

Why is that? Because the study also found that smell wasn’t the be-all and end-all. When it comes to overall relationship satisfaction, there are more significant predictors.

Such as what? Such as personality and competence.

Oh no. And looks too, come to think of it.

This is a disaster! When will fate finally smile upon the useless and ugly and horrible? Hey, don’t be like that. There is someone out there for everyone. Maybe working on your natural scent is a good first step. Actually, what is your natural scent?

Well, I’m a chainsmoking durian fanatic who works in a fish factory and lives in a house made of burnt hair. There is lots to be said for longterm singledom too.

Maybe you can love me. Come here and smell my T-shirt. Smell it! Well, this has all been rather pleasant, but I’m afraid I must be off.

Do say: “Darling, I am aroused by your smell.”

Don’t say: “That said, would it be too much trouble to occasionally have a wash?”

‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:22:20 GMT

A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised?

Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked.

But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since.

Using his ideas on botanical form, he created designs strikingly at odds with the aesthetic of the times. He took the everyday – teapots, toast racks and pitchers – and made them unfamiliar and futuristic. But his achievements are now not widely known.

“Everyone knows about William Morris and the Arts and Craft movement,” says Ian Robinson, a collector of Dresser’s work. “Morris’s politics kept him in with the era’s movers and shakers, and subsequently on the radars of curators and historians. But Dresser was focused on technological developments and using mass production to bring design to every home, which didn’t sound as sexy. It’s interesting how history plays out in these stories. Dresser was embracing new methods; Morris was looking backwards.”

A new exhibition, Christopher Dresser: The Pursuit of Beauty at the Hub, a centre for craft and design in Sleaford, hopes to reinstate the designer’s legacy with a survey of his modernist ceramics, fluid glassware and sharply angular metalwork.

“Ask your friends if they’ve heard of Christopher Dresser, and nine times out of 10 they’ll say no,” says Joshua Lockwood, exhibitions manager and curator at the Hub. Robinson, who has lent work to the exhibition, is such a Dresser fan that he’s got one eye on an online auction for a piece while we talk on a video call.

“If I show people his designs, they recognise some pieces, such as the sugar bowl that Italian design brand Alessi brought back into production in the 1990s, but they don’t know who made them,” Robinson says. “He was the Terence Conran of his day, but he’s not remembered.”

Dresser was born in Glasgow and studied structure and science at the Government School of Design (later renamed the Royal College of Art) under influential academics architect Owen Jones and art critic Gottfried Semper. He became professor of artistic botany there himself, but after missing out on the chair of botany at London University in 1860, Dresser ditched academia and worked instead as a consultant for businesses such as Wedgwood pottery, Minton’s porcelain, Liberty of London and Tiffany & Co.

He created an experimental body of work, remarkable in terms of technology and influence. In his metalwork, Dresser experimented with unusual metal alloys and then cutting-edge processes such as electroplating to make exceptionally sleek household objects. He was co-founder and art director at Linthorpe Art Pottery, a revolutionary workshop set up in 1879 that was the first in the country to use gas-powered kilns. This innovation let Dresser develop his signature mottled glazes, and he designed over 1,000 vessels in the three years he worked there.

He travelled to Japan in 1876 on behalf of the South Kensington Museum (now the V&A), and helped start the Victorian craze for Japonisme. “That was his thing, to bring beautiful things to the home,” says Robinson. “He wanted to bring good design to as many people as possible. To buy Morris’s furniture you had to be very wealthy. Dresser mainly worked in silverplate or even painted tin. It was beautiful design but it was also affordable.”

Dresser’s family tried to continue his design studio after his death in 1904, but when that proved unsuccessful they disposed of all his account books and drawings, effectively destroying his archive. “I think they burned everything,” says Robinson. “All the documents were lost and it wasn’t until the 1970s that anyone started looking into his work again.”

Designers Philippe Starck, Terence Conran and Alberto Alessi have all expressed admiration for Dresser’s ability to bridge great design, mass production and respect for the middle-class consumer; and artists such as ceramicist Magdalene Odundo and sculptor Alice Channer have been influenced by the sleek, sinuous botanical shapes that define his work. Odundo saw Dresser’s ceramics at the British Museum as a student, and was inspired by the way he pulled ideas together to create something new, rather than to emulate what already exists. Her work will also be on show at the Hub alongside Channer and artists Coco Crampton and Gabriele Beveridge.

“Hopefully this exhibition will bring more awareness of Dresser,” says Lockwood. “Not just his production of objects but that his work has lineage. This history hasn’t really been told and I want to bring this wonderful designer to the forefront.”

Christopher Dresser: The Pursuit of Beauty is at the Hub, Sleaford, from 28 November to 7 March

More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 16:00:50 GMT

Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa

When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.

In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.

Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.

“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.

Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.

Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.

A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.

“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

Senegal restored as Africa Cup of Nations champions after court ruling

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 14:22:36 GMT

Senegal won January’s final 1-0 after walking off

Result was overturned in March as 3-0 win for Morocco

Senegal have been reinstated as the champions of Africa, and their controversial 1-0 victory against Morocco confirmed in the record books, after the scandal over January’s Africa Cup of Nations final was resolved in a Swiss courtroom.

The court of arbitration for sport (Cas) ruled that a decision to award the 2025 Afcon title to Morocco on appeal should be set aside. Senegal celebrated with a social media post proclaiming the team to have won the title twice: first on the field and then at Cas. Morocco, who are due to co-host the World Cup in 2030, declared their intention to “pursue all legal avenues” to challenge the ruling.

A Cas panel of three legal experts agreed unanimously that the original result should stand because of the primacy of decisions made on “the field of play”. The referee’s decision to complete the fixture was held to be a definitive act that could not be overturned by Senegal’s breach of Afcon’s rules when they walked off and caused a 15-minute delay in one of the most notorious encounters in the competition’s history.

The final was held in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, on 18 January. With the match goalless in second-half added time, the then Senegal coach, Pape Thiaw, withdrew his team from the field in protest at Morocco being awarded a penalty, shortly after Senegal had a goal disallowed. After Senegal returned to the pitch, Brahim Díaz missed the spot-kick with a Panenka. Senegal went on to win with a goal in extra time.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

The result caused huge ructions in African football and became a media sensation. An initial appeal by the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) to the Confederation of African Football (Caf) argued that Senegal’s behaviour had contravened Afcon rules, which prevent teams from leaving the field without the referee’s authorisation. The argument was accepted by a Caf appeal board, which overturned the result in March, awarding Morocco the title in a 3-0 walkover.

Senegal responded with an appeal, and an in-person hearing took place behind closed doors at Cas on 8 October. Cas verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland’s supreme court only on limited procedural grounds.

The judging panel concluded that the “field of play doctrine” which prevents the court from reviewing decisions taken on the pitch by match officials must hold sway, and that because the referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had not chosen to call the match off the result should stand.

“By blowing his whistle to resume his match at the 109th minute the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” said Matthieu Reeb, the director general of Cas. “Both teams were on the pitch again and both expressed their willingness to resume. The Cas panel found that the referee’s decision fell solely within the scope of the rules of the game and was therefore within his sole authority. The Caf rules [Afcon regulations] would have been applicable if the referee had blown the final whistle which would have resulted in Senegal’s forfeit loss, but this was not the case.”

In a trenchant statement the FRMF announced its determination to continue fighting the result, saying it “reaffirms its determination to pursue all available legal avenues to challenge this Cas decision”.

The FRMF argued that the Cas decision “failed to take into account the stance recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (Ifab) and the International Federation of Association Football (Fifa) regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee’s authorisation, as well as the associated responsibilities and disciplinary sanctions”.

It also expressed “astonishment” that Cas had not delayed its verdict after being presented with claims by the FRMF that one of the three panel members, Professor Dr Ulrich Haas, had a private telephone conversation with the president of the Senegalese Football Federation on Sunday.

Cas said: “The [international council of arbitration for sport] challenge commission found that there was not enough evidence at the time of the challenge to delay the issuing of the decision. Ulrich Haas strongly denies any direct contact at any moment with the parties involved in this procedure.”

Senegal’s Sadio Mané said on Instagram that the Cas decision “fills us with joy”. He spoke of the “efforts and sacrifices everyone has put into for this second star” and thanked fans for their support. He also expressed solidarity with Morocco, saying: “Senegal and Morocco are two brother peoples. May the passion of football continue to bring us closer.”

Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 14:11:15 GMT

Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next

For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017.

The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel.

Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove: If Benjamin Netanyahu were prosecuted, it would be hard for the prosecution to show that he had the necessary specific intent to kill Palestinians “as such” (the term used in international law) given his frequently proclaimed intention to liquidate Hamas as a political organisation.

This distinction may be legalistic, but it stems from the definition of the crime. Hence Pol Pot’s henchpeople could not be prosecuted for genocide for killing about 1.7 million Cambodian citizens, because of their crazed political intention to return the country to “year zero”. This might be termed “politicide” but that is not a crime under international law. The distinction was the basis of Myanmar’s defence that its intention was to conduct counterinsurgency operations to clear out terrorists. But the court examined the history of the conflict and conducted its own investigation, which established the racial and religious roots of the massacres.

The intention of an individual defendant may be difficult to fathom, but to discern the “mind” of a state the court must draw inferences from a much wider set of facts, including the historical context of the atrocities and the previous behaviour of the government – for example, whether it has introduced apartheid-type laws oppressing or discriminating against the targeted group and whether its ministers have used hate speech against the group. Israel is vulnerable on these grounds.

Although the court insisted that the burden of proof required the evidence against the state to be “fully conclusive” (ie beyond reasonable doubt), the means of establishing liability will be inferential rather than direct. As one influential judge, Prof Hilary Charlesworth, put it, the true test of state liability is whether genocide is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence as a whole.

The evidence against Israel includes the destruction of 90% of Gaza’s infrastructure and about 75,000 deaths so far (compared with an estimated 10,000 deaths in Rakhine state and about 43,000 in the blitz). This disproportionality alone means that Israel will have a case to answer.

Israel may also be discomforted by the way the ICJ examined and interpreted the actual atrocities in Myanmar. In order to assist the inference of genocide, it focused on the killing of children – usually an indication of an intention to stop the propagation of part of a race. It drew attention to sexual violence for the same reason and to the shooting of soldiers as they were running away or after their capture. This showed that they were not simply engaged in a “clearance operation”. Importantly, the court made the point that state actions may have a number of purposes – if racial or religious hatred is among them, it may be arraigned for genocide.

The further advantage of indicting a state is that it may be ordered, as Myanmar was, to provide compensation, to pay for rebuilding and to allow the return of those of the targeted group who have fled. The government can be ordered to prosecute those of its politicians or army commanders who personally directed the genocidal attacks. This is important because individual defendants, by the time they appear in the dock of the international criminal court (like Ratko Mladić and his generals found guilty of genocide at Srebrenica), have no power and little money. States like Myanmar and (especially) Israel, have both.

Will the court’s orders be enforced? The genocide convention requires all 154 states’ signatories to assist, and Britain has made a tiny effort to do so by expelling Myanmar’s military attache. But nations must go much further by imposing severe economic sanctions and seizing bank accounts traceable to members of the junta.

The ICJ has no police to enforce its judgment – this is the duty of the UN security council, which is now a useless body, pole-axed by vetoes allotted to its permanent members and wielded in their own interest by Russia and China and by the US in the interest of Israel.

It was deeply ironic that on the same day as the judgment against Myanmar was delivered, three men accused of crimes against humanity – Putin, Trump and Xi – met in Shenzhen to announce that they have agreed “the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the ICC and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Decoded, this meant that international courts should not prosecute them or their officials for crimes against humanity.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Putin has without doubt committed the crime of aggression by invading Ukraine and starting a war that has caused the death of nearly 500,000 Russians since 2022. Trump has unlawfully invaded Iran, killing its supreme leader and 120 children on the first day alone. Xi awaits condemnation for persecuting Uyghurs and keeps threatening the option of invading Taiwan. This trio is opposed to any form of justice, international or otherwise, and Trump has already begun to “dismantle” (in Marco Rubio’s words) the ICC, with wide-ranging sanctions on its judges and its staff.

At least it will be difficult for Trump to dismantle the genocide convention, because the US’s ratification was the work of Ronald Reagan. Of course, the crime of genocide should be redefined to include the destruction of groups for political or cultural reasons, but in these difficult days for international justice, the convention at least offers states the possibility of making other states accountable for some heinous crimes.

The ICJ may yet decide – probably in 2028 – that Israel has been guilty of genocide. Any action on that verdict would be vetoed by the US if Trump is still in power. But this weakness in the enforcement mechanism of the UN does not mean that ICJ decisions are inconsequential. It is a court that declares the content of international law, and however much the result may be resented by governments and their immoral leaders, its verdicts represent the still, small voice of truth and justice.

Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond

Ministers approve fast-track disability payments in England and Wales

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 13:30:46 GMT

Benefit claims made easier in first stage of shake-up of welfare system

Disabled people with severe and lifelong conditions will be able to claim disability benefits more easily after a major review of the system by ministers.

The Department for Work and Pensions said on Tuesday it would immediately commit to speeding up the personal independence payment (Pip) system for adults in England and Wales who have severe conditions or ones that are unlikely to change.

Ministers are working on a broader response, however, which the Guardian understands is likely to include cuts to cash payments for those who do not meet the threshold for the new fast-track system.

The proposals will be included in a white paper to be published next year as the first step in what is likely to be the biggest shake-up of the welfare system in over a decade.

Stephen Timms, the minister for social security and disability who led the review, said: “The Timms review’s interim report was clear that while Pip is valued, the system is no longer fit for purpose.

“That’s why the government is today accepting two of its key recommendations: reducing unnecessary award reviews for people whose health conditions are lifelong, progressive or unlikely to improve, and introducing a fast-track route for people with severe, well-evidenced conditions and those nearing the end of life.

“These changes are a first step to building a system which gives greater security for those with the most severe conditions.”

The recommendations were broadly welcomed by campaigners and disability charities who said the report, drawn up in consultation with disabled people, provided the basis for a potentially fairer and more compassionate system.

But there is widespread nervousness that some claimants will fail to qualify for cash payments under a new “impact assessment” of needs. Campaigners will seek assurances that vulnerable people are not left without a financial lifeline.

Alexa Knight of the Mental Health Foundation said: “No one receiving Pip should be pushed into deeper poverty as a result of these changes, even in the short term. The consequences for individuals and their families can be devastating if support is removed before suitable alternatives are in place.”

Timms began his review last year after Keir Starmer’s government dropped a plan to cut the Pip system by £5bn in the face of a backlash from backbench MPs.

Timms defended those proposed cuts as a minister at the time, warning that without spending reductions the welfare bill would become unsustainable. The Office for Budget Responsibility has forecast that without changes, spending on Pips will rise from around £16bn in 2019-20 to just over £41bn by the end of the decade.

His final report, which was written with disability rights advocates Sharon Brennan and Clenton Farquharson, does not identify any specific areas where the overall bill could be cut.

Instead, Timms makes a series of recommendations to make the system easier to use for people with serious conditions and more tailored for those with less severe needs.

after newsletter promotion

The report recommends a fast-track route for people with what Timms calls “severe, well-evidenced conditions”. It also proposes reducing the number of reviews for those with lifelong or degenerative conditions and making sure these reviews look only at what has changed rather than starting from scratch.

For others, the report calls for the system to be changed so that it better suits their needs, rather than paying out the current set rates of up to £194.60 a week.

Those who are not being fast tracked will undergo an assessment on how their condition affects their daily life to decide what cash payment they should receive. The government should spend more on face-to-face assessments, the report recommends.

The Department for Work and Pensions said the new system would “help disabled people achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence”.

Timms insists that cash payments should remain at the heart of the system, unlike Alan Milburn, who recommended in a separate report on youth joblessness that under-25s should no longer be able to claim Pip. Milburn recommended the money saved should be spent instead on schemes to help young people get into the workplace.

Ministers are now working on a formal government response, which is expected next month before a white paper in the spring.

If they follow the proposals made by Milburn and Timms, it will lead to two separate welfare systems where those aged 25 and over can claim disability benefits but younger adults cannot.

Timms’ report does leave space, however, for ministers to save money from Pip by reducing cash payments to many of those who claim it.

The Guardian has been told that ministers are working on a Pip system that would apply the Milburn model of extra work and training support combined with cash cuts for all ages who do not meet the threshold for the new fast-track system.

$150 for photos of Melania looking like a waxwork? Will the Trumps ever run out of money-making ideas?

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 13:20:28 GMT

From the first lady’s Amazon documentary to Barron’s energy drink, the family is raking it in during Donald’s second term. And that includes the president

Melania Trump is not a regular mom. She’s “a very cool mom”. We know this because she says so in her very cool new TV docuseries, which no one asked for, but which Amazon made anyway. I should clarify that Melania: The Series is not to be confused with Melania, the 104-minute-long $75m (£57m) movie Amazon released earlier this year. You know, the one an industry insider called “the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing”. Various people insinuated nasty things about alleged corruption when that film came out, but I think it’s sweet how patriotic Amazon seems to be.

While our cup may runneth over with Melania content, I have good news for first lady fans. We’ve been graced with even more Melania merch. At the weekend, Melania announced an “exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed photographer Ellen von Unwerth” to complement her new docuseries. For the non-refundable price of $150 (£115) you get one black-and-white digital image of the first lady sitting on a chair and one photo in which she is posing next to a clapperboard. According to Melania’s website, she and “Ms von Unwerth worked collaboratively during a two-day shoot to develop this visual narrative”.

Von Unwerth is known for her provocative and playful fashion photography; far be it from me to tell her how to do her job. But I’m going to do so anyway because I can think of way more appropriate visual narratives. She could, for example, have had the first lady wearing her “I really don’t care, do u?” jacket (the one she wore while visiting jailed migrant children) and jumping in a pool full of money like Scrooge McDuck. Or Von Unwerth, who was briefly a magician’s assistant, could have leaned into Vogue’s description of Melania looking like a “freelance magician” in her official portrait, and had her waving a wand, turning Jeff Bezos into a toad.

All I’m saying is that for $150, I’d expect a bit more of Von Unwerth’s signature style. The German photographer once said she loves seeing women “being powerful and oozing femininity and oozing their personality”, but there’s no oozing in the new Melania photos; an anaconda couldn’t squeeze a drop of personality out of them. The first lady just looks how she always looks to me: like a Madame Tussauds waxwork figure who was brought to life by an evil sorcerer.

Still, I suppose you don’t need much personality when you’re oozing money. The entire Trump family has turned Donald’s second term into an unprecedented wealth-building opportunity. According to the president’s financial disclosure report, released in June, Melania earned about $17m in 2025 from her Amazon documentary and other ventures, including her coffee-table memoir and collectibles. And the collectibles keep coming: as well as the new $150 photos, Melania’s website is hawking a $90 limited-edition 2026 Christmas ornament called the “Starlight Star”. Which is weird, since Melania is on record saying: “Who gives a fuck about Christmas?” Still, I suppose it is holiday grifting season.

Barron Trump, meanwhile, has learned a lot from his cool mom, and has lucrative crypto interests and an energy drink venture. Kai Trump, Donald’s granddaughter, is also hawking a soft drink, along with a clothing collection. Lara Trump (Eric’s wife) has an activewear line. Eric and Donald Jr, the large adult sons, are making a fortune on defence tech. And Jared Kushner seems to be profiting from his father-in-law’s foreign policy adventures.

As for the president, is there a pie he doesn’t have his little fingers in? Dwarfing this week’s windfall from Nvidia, Trump made at least $2.2bn in the first year of his second term, largely from his family’s crypto dealings. Indeed, while Melania was promoting her new photo collection over the weekend, Donald was throwing his third cryptocurrency gala at his Virginia golf club for top investors in the $Trump meme coin, which has earned the Trump family about $635m. The coin’s value crashed recently, but gala attenders were consoled with a goody bag containing a Trump “victory” perfume, and a commemorative poster. A lucky few even got a “Trump 18K gold watch”. It’s all very depressing, but the political tides are turning and investigations into Trump’s family finances are in the works. I don’t need a gold watch to tell you the president’s time is finally running out.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 13:19:22 GMT

Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. The stale previous seasons are fast becoming a mere memory

When Nigella Lawson helps crown the new champion of The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday night, two other winners will also be celebrating: the show itself and broadcaster Channel 4. The fabled “Nigella effect” has freshened up a franchise that was beginning to taste distinctly stale.

Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence.

She has certainly been a raising agent in ratings terms. Terrestrial TV is in a state of managed decline nowadays but Bake Off has bucked the trend. Viewing figures overtook Strictly Come Dancing this series, with the first episode drawing 7.1 million viewers compared with 6.4 million for the BBC’s Saturday night flagship’s launch show. This might ring alarm bells in the ballroom. Perhaps the BBC needs to find a hoofing equivalent of Lawson to put some pep in its dance step.

Ahead of Tuesday’s all-male, all-25-or-under grand final – doing doughy battle are law student Mo Mahir, political economy graduate Moyin Odeniran and hairdresser Tom Whittaker, a three-time Star Baker and the bookies’ favourite – the new judge’s debut run can be deemed a resounding hit.

After nine weeks in the tent, Lawson feels like a fixture. It’s strange to think that she had to be persuaded to accept the job in the first place. The 66-year-old food writer was understandably nervous about joining such a beloved franchise, uncertain whether she had sufficient baking expertise.

In fact, media coverage has been overwhelmingly positive. Critics have hailed her as the “icing on the cake”. As producers reassured her, Lawson was hired to talk about taste rather than technicalities. After she went viral for taking large forkfuls, she unrepentantly explained: “I like to be able to taste things properly. I’m an eater. Eating is my superpower.” When Hollywood described a chocolate cookie as “indulgent and naughty”, she shot back: “I don’t approve of talking about food as naughty. We need to take our pleasures where we can in life.”

She’s passionate about flavour and conveys that sensory experience to audiences. Hollywood would happily admit that he’s a master baker, not a natural wordsmith. By contrast, Lawson is a bestselling author and former literary editor with the vocabulary to match. She relishes wrapping her mouth around tasty descriptions almost as much as the treats themselves. When she purred the word “sumptuous” in her debut episode, co-presenter Noel Fielding said: “I think I might be pregnant.”

Cakes have been “bejewelled with embellishments”. Stout in a sponge added “a ferrous tang … a savage bite”. Spiced gingerbread showed “elegant restraint”. Pasties were “plump little pillows”. A fortnight ago, Lawson compared Mo’s nougatine showstopper to “a Renaissance sculpture”. Remember when her pronunciation of microwave as “mee-cro-wah-vay” was nominated for Bafta’s TV moment of the year? Bake Off viewers went almost as wild when she rolled her Rs while pronouncing “Parmigiano Reggiano” and renamed Worcestershire sauce “Worcester shushter” (“we always call it that at home”).

When she’s not rhapsodising, Lawson imbues proceedings with a certain regal campness. She glides around the tent with an impish twinkle in her eye, greeting any innuendo with an arched eyebrow or “Boys, behave”. She has serious star presence, bringing glamour, wit and poise to the home-spun contest. Her arrival has been accompanied by format tweaks, including an Audience Choice week, pantry-raiding challenges and baking from illustrations rather than recipes. After 16 years, it’s helped rejuvenate the show.

Lawson’s quotable utterances, hearty mouthfuls and reaction faces make her highly meme-able. For all 86-year-old Leith’s qualities, being a social media darling wasn’t one of them. The only time she went viral is when she accidentally tweeted her congratulations to the 2017 winner, six hours before the final was broadcast. Talk about a spoiler.

Lawson’s relationship with the bakers is sweetly supportive. If Hollywood is their stern teacher, Lawson is their worshipped big sister. He issues firm handshakes; she dispenses warm cuddles. Yet she’s no soft touch as a judge. She gives constructive criticism, generously sharing tips on how to improve. As has become a running joke, this often involves adding salt.

When a challenge involves one of Lawson’s own recipes, she vibrates with pleasure and the bakers are desperate to impress. Several have hailed her as “an inspiration”. They light up with pride when she praises them, gazing awestruck across their workbenches. Semi-finalist Gabe called her “iconic”. Tom said he wanted a Nigella air kiss more than a Hollywood handshake.

Before the series aired, tabloids stoked rumours of tension between the judging duo. On the contrary, Lawson and Hollywood have fizzing chemistry. More than her predecessors Leith and Mary Berry – as he says, he’s gone “Dame, Dame, Queen” – Nigella gives ol’ blue eyes a run for his money. Their back-and-forth veers from mildly flirtatious to spiky differences of opinion, often within the same conversation. She teasingly calls him “The Professor” or “Mr Precision”, and promised to beat him in an arm wrestle. If this was a romcom, they’d be a textbook will-they-or-won’t they couple. (Rest assured, they won’t.)

When Lawson’s casting was announced, she correctly called Bake Off a “national treasure”. Well, she should know. With her first-name recognition factor and dazzling full-beam charm, Queen Nigella has single-handedly given the show a new lease of life. Applications to enter next year’s contest are said to be “booming”. Channel 4 bosses are so happy, they’ve signed her up for a second series, reportedly for £500,000. Long may she reign.

The Great British Bake Off final airs on Tuesday 24 November at 8pm on Channel 4.

I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 12:00:46 GMT

A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us?

Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy.

What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society.

“Few would argue that family life is unimportant,” I had written. “Yet authoritarian movements have long politicized it, reframing it as women’s sole purpose and a substitute for autonomy and rights.”

Wayne, whose name I’ve changed out of an overabundance of generosity and grace, didn’t read the article as a structural critique, but a personal attack. With his wife CC’ed, he wrote with a bloviator’s panache: “One assumes you’re neither wife nor mother, and older than my beautiful 33 y/o wife, Liz.”

He continued: “You might think you’re truly happy and empowered, but clearly, you’re not.”

Because I am currently without children by choice, and am not struggling with loss or infertility, Wayne’s missive struck me less as hurtful than as bewilderingly absurd.

Things only got stranger from there.

Wayne went on to tell me that Liz – whose name I also changed – on hiatus from nursing school, stays with the couple’s three children at home in the Pacific north-west and has had “four miscarriages”, her husband seemed to brag. “Three in the last year.”

That was an intimate detail to offer, but Wayne wasn’t finished. He attached photos of all his children to the email, their names in the jpeg files.

I looked at their lovely faces and thought: “Does this man think I’ve never seen children?”

I didn’t reply.

A year passed, and Liz had another baby. I know this because shortly after the birth, Wayne sent me pictures of the tiny infant, their “latest miracle”, swaddled in blue.

“It’s never too late to do the right thing,” Wayne wrote. “Find a good man. Get married. Have a family.”

This time, I had to ask him: “Wayne, do you send unsolicited pictures of your children to other strangers, or just me?”

Just me, he responded. “The better question is, ‘Why did I send them to you?’ The answer: so, you can see what you’re giving up. You’re literally giving up everything.”

Wayne and Liz had formed an idea of me as a person whose reproductive choices looked different from theirs. On that much they were right, though several of their assumptions were off. I do, for instance, have a good man in my life, though that phrase makes me want to eat a brick.

Wayne felt he must command me of what I should do, reproductively and existentially, in order to be “happy”. His family was blissfully content, he told me – and yet, there he was, in a house with three little ones and a fresh baby, emailing a person he had never met, fretting over whether I would miss my chance to replicate his life.

I was curious to learn more about this couple and suggested an in-person interview, but while they claimed I was welcome at their church, their tone veered hostile.

“I don’t care if you die childless, it’s probably for the best,” Liz wrote. “Let those who believe in the future inherit it.”

I was surprised by how angry Wayne and Liz were. After all, I wasn’t the one reaching out to them repeatedly with gloating updates on my clean house and uninterrupted nights of sleep.

What’s it to them how I die? And why can’t they leave me in peace?

While I think my experience with Wayne and Liz was particularly surreal, it’s becoming strikingly common for people to opine on each other’s reproductive choices. Parents become mindless “breeders” on forums like Reddit’s r/childfree; while the childfree are sad losers who stand to be eaten by their own cats. Nobody is spared criticism.

Take, for instance, one-and-done parents. You might think they were beyond reproach, tasteful minimalists who did their part for the species. Nope.

Writer Jessica Valenti recently took to social media describing a “really intense backlash against moms of only children”. Whenever a mother who has decided to just have one child posts a video about how much she enjoys her life, the comments are a wreck. Why?

“The thing that seems to set people off the most is when women talk about enjoying their lives,” particularly their free time, she says. She argues this backlash reinforces conservative propaganda portraying good motherhood as requiring women to sacrifice their identities, personal interests or public lives.

Valenti is absolutely right; there are political and religious dimensions to trying to control the reproductive choices of others – including the idea that having too much free time and too few children makes a woman “immoral” or “a threat” to interests of the nation. Procreative choices are becoming increasingly politicized, with Erika Kirk infamously advising the Turning Point USA Women’s Leadership Summit to have “more kids than you can afford” (try enjoying your free time then).

Writers such as Tia Levings explore how Christian patriarchy works to convince women that happiness is a sole product of their all-consuming devotion to a controlling system that doesn’t keep them or their children safe. Criticism of that system is not tantamount to personal criticism of any large family itself, but it’s understandable that it may feel provocative – especially when so many of us seem to be picking sides.

Families with things in common have taken to “conceiving themselves as an identity group”, says Anastasia Berg, co-author of What Are Children For? On Ambivalence and Choice, a book on seriously contemplating the question of motherhood. Each group, she says, seeks “camaraderie and self-understanding, then defines themselves in terms of what uniquely they have”.

For the childfree, it may be freedom and flexibility; for parents, the experience of special bonds. People in different groups, she says, can see each other’s goods and start thinking, “Well, that’s a slight against me.”

In her research, Berg found it was often the case that people feel pressured toward whichever reproductive choice they didn’t make. Whether they have kids or not, “People are very sensitive to affirmation of the opposite choice,” she says. This perspective can make each side feel stigmatized by the other – every choice is against the grain.

Maybe the aspect of reproductive choice that is most triggering is the idea of parenthood as being a choice at all.

The freedom to control our reproductive destinies is relatively new; the concept of abstaining from parenthood by choice, let alone being vocal and positive about that decision, is newer still. Having children was once a default position, and those without them were stigmatized and pitied.

That norm is broken. A 2024 Pew survey found that 57% of adults under 50 without children say they’re unlikely to ever have children because they just don’t want them.

“I remember one gentleman I was talking to quite literally responded, ‘What do you mean choose?’” to have children, says Keltie Maguire, a coach who helps people decide whether they want to become parents. For those who never questioned parenthood, the existence of an alternate path can be deeply confronting. “Nobody wants the thing they like to be the wrong choice,” says Maguire. Seeing someone happy with a different life can feel like a dismissal of the sacrifices they made to build their own – three miscarriages in a year, for instance.

Left to ferment, pangs of impotent rancor can harden into something akin to what the philosopher Max Scheler, building on Nietzsche, called ressentiment: a “self-poisoning of the mind”.

Rather than live with the sting of seeing a good in someone else’s life that you don’t have, you come to believe it was never a good at all. Scheler thought this distortion happened below conscious thought. Operating from such a place, we might believe we see other people’s lives more clearly than even they do. And unable to actually change them, we may settle for “imaginary revenge”: the fantasy of the day they realize they’re as bereft as we’ve decided they are.

Sometimes, the urge to rescue is hostility in disguise.

Madeline Lillis, a 31-year-old childfree content creator who works with children as a speech pathologist, says some commenters seem determined to change her mind. “I will have somebody who, it appears, genuinely does not like my content … then they decide it is their mission to get me to see the light,” and have children.

Lillis has built her platform around the idea of providing realistic, neutral perspectives on life with and without kids. Still, when commenters come at her, it “definitely feels like they’re defending something. They feel this urge to prove to you that their choice was the best one.”

“The most common comment I get is that I’m going to be lonely in my old age,” says Lillis.

Ah yes, that old chestnut, the threat of misery, as if sadness and loneliness are not inevitable elements of the human condition, part and parcel with everything else a person feels.

Take it from Berg, who overcame initial ambivalence and became a parent, that happiness makes a poor case for parenthood: if you’re having children because “‘I want to get some happiness out of it,’” she told me, “there’s gonna be a lot of moments where you’re gonna want to jump out the window.” Whatever you want from a child, “they’re going to exceed that. And they’re gonna disappoint that.”

When Jaime Fisher, 43, was raising her four children, she never heard any counter-narratives to the idea that people felt anything but blissed-out to become a mother. “It’s only something I’ve seen widespread in the last four to five years of my life,” says the content creator, who has spoken on topics including her experience of maternal regret.

“I have found so much freedom, delight, and even joy watching women who are childfree get to tell their own stories,” says Fisher, “how they’ve enjoyed it or not enjoyed it. Because for so long, women weren’t allowed to share their own narratives.”

Not everyone is equipped to see the good in a path they never knew was open to them.

“I think many people have a weak worldview and they don’t even know it. Which is why it becomes so tender the minute you press on it,” she says.

Some, like Wayne, brandishing his children like a despot’s spoils, dictate what others should do in an effort to exercise the authority they crave. “I don’t think a lot of people have recognized the narcissism or the arrogance,” of wanting to control the narrative of what makes a good life, says Fisher.

Fisher is right, there is no one way to live a good life. There’s no data to show that older people are any more regretful, with or without kids; there’s no reason to feel like you’re doing something bad if you want no, one, or six children.

There is, however, research affirming that social networks that “bridge”, or include people with different life circumstances, are beneficial for everyone’s cognitive health, as well as provide practical help, and expose members to a wider range of life experiences. In healthy societies parents and non-parents are seen and included to the benefit of all.

Presented with the choice to build community or fight on the internet, it’s clear which would make us happier. Whether to have children isn’t so simple, and no one can promise you’ll be happier either way. But that’s OK. Your choices don’t have to make you happy. They just have to be yours.

‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 12:00:45 GMT

Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out

The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff.

Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event.

The concerns were ignored for nearly a decade, according to multiple sources, who said employees would instead warn each other to avoid him. It was not until 2023 when managers took action and brought in the City law firm Allen & Overy to investigate the allegations.

At least five women spoke to the inquiry, some with first-hand experience of the alleged misconduct. Walliams was never interviewed. His lawyers subsequently said he denied all allegations of harassment or inappropriate behaviour in the workplace.

The inquiry quietly wrapped up in early 2024 with no consequences at the time for the author. Walliams, whose bestselling children’s books have been compared to those of Roald Dahl, went on to publish a further five books before HarperCollins severed ties with him in December 2025.

Several former employees said they believed the inquiry was a means to shut down complaints. One, who would only speak anonymously, said: “It was not an inquiry, it was a cover-up.”

For one woman who spoke to the inquiry, it led to the end of her career at the publishing company. She was reportedly given a five-figure payout.

She told the Guardian and ITV News she wanted to speak out but could not. It is understood she is prevented from doing so because she was gagged by a strict non-disclosure agreement (NDA) as part of her settlement.

The women questioned were told they could not discuss anything related to the inquiry or their concerns about Walliams, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the process, and they still feel unable to speak openly.

The development comes after a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News revealed accusations that Walliams used his celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex. Two were aged 15 when he first contacted them. Walliams’ lawyers said he denied being a sexual predator or abusing his power.

Walliams is now the focus of an investigation by the Metropolitan police into separate “serious sexual misconduct” allegations. Walliams earlier told the Guardian and ITV News he had not broken the law.

The new claims about HarperCollins’ handling of complaints raise significant questions for the Rupert Murdoch-owned company, one of the biggest publishers in the world.

Leading figures said the law should not be used to silence concerns about inappropriate behaviour in the workplace. Zelda Perkins, who broke an NDA to reveal the sexual misconduct of the Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein and is currently speaking to the UK government about further changing the law to prevent their misuse, said: “Nobody can ever understand what having your voice taken away means.”

Victoria Barnsley, who was the chief executive of HarperCollins in the UK until 2013, said it was “absolutely outrageous” how the company allegedly dealt with its bestselling author. She said it was not right that the women “have to move to other companies or be forced out or paid off. That really shouldn’t be happening.”

A spokesperson for the publisher said: “We are shocked by the allegations contained in the ITV and Guardian reporting relating to teenage girls.

“HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams. We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously.”

When the Guardian and ITV News published the allegations against Walliams, Kate Elton, who took over as CEO of HarperCollins UK in October last year, made a short online address to employees. Apparently reading from a written statement, she explained that she decided to stop publishing Walliams shortly after taking over as chief executive, and that “it was a decision I felt had to be taken”.

Elton, who has worked at HarperCollins since 2011, spoke about the “deeply upsetting accounts” in the news reports and said she wished she did not have to speak to staff about the situation. She went on to reassure people that their wellbeing was important to the company: “If you ever have any concerns or issues, you can speak up in confidence and you will be heard.”

Elton’s address to staff contrasts with accounts from multiple sources who said women tried to raise concerns or blow the whistle on the star author, only to be ignored by managers or shut down by the lawyer-run inquiry.

Walliams was signed up to HarperCollins’ children’s division and in 2008 published his first book, The Boy in the Dress, which proved an immediate hit. He went on to become the UK’s fourth-bestselling author since accurate records began, publishing more than 40 children’s titles and generating around £156m of sales in the UK alone.

It was this commercial success that several former employees said they believed protected the author.

“Because he was responsible for HarperCollins hitting [its] targets every year, nothing ever happened,” said one woman who shared her misgivings about Walliams’ behaviour with managers in 2015.

Another woman, who worked in the children’s division in 2017, said that in her opinion: “If he hadn’t been making them money, if he hadn’t been this big TV guy … they would have got rid of him.”

Several sources said they believed the reluctance to tackle concerns about Walliams came from the top, linking it to Charlie Redmayne, who succeeded Barnsley in 2013 and left suddenly in October 2025, two months before Walliams was dropped. Redmayne did not respond to requests for comment.

In spring 2015, Walliams separated from his wife, Lara Stone. A few months later, a junior member of staff showed a manager emails she had received from him. He had met the young woman at a book promotion event in a primary school, then asked her out over email, and tried again a few months later, according to the manager.

Lawyers for Walliams said he had messaged the woman when he was “heartbroken and lonely after his divorce and was hoping to meet someone to spend time with”. It is understood the woman ignored his emails.

“She was just so young,” said the employee who saw the emails. “It’s just not appropriate for an author to be messaging a member of staff like that.”

She said she brought the incident to the attention of the human resources (HR) department, but that she felt she was ignored. It was one of at least six occasions, the Guardian and ITV News were told, when women alerted management to their concerns about what they felt was Walliams’ inappropriate conduct.

In 2017, Walliams started a sexual relationship with a junior employee, according to multiple sources. He met the young woman, who was an intern for the company, at a promotional book event at a school. She was later sent to his house alone to deliver paperwork. She was in her mid-20s and Walliams was 45. The woman told colleagues that while it was consensual looking back she considered the relationship to be the result of “an abuse of power”.

after newsletter promotion

News that Walliams was having a relationship with a junior employee spread around the company. One former manager said he felt uncomfortable to learn that the young woman had been sent to Walliams’ house. A second source said Walliams sent a large bunch of flowers to the woman’s desk, and another colleague saw the woman crying about Walliams in the office bathrooms.

Senior management, including Redmayne, were aware of the relationship, according to former employees.

Lawyers for Walliams said it was a “consensual sexual” relationship.

At a book signing event a year later, Walliams was seen approaching a girl who appeared to be in her mid-teens. A former HarperCollins employee who was helping to arrange the signing witnessed the interaction. She said it seemed as if he was asking for her Instagram handle. “I just was like, no, no, no, no, no, no. This is a fucking children’s bookstore. Are you out of your mind?” She said she and another colleague reported what they had seen to a manager.

Walliams’ lawyers said he did not recall the interaction. They said if he had been asking for Instagram details it would have been to tag the bookshop in his own posts. Walliams did post two photos from the event, but he did not tag the shop.

In the face of apparent inaction from bosses, women took it upon themselves to warn each other about Walliams’ behaviour. Two women said colleagues had advised them to take care when they had been asked to deliver paperwork to his house.

A young woman who was in her early 20s when she worked at HarperCollins said she was told to be careful as she was blonde and considered by colleagues to be “his type”. She said there was an “unwritten rule” that young women should not be alone around him.

Worried, she said she raised concerns with senior managers and HR at least twice. “I was reassured by them that there was no proof and we would never be put in bad situations,” she said. “Now I think maybe we weren’t necessarily safe.”

Not all former employees spoke negatively about Walliams. Three former staff members said they had not witnessed any inappropriate behaviour themselves, with one saying they found him to be professional and quite introverted.

Beyond the office, Walliams’ reputation caused consternation for the publisher. In 2020, he faced criticism online about the content of his books after the anti-poverty campaigner Jack Monroe posted on Twitter (now X) that they were “sneering classist fatshaming grim nonsense”. Soon afterwards a young woman started posting about her interactions with him in his role as a judge on the TV show Britain’s Got Talent.

A group of authors published by HarperCollins UK sent an email to the company to express their concern about the tweets.

Then, in November 2022 Walliams was dropped by BGT after a hot mic incident, revealed by the Guardian, caught him making derogatory comments about contestants.

HarperCollins continued to publish his books.

In October 2023, Walliams was the guest of honour at a tea party at the HarperCollins office to mark the launch of his latest title, The Blunders.

Days earlier, managers had launched the internal inquiry into his conduct. A new head of the children’s department, Cally Poplak, was told of the concerns about Walliams’ behaviour. She told one colleague she felt there was a culture within the company of managers looking the other way.

Oversight of the internal investigation was taken up by the publisher’s head of global compliance, Isha Mehmood, based in New York.

The inquiry was then passed to Allen & Overy (now known as A&O Shearman) and run by Sarah Henchoz, a lawyer described on the firm’s website as having a particular specialism in “business protection and workplace conduct issues”.

At least five women were interviewed as part of the process, according to sources. It is understood the women were warned not to discuss the inquiry with colleagues, and that if they did it would be a disciplinary matter.

In early 2024, the law firm handed over the report on its findings. A&O Shearman did not respond to a request for comment.

Several sources told the Guardian they believed the inquiry was just a way to scope the company’s legal liability and shut down complaints.

A source with knowledge of the process said the women were never told the outcome of the inquiry but were “left in the dark” and still fear speaking out.

One woman left the company after agreeing to a settlement, which is understood to have included a strict NDA. Some of the other women, according to multiple sources, said they felt “isolated”, “overwhelmed” and “shut down”. Some were told they could avoid going to the office when Walliams was present.

A spokesperson for HarperCollins said: “To respect the privacy of staff we cannot comment on individual employee matters but can confirm that in 2024 an investigation was concluded by an external law firm and recommendations were implemented.”

For nearly two years HarperCollins continued to publish Walliams’ books.

Walliams’ departure from the publisher in December 2025 came just two months after another seismic event. After more than 10 years with the company, Redmayne had left suddenly that October. There was no internal announcement and no big leaving event. Redmayne did not respond to requests for comment.

He was replaced by Elton, who was promoted internally. She had been in post for two months when the company was approached by the Telegraph with questions about the internal inquiry. Days after receiving those questions, Walliams was dropped.

In her address to staff, Elton said she was positive about the company’s future.

Industry insiders have said there is much work to be done. Philip Jones, the editor of the Bookseller magazine, called the revelations about HarperCollins the biggest scandal in publishing in his 20 years in the sector. “This is a #MeToo movement moment for the industry,” he said. “HarperCollins now need to step up, come clean and don’t let it happen again.”

He said company executives needed to investigate “what they knew, what they condoned, what they thought was permissible and what they thought they could manage”.

“This is a moment where the entire sector needs to stop burying their heads in the sand and do something.”

Barnsley, the former CEO of HarperCollins, said: “What’s staggering is that everyone is relating it to 90s and 00s culture, but it’s not, it’s still happening. That’s what people have to understand. They have to stop trying to comfort themselves by saying it happened a long time ago.”

‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 11:59:18 GMT

London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless

‘An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture

The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens. But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield.

History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. When Sharon Ament, the director, asked me if I liked it, I couldn’t find the words. I was heartbroken, speechless, unlike the museum’s management who have their own way with language. Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London?

Two vast ground floor spaces are called Real Time and Our Time. Neither has much to see in the way of exhibits – a bell, a stuffed giraffe, the Lord Mayor’s coach in an absurd vitrine. But that’s not the point, for really they are all about the cafes and restaurants, chill-out spaces and vibing. I was proudly told the 24-hour Temperance cafe will serve people coming out of nearby Fabric.

This place wants to be up there with the club, to be more than a stuffy old museum. It ends up being so much less. It strains to be part of the city and definitely is a good indoor piazza to hang out, have coffee, read your texts. But so is nearby St Pancras station and it has more respect for its Victorian heritage.

Where is the heart of this museum, its vast and fascinating collection of artefacts from London’s long history and even prehistory? That has been shoved downstairs into a third space called Past Time. The assumption seems to be the past is dead in contrast to the living present, though surely history is the process of change in which we all live.

Past Time doesn’t have galleries of different periods: just one long open space telling the entire story of London in a potted, bullet-point version addressed to someone who in the curators’ imaginations can’t cope with the least hint of complexity. I say entire, but it cuts out the prehistory of the Thames landscape, which got its own gallery in the old museum. Ament told me that the gallery was not “popular”, so it’s sayonara to the stone age handaxes.

Yet the lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content. I may have made the old Museum of London sound serious, but it found space for a son et Lumiere 18th-century pleasure garden, Victorian shops, a Roman house. There’s nothing like that here. Instead everything is presented with chic conceptualism, like a taster menu. There is a Roman shop and tavern, yet this is done in such a minimalist, cool way it has no atmosphere. Kids will shrug.

The whirl through time continues as medieval London is jumbled into the Tudors and Stuarts. In next to no time, you reach a single case covering both world wars. Well, I don’t suppose they made much impact on London … but wasn’t there a blitz or something? The lack of space or time to explore the collections in depth destroys any chance to connect with objects emotionally: as you proceed from chronological displays to themed ones, the randomisation is numbing.

London is a venerable place yet also a city of amnesias. Accidental destruction by the Great Fire and attempted obliteration by Nazi bombs are not the only enemies of its past. Many medieval and Tudor buildings were demolished by the Victorians and today the character of whole neighbourhoods is casually undermined by cynical building – it recently took Mick Jagger to stop a tower dominating the riverside at Chelsea. So a London Museum is necessary, a place where Londoners and visitors to the “monster city”, as Defoe called it, can understand its immense yet fragile history.

But the London Museum treats it as an eternal entity, always in the now, never changing. A painting of the Annunciation, a Roman inscription, modern badges are shoved together in London as Ritual but don’t spark new meanings by being juxtaposed. Everything starts to feel meaningless: Punch and Judy next to a painting of an ice fair, a mannequin of the actor Edmund Kean, Charles Booth’s map of London wealth – the supposedly imaginative rejection of chronology is just baffling and disengaging.

It’s one thing to lack a brain but this museum has lost its soul. At least if you live far outside the capital and are sick of London getting all the fuss, you can take satisfaction that your own local museum is almost certainly more interesting and charming than this.

London Museum Smithfield opens 28 November
