You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you?

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 11:52:44 GMT

The idea that seeing is believing is turned on its head in this documentary about the inscrutable Theranos founder, a world-class liar who may just be completely unreadable

Warning: this article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything

Elizabeth Holmes doesn’t believe that she’s ever told a lie. She “knows” that she hasn’t committed any crime. And she has no reason to deceive you. While speaking, she is gazing at her interviewer, Nathan Fielder, with those enormous, blue, vacant, unsettling, unblinking eyes. She doesn’t break eye contact.

This is You Can See Everything, Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, which, at her invitation, follows Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at their home in San Diego in the weeks up to her surrender to custody at federal prison. Holmes is the disgraced tech ex-billionaire whose startup Theranos claimed the ability to run hundreds of comprehensive blood tests from a single pinprick of blood. This false claim posed “immediate jeopardy” to the health of thousands of patients and defrauded investors of more than $700m.

What the film promises is what it says: that you can see everything, because the couple have nothing to hide. Unprecedented access is given to their lives: the cameras come in, and they don’t leave. You can see them discussing plans for a Theranos 2.0, you can see Billy’s penis in the shower, Elizabeth, or “Liz”, breastfeeding. You can see that Liz doesn’t whisk eggs vigorously enough for Billy’s liking. You can, following their logic, see that Holmes is innocent.

You Can See Everything has become a phenomenon, surpassing $100m globally since its release in the US last month, and breaking the record for the biggest opening weekend for a non-music documentary in the UK since opening here last Friday.

But why does Holmes’s story remain such a draw, 11 years on from Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyro’s exposé? Fraudsters fascinate, of course. Anna Delvey posing as a wealthy German heiress; “the Monster of Wall Street” Bernie Madoff’s decades-long Ponzi scheme; the Tinder Swindler. Yet beyond the thrill and dreadful amazement, there is another pull: the question: “Could you detect a fraudster?” And if reality is broken down and blurred right in front of you, would you have the mental fortitude to withstand such an orchestrated illusion in real time? While watching the film, you ask whether Holmes is manipulating us, or being manipulated herself? Or does the answer lie somewhere in between? Did she genuinely believe in Theranos or did she know all along that it was bunk? Is she really just that good at deceiving people?

You Can See Everything asks whether you can ever know where someone’s performance begins and ends. That is what the cameras go in to find, but thanks to the limits on what can be recorded, a documentary premised on observation and seeking truth is forced to rely on the techniques of fiction: performance, reenactment and selective disclosures. After Holmes is shown being sent to prison, the actor Amanda Seyfried, whose portrayal of Holmes in the 2022 series The Dropout earned her an Emmy, enters the frame – literally walking into Holmes’s home and making porridge on her stove in a reenactment.

There’s an unsettled dispute around a New York Times interview in which Holmes, in reference to The Dropout, is quoted as saying: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” Holmes claims she said “a character they created”. But in the documentary she seems to have dropped certain memorable elements of her previous public persona: the baritone voice, the Steve Jobs-apeing turtlenecks, the private headbanging to hip-hop music. The home Holmes invites the film-makers into is so devoid of character or lived-inness that it may as well be a film set. So if Elizabeth Holmes is a performance then who, or what, are we watching in You Can See Everything?

That is why we are so fascinated by Holmes’s eyes. The film-makers know this; a single eye is the centrepiece of the film’s poster. Even while overwhelmed by the scale of Holmes’s deception, it’s her piercing eyes that Seyfried is most invested in imitating.

But what can we ever really learn from looking into a person’s eyes? Pop-psychology myths have long abounded that eyes are a reliable indicator of whether or not a person is lying to you. Liars avoid eye contact, say some. Or do they maintain intense eye contact as overcompensation? Others say they look in one direction or another. Body-language experts have weighed in to say that Holmes engages in “gaze aversion suppression” with Fielder, refusing to cut the tension when she’s questioned on her crimes. Academics have long dismissed the “lying eyes” theory, yet we stubbornly cling on: if we want to know if a child is lying to us, we ask them to repeat the statement while looking us in the eyes.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Holmes’s unnerving gaze exposes one misconception about our voyeuristic age of media, reality television and tell-all documentaries: that if we are able to look closely enough at someone, see enough of their private life, and scrutinise every flicker of their expression, we will eventually be able to excavate their interiority, to tell good from bad, truth from lies.

In a film that becomes something of a conspiratorial thriller, you may leave with firm conclusions that Holmes is lying, a fantasist, a victim or some combination. But no matter how certain we are, we have no real way of knowing what is inside another person’s head. So in the end all you can do is look into her eyes and wonder.

Jason Okundaye is assistant editor of Guardian Opinion

UK nations in dark over whether they will get automatic entry to 2035 Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 11:00:43 GMT

Fifa will make decision on qualifying procedures

Four 2031 hosts have been given automatic places

England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are in the dark about whether they will be granted automatic qualification as hosts for the 2035 Women’s World Cup.

The decision on qualification procedures will be made by Fifa, with sources at the domestic football associations telling the Guardian they had yet to be informed of the plan after their bid was formally accepted.

Jess Carter says there is more 'kindness' in America's NWSL

The England defender Jess Carter says fan bases are kinder in America's National Women's Soccer League than in the Women's Super League.

The 29-year-old former Chelsea centre-back, who signed for Bay FC this month on a free transfer from the 2026 NWSL shield winners, Gotham FC, was subjected to racist abuse online during England's run to the Euro 2025 final but says the supporters in the USA have made her feel at home.

"The Gotham fans have beyond lovely to me," Carter said, when discussing the differences she's noticed between England and the US. "They are so kind that [I could] probably score an own goal and they’d still go: ‘Jess, well done.’

"Sometimes they're a little bit too nice, but here [in England] there was just a lot more scrutiny within the game, maybe because the love of the game is more, it's the main sport here, whereas in America, football's competing with every other sport [but] in America I can just go and be whoever and there's no camera on me or [pressure to] act a certain way.

"I think there's a bit more kindness out in the NWSL than there is here and I'm probably going to get a bit of scrutiny for saying that but that's just my personal experience."

Carter was speaking before England's must-win Women's World Cup qualifying playoff against Ukraine, as the Lionesses seek to secure a place at the 2027 finals in Brazil. The 2031 edition will be co-hosted by the US and she added: "I think that'd be incredible – the love for football out there is huge. I get to see how they make championship weekend a really special occasion. So I think it's going to be an incredible tournament out there." Tom Garry

Such doubts contrasted with the certainty expressed by the newly confirmed hosts of the 2031 World Cup, the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, who said they had assurances that all four countries would take part.

“All four countries will qualify automatically,” said Cindy Parlow Cone, the president of US Soccer. “That’s what happened in 2026,” a reference to the US, Mexico and Canada being given automatic qualification for last summer’s men’s World Cup.

Michael Ricketts, president of the Jamaican Football Federation, said: “We will qualify automatically and will be seeded. Once we are one of the host teams we will definitely be in. And in fact, we have had discussions about hosting most of the games that Jamaica will actually play.”

It is unclear whether the uncertainty in the UK is a byproduct of Fifa’s strained relationship with Uefa, which will run the European qualification tournament, or the differing nature of the bids. Whereas the UK bid was always a four-nation proposal, Costa Rica and Jamaica joined the previously existing US-Mexico bid for 2031 last year, at which point it is understood assurances were given that they would all qualify.

The 2031 World Cup will be the first women’s tournament to feature 48 teams, which in theory should enable Fifa to be more flexible in granting automatic qualification. An automatic spot would be a major boost in particular for Wales and Northern Ireland, who have never qualified for a Women’s World Cup.

Uefa granted two automatic qualification places for the 2028 European Championship, which will take place in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland. All four countries will take part in qualifying tournament, the draw for which will take place in Belfast next month, but two “safety net” places have been reserved in the event that some fail to make it through.

after newsletter promotion

Fifa has yet to allocate the number of qualification places for each confederation for the expanded Women’s World Cup. Next summer’s 32-team tournament in Brazil will feature 11 or 12 teams from Europe and six from Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation. Concacaf was given nine places at last summer’s 48-team men’s World Cup, six qualifiers plus the three hosts, with 16 teams qualifying from Europe.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “The slot allocation for the 2031 and 2035 editions of the Fifa Women’s World Cup will be confirmed in due course by the Fifa council.”

The UK government has set out its ambition for one million more girls to be involved in sport by the time of the 2035 tournament and for women and girls to have equal access to primetime slots at grassroots facilities by then. It said that under new rules sports risked losing public funding if they did not create equal environments and allow men and women to share decision-making power.

Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 10:00:13 GMT

With the British actor securing the role of James Bond, speculation has now begun over who should join him in Denis Villeneuve’s much-anticipated caper

After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment.

Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl.

It’s possible to draw a line between Sweeney’s bombshell status and the most recent wholly American Bond girls; Teri Hatcher in Tomorrow Never Dies and Denise Richards in The World Is Not Enough were both well-known actors with substantial pin-up appeal when they were cast. But Sweeney is a bigger deal than those actors – neither of them ever had a non-Bond hit as substantial as The Housemaid or Anyone But You – while also seeming like a profound mismatch with whatever form Pattinson might take for this role. In terms of performance styles, Pattinson’s slightly alien affect, even at its most charming, feels too eccentric to sync up with Sweeney, who has specialized in 1990s throwbacks. Smirky suggestions of Pattinson’s The Drama co-star Zendaya feel off for a similar-yet-opposite reason: She’s both too big a star on her own to be Bond’s second banana, and almost too much of a temperamental match with her partner in an off-kilter black comedy.

Yet Pattinson’s presence does allow for a bit more leeway in fantasy-casting Bond girls, going beyond the Craig era’s mix of continental prestige hotties (Léa Seydoux, Eva Green, Monica Bellucci) and more genre-friendly variations on that theme (Gemma Arterton, Olga Kurylenko, Ana de Armas). Those Craig entries largely eschewed the traditional dichotomy between good-girl sidekick and femme fatale betrayer – Paloma (de Armas), for example, neither sticks by Bond’s side for the entire film nor sells him out to the bad guys in No Time to Die – and hopefully the Villeneuve film will similarly allow for less rigorously defined gender roles while still having some fun with the archetypes. All that said, wouldn’t it be fun to see Lily James play a femme fatale? She has a sunny countenance that made her excellent casting as a Disney princess as a younger woman, and an adorably underwritten love interest in Danny Boyle’s disappointing Beatles sorta-musical Yesterday. She might look like a damsel in distress as Bond’s main love interest. But as a character with more noirish ambiguities, she could make an oft-thankless role feel like a personal challenge.

The Craig period also seemed to pause (or at least de-emphasize) the Brosnan-era lip service to the idea of an allied female agent who is supposed to be Bond’s equal, a part with a surprisingly strong Oscar track record; Michelle Yeoh was in Tomorrow Never Dies decades before her Everything Everywhere All at Once Oscar, while Halle Berry shot her role as Jinx (once earmarked for a spin-off!) shortly before winning hers for Monster’s Ball. Let’s not presume, though, that only seeming Oscar inevitabilities like Carey Mulligan or Amanda Seyfried may apply to a newer version of this type. Callina Liang is still early in her career, but she buffed up for the recent Street Fighter and could be equally believable fighting at Bond’s side or beating the holy hell out of him. Amber Midthunder is another genre actor with a ton of charisma, first shown off fighting a Predator in the franchise-reviving Prey. (The only drawback? She’s the rare potential Bond actor who might well have a more interesting real name than her character.) Cassandra Naud, who, like Midthunder, appeared in the recent Carrie TV series, isn’t as well-known, but in the indie horror influencer movies, she can be seductive, scary, and likable within the space of a few minutes.

Though this kind of role seems well beneath Zendaya’s stature, Pattinson does have another 2026 co-star who might bring an unusual and welcome energy: Phoebe Bridgers, the indie-rock singer who made her acting debut alongside Pattinson in the recent Primetime, and contributed a song to the soundtrack to boot. Between her strong solo albums and her supergroup boygenius, Bridgers seems too busy for a full-time acting career. But there’s no reason she couldn’t pull double duty here as one of those Bond girls with a little less screen time (de Armas only has one extended sequence in No Time to Die; the Moore and Brosnan entries often included a smaller role that was neither sidekick nor femme fatale) while also providing an eerie yet catchy opening-credits number.

Finally, there’s one more former Pattinson co-star that some have floated as a joke but deserves to be taken seriously: Kristen Stewart. Yes, some would immediately scoff or shudder at a Bond film serving as a Twilight reunion. But look at it this way: Since Twilight, both Pattinson and Stewart have proved themselves far more capable actors than the Twilight film-makers were able to fully showcase, shackled as they were by the dubious source material. They clearly share an offbeat, thoughtful sensibility; they’ve even both worked with Cronenberg, albeit not at the same time. If Twilight never existed but A24 announced a vampire romance starring Stewart and Pattinson coming out next summer, it would shoot to the top of countless anticipation lists on the basis of the actors’ reputations.

Stewart would also match Pattinson’s exciting flexibility. Just as we’ve seen him both debonairly quasi-auditioning for Bond in Tenet and making Batman into even more of a little weirdo, Stewart can play frazzled nerves in a movie like Personal Shopper as readily as she can look as if she’s genuinely having a great time in a middling reboot of Charlie’s Angels. She could play a live-wire Bond sidekick, an aggressive femme fatale, or, as some have suggested, the actual lead villain of the piece. It may not be likely for any number of reasons, but it would make for a fascinating bookend to their impressive post-Twilight careers. Despite the nomenclature, Bond girls don’t need to be accessories, especially not with Pattinson at the wheel. What most of these suggestions have in common, and Stewart has in abundance, is an ability to match the new 007’s freak.

Cookie fever! How does Marks & Spencer knock out so many viral food sensations?

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 10:00:12 GMT

Chicken kievs, ‘picky bits’, strawberry and cream sandwiches: the hits have been coming for almost half a century. Now Kathryn Turner, M&S’s head of product development, has become a social media celebrity. What’s the secret ingredient?

The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer, after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster. How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits?

You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatever the flavour, there is always chocolate in them, and always more of it than you’d credit. Even the packaging on the M&S cookies – clear, crinkly – has the main-event feel of a bouquet or a hamper. Except if you put these cookies in a box, that box would be ginormous, and people would say: “I can’t eat five of those – don’t be stupid.”

Seraphi Bouchier Hayes, 23, works in marketing and speaks digital like, well, a native. “Everyone’s always loved M&S for the summer – picnics and stuff; they have their own song – and for any journey, you’d get a premixed drink. People call it ‘journey juice’, but it would cringe me out to say that.”

Their own song? She sings it for me: “It is the season of picky bits / If you can stick a toothpick in it / Then you can bring it to my pic-a-nic.” I’m not convinced it’s been signed off by M&S’s product team.

The TikTok crowd aren’t in the store for meals. M&S is very good at picking up on a viral food trend and tailoring it. When Dubai chocolate was everywhere, it brought out a line of pistachio products. “The big thing two summers ago was the strawberries and cream sandwich during Wimbledon,” says Bouchier Hayes. “It’s a Japanese thing, but they made it into the tennis sandwich, and apparently it was quite nice.”

M&S also has a “dot cake”, a sponge with tooth-achingly sweet buttercream icing that you eat out of a pot with a spoon. This is a homage to a New York bakery’s cake that hit the sweet spot of unboxing (people filmed themselves cracking into the virgin, individuated pots), ASMR (they make a lot of cracking, squelching noises) and slightly outlandish expense (they were between $8 and $12 each, or about £6 to £9). Marks and Sparks’s take was less garish, much cheaper (£1.10) and perfectly tasty. It became an instant TikTok pilgrimage item.

M&S stampede foods are often more about plugging in and “belongingness” than they are about originality. People make mini-careers on Instagram out of just going into the shop to try things, such as the double chocolate bloomer (a loaf of bread with added chocolate). These viral foods are often in-store only; you don’t create an internet sensation with stuff you can buy on the internet, paradoxically but understandably.

This has something in common with the psychodynamics of the mukbang, a trend that originated in South Korea. The word is a portmanteau of “eating” (meokneun) and “broadcast” (bangsong). Basically, some (usually beautiful) person will film themselves eating an awesome amount of food. And that’s it. A 2020 review of the mukbang literature yielded some insights that were quite sad: for example, that people are lonely, and the mukbang makes them feel as though they’re eating with others. But there’s also an interesting, childlike, fantasy excess about it all. Ultimately, who stops you eating 17 eggs, or an entire tin of differently shaped tiny sweets, or bread with added chocolate? Your mum. It’s like a portal to a childhood where everything’s taken to the max, and the cold, dead hand of responsible adulthood does not exist – which is to say, paradise.

That makes sense of the Turner phenomenon: she is a 56-year-old mother of three, yet she would never tell you not to overdo it – the opposite. In her kitchen, it’s liberty hall. She is wildly enthusiastic over every pretzel, but her enthusiasm is the only thing about her that’s wild. She is every inch the kind authority figure, completely normal except for her snacks, and so alluring that gen Z influencers were dressing up as her for Halloween. “It wasn’t hard,” says Bouchier Hayes. “You just had to stand outside M&S wearing what she wears. And if no one got it, you’d say: ‘I’m Kathryn Turner, the product developer for M&S.’”

I know this isn’t about me, but I contacted M&S to ask if Turner would speak to me, and when it refused, I was gobsmacked. We’re both women of a similar age, I’m nice, she seems nice, all I want to do is ask how come she’s so good at her job … It was honestly the maddest rejection I’ve ever had. But then I spoke to friends who work for the tabloids and it transpires I am the mad one: everyone has been asking to speak to her for 18 months, and the Sun and Vogue have given up and printed profiles with quotes they’ve pulled off Instagram. Again, without wishing to be either solipsistic or insider-y, this is absolutely unheard of. Aloof, private and always in control of her own image, Turner is the Kate Moss of supermarket product development. There has never been a Kate Moss of supermarket product development.

But Turner has worked at the retailer since the 1990s, and the commitment to zeitgeist did not start in the past few years, nor did it originate with her. M&S, which began as a market stall 142 years ago, was the first store to sell sandwiches in a skillet (the triangular pack with the film cover). This was 1980, and it started in scattered stores in Edinburgh, Leeds, Croydon and Cambridge. Staff were making them overnight, and they were so popular that the Cambridge staff started throwing pilchards in just to keep the production line going. “That enables a lunchtime food market,” recalls Polly Russell, who was a product developer in the fish department in the late 90s, and is now an author, food historian and curator at the British Library. “This really transforms that move towards not eating in a canteen or cafe or bringing in a packed lunch.”

Before that was M&S’s most famous launch: the chicken kiev ready meal, in 1979. “That was classic French restaurant fare, but also the sort of thing that a housewife would like to serve up to her husband’s boss,” Russell summarises. “Dinner-party elegance and status, appealing to people who wanted to be comfortable in that register. Off the back of that, you get the development of the ready meal: it’s a mixture of TV dinner convenience, but also luxury, things that you can’t make yourself.” That’s an interesting through-line, from the kiev to the cookie – things that are actually quite hard to make at home. “Biscuits are harder than cakes,” Sykes says. “I’ve been a cook for 35 years, and I know that you can make a biscuit recipe many times, and it won’t necessarily turn out the same. There are a lot of variables. If the weather’s hotter and the flour’s drier … with a cake, that’s not so much the case.”

Russell’s heyday was when they reinvented sushi. Yo! Sushi was on manoeuvres with real sushi and fancy conveyor belts in 1997, but M&S was the first supermarket to launch prepacked sushi. “They didn’t go into the market with raw fish, because at that time sushi was weird,” Russell says. “They could see it was going to be big, so they went in with fish people already understood: smoked mackerel, smoked salmon, prawns. It was a version that was delicious but it was still British. It was massive when it launched. It was the new sandwich.” If you remember that era, you’ll also remember the salmon pinwheel. Unbelievably tasty.

Soon the other supermarkets had caught up, as they always do. But if you want to know why M&S was first, it’s the same reason US drama used to seem so flawless, so failsafe, while we were constantly surprised by random flashes of British genius such as Fawlty Towers or The Office: the sheer size of the writers’ room, or in M&S’s case, the product development room. It was bursting at the seams with developers – a score of people just on fish.

“In the development kitchen, you were working really closely with suppliers, with other product developers, a buyer and a technologist,” Russell says. “They really did invest in supporting product developers’ research, talking to chefs, trying to work out what was happening outside the mainstream, as well as trying to understand the technological innovation that could take these things mass-market.”

She remembers her job interview, when they asked: “Can you give an example of when you’ve done something really innovative in order to save money and you were pleased with the result?” Her example wasn’t even about food – she’d had to go to a fancy wedding, skint, and she’d bought a huge straw hat plus some feathers from John Lewis. “I looked posh for 12 quid. They loved that.”

M&S freely accepts, even boasts, that it created the term “picky bits”, a phrase that doesn’t even feel class-coded since everyone hates it. But it has historically been the pioneer of everything, from packed lunches to husband’s boss dinner parties, through party food, deli Christmas, romantic main meal, side and wine deals, picnics. It has always been remarkably successful at capturing a food trend or just a mood, and making it edible. “They understand a social and cultural moment,” Russell says, “about feeling special, treating yourself – but what that looks like is always slightly different. Now, with food, there’s less of a fixation on being smart or impressing people; it’s about pleasure and fun and conviviality. It’s almost as though you’re in a gang of co-conspirators to have the best fun you can. And what you’re being offered through that cookie range is the most joyful, exuberant, over-the-top ingredient.”

It’s generation-specific – gen Z and younger millennials – because it’s about a precise relationship with social media: in part, surely, a rejection of the wellness scene, all giant water bottles and two yoga mats, which is getting a bit tired. But also, a passion for physically going somewhere, tasting something, being in the world. AI might take your job, but it cannot mimic or ever understand your delight in a cookie.

Honestly, the only food I go into M&S for is the combo mix potato snacks and “they’re not viral”, says Bouchier Hayes. “I feel like I would have them at a service station.” Doesn’t matter – M&S know where the viral is. It knows it’s not gen X, and it makes crisps for us anyway. Which, sincerely, we all appreciate; we’re just not about to make up a song about it.

‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 09:34:21 GMT

Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for

The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling.

From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football.

“It’s so lovely to hear them,” said Alman, whose son is in year 5. “I used to hear them before Charlie was in there, and now I go out there and I know he’s one of them, and it’s really nice to see him playing. I’ll drive by there, and there’ll be a couple of footballs that have gone over the fence and rolled to the verge. They try to flag someone down to throw back the ball so the game’s back on. It’s the heartbeat of the village, you know.”

Gladestry is home to 400 people and sits (just) on the Welsh side of the border with England. Indeed, if you’ve ever walked the Offa’s Dyke footpath that runs, more or less, along that border, you’ll have passed right through the small cluster of buildings that mark its centre. The school has been educating Almans since Joseph’s grandfather and great-uncle arrived in 1917, but Charlie could be the last. In June, just before the start of the summer holidays, Powys county council announced that it wanted to close the school.

“It all seemed to come as a bit of a bolt out of blue,” said Alman. “We didn’t know nothing about it.” It was, however, just the latest episode in a slow-motion erosion of the foundations of life in mid-Wales, which is caused by generations of politicians failing to engage with an important question: how do you provide adequate services to a sparsely populated place if you’re not willing to spend more money? In other words, how do you solve a problem like Powys?

Powys was once a kingdom, from which Britain’s native population resisted the remorseless westwards expansion of the Anglo-Saxons for half a millennium or more. The kingdom disappeared in the 13th century, when the English conquered the last independent Britons, but seven centuries later – in 1974 to be precise – its name was dredged out of obscurity. (The word itself derives from pagus, the Latin word for countryside.)

At the time, the government in London was trying to rationalise local administration by combining smaller units into larger ones that were better able to meet the needs of their populations. The result was new inventions such as Greater Manchester, Avon, Humberside and Mid Glamorgan. A basic principle of the reform was that local authority areas needed at least 250,000 people to be viable. And this is where mid-Wales ran into trouble.

The existing counties of Breconshire, Radnorshire and Montgomeryshire were clearly too tiny to justify their continued administrative existence. Even combined into a single entity called Powys, however, the population was less than half the supposed minimum. “There are more sheepdog exemption licences than there are members of the population,” one peer said when the House of Lords debated the reform in 1972. “Powys, as we all recognise, is a county with too few people and too few resources,” said another.

There was no easy answer. The new county already covered 5,200 sq km (2,000 sq miles), and combining it with yet more parts of Wales risked creating something too unwieldy to be manageable. Merging it with anywhere in England was clearly unacceptable, so Powys was left as a vast underpopulated exception – its population density lower than any part of Britain south of the Highlands, its properties cumulatively worth less than any other county in England and Wales.

Mid-Wales is a unique place. Unlike other parts of Wales – with their coal, steel and slate – Powys was largely untouched by the industrial revolution. Much of the county lived by producing meat for export, sending its livestock to the market towns of England. As a result, in contrast to farming communities elsewhere in Wales, most of Powys is English-speaking, which means it’s linguistically cut off from rural areas to the north and west, and culturally distinct from places to the south.

It is unassuming, and it is beautiful; the kind of place that hippies such as my parents sought out in the 1970s when they wanted somewhere quiet to build a new kind of life. It is also empty. Even today, the county’s entire population – 135,000 – is barely equal to that of St Albans, yet it is spread over an area larger than Northumberland. That’s a quarter of Wales’s landmass with 4% of its population. If you were to add Powys’s two largest settlements together – Newtown, on the English border near Shrewsbury, and Ystradgynlais, 85km away in the Swansea valley – you still wouldn’t have enough people to reach the Office for National Statistics’ threshold for a “medium-sized town”.

It takes two and half hours to drive from one end of Powys to the other, from Eryri (Snowdonia) to the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons), though you might want to allow yourself more time in July, when visitors to the four-day agricultural jamboree that is the Royal Welsh Show throng the centre of the county; or in August, when caravans clog the county’s B-roads; or, at other times, in case of incidents on the A470.

The county is bumpy. It is for this reason that if you take a train between south and north Wales, you bypass Powys altogether and travel instead through the smooth green fields of England. That feels appropriate because, when it comes to Welsh politics, Powys residents feel ignored – as if their home county were just a blank between the electorally significant places above and below it.

“The truth is, civil servants in Cardiff have always viewed Powys as a nuisance,” one local politician told me recently. “We’re a policy nightmare, aren’t we? Hardly any people. Lots of sheep. We haven’t got a big city, we haven’t got a university, we haven’t got a general hospital. Miles and miles and miles of roads to maintain. We’re just very expensive.”

And this is why Gladestry Church in Wales primary school was slated for closure. It was not because of something it did or didn’t do, but because the council decided that it couldn’t afford it any more. “This is one of those papers that none of us like to have to present,” said James Gibson-Watt, the councillor responsible for education in Powys county council’s cabinet, when he formally proposed the closure at a council meeting in July, “but the numbers are very stark.”

My family left the village 40 years ago, when our parents sold our farm, but our old teacher had told my brother Tom of the threat to the school, and Tom had told me, so we drove to Gladestry in September, when we heard that a public meeting had been called to discuss how the village could fight back against this threat to its future.

While we waited for everyone to file into the village hall, we reminisced about our own star turns on its stage. In December 1983, Tom had been Good King Wenceslas’ page, and I’d been Joseph, sinfully proud in dishcloth and dressing gown. Neither of us could quite remember why Wenceslas had been present at the birth of Christ.

It was shortly after that nativity play that the council first tried to close Gladestry school, and it tried again in 2012, when the pupils recorded a song to highlight their plight. Both times, the village mobilised and saw off the threat, and everyone sitting in the hall that evening hoped it could do so again.

Of the 100 or so people in attendance, probably everyone had at one time or another either performed on that stage, seen their children perform on it, or both. That’s what a school brings to a village: the one thing that everyone has in common. “We supported each other, we learned far more from each other than any lesson plan can provide, and that is what makes Gladestry school outstanding,” said one 17-year-old alumna, Eva Lloyd. Lloyd is the fourth generation of her family to pass through the school. Her speech was so eloquent she was immediately asked to repeat it, so it could be filmed and posted to the village Facebook page, which has 1,500 members – almost four times Gladestry’s population.

Inspectors from Estyn, the Welsh equivalent of Ofsted, published their most recent report into the school three years ago, and it could barely have been more glowing: pupils were proud of the school, they were well behaved, and their reading, maths and Welsh-language skills were impressive.

“That was 2023,” Hannah Price, who chairs the school governors, told me one evening over coffee after she’d finished her day’s work as a veterinary physiotherapist. “Mrs Beck [the head] sent four children to give the inspectors a guided tour and thought it would take them 10 minutes. Forty-five minutes later, she had to go and rescue the inspectors because they got shown every inch of the school with such, you know, animation and enthusiasm. It was all about the motto that we’re small but mighty, and how we won a maths competition, a cricket festival. They are amazing kids.”

But no matter how amazing these kids are, you can’t help but notice that there are very few of them. When the Estyn report was published, 40 pupils attended the school. By the time the council proposed closing it two and a half years later, there were only 31. The Welsh government’s definition of a small school is one with fewer than 91 pupils, so – with barely a third of that – Gladestry was very small indeed.

Welsh politics could, until the recent rise of Reform UK, be crudely but not unfairly caricatured as a battle between Labour in the south of the country and Plaid Cymru in the north and west. Powys is unique here too, and has in recent decades been more of a contest between the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats and an unruly gaggle of independents.

All of the governments in the UK have a presumption against closing rural schools, which are considered to be at the heart of their communities. In Powys, however, this policy is more of an ambition than a reality, and more than 15% of the county’s primary schools have gone in the past decade. The 2018 version of the Welsh government’s school organisation code listed all the schools deemed to be rural, and therefore to be worthy of protection. By the time a new edition was published this year, however, nine of the Powys schools had vanished off the list and another one – Llandinam, in the north of the county – closed in August.

Although primary schools have been closing all over the country, particularly in London where the birthrate is low and house prices are high, the effect is particularly dramatic in a rural setting because distances are greater and there is often little else to bring a village together.

Parts of rural Scotland have also seen their schools close, but there councils wait until the pupil numbers are in single figures before taking action. Powys acts far sooner, and it is so cash-strapped that it can’t even afford to repurpose these shuttered buildings, which often still have sports facilities that everyone used to use. They are simply left to rot. At the closed schools of places such as Llanigon and Rhosgoch, the paint has lost its brightness, weeds have pushed up through the playground, ivy has climbed the walls.

“Nobody, nobody wants to see their local school closed. I mean, I don’t want to see Gladestry closed, I’d love to keep it,” said Gibson-Watt, who represents the Liberal Democrats, as we sat and talked in a cafe in Hay-on-Wye recently. “But when the report for the cabinet was prepared, there were 31 pupils there. There are now 23, and it’s projected to go to 19 in two years’ time. I mean, where do we draw the line?”

The trouble with primary schools is that, no matter how small they get, they will always need at least two teachers, as well as heat and light. There is always a minimum cost that can’t be reduced. The fewer pupils a school has, the more expensive each pupil becomes, which is tough when councils receive funding on a per-pupil basis. That means schools with surplus capacity are effectively being subsidised by the rest. Even before those extra pupils left, Powys county council was spending £7,696 a year to educate every child at Gladestry, compared with an average of £5,710 across the county as a whole. The school apparently also has, for what it’s worth, a maintenance backlog worth £184,452.

If you spend time reading the budget reports published by Powys county council, you can see why this is a problem. Year after year, the allocations it receives from Cardiff have failed to keep up with inflation, so the council has had to cut huge chunks from its budget – adding up to £100m over the past decade – to keep afloat. In the last financial year, the administration has budgeted to spend £379.3m, but that’s £12.3m more than it’s going to get, which means more cuts for this dwindling administrative machine. “It’s going to have to get a lot leaner again to survive, just to be solvent,” said Gibson-Watt.

Council officials expect they’ll need to cut another £40m from the budget over the next five years, but are well past the point when they can save money by cancelling whole programmes; those went years ago. Instead, they pore over spreadsheets, looking for a £2,000 saving here, a £3,000 saving there, which means the effort to make the budget balance consumes a huge amount of their time, and services are gradually degraded. This is particularly stark in education, where new technologies are introduced all the time and schools have to spend money to keep up.

And it’s striking in healthcare too. The Powys health board, which is funded separately but faces the same kind of challenges, ended the last financial year having overspent by £33m. In response, it has proposed to close most of the county’s eight community hospitals, reducing inpatient beds from about 146 to as few as 60.

Austerity is not just about the loss of big headline services. It is also about small indignities that add up to a lot: fewer roads get gritted in winter, which makes getting around harder; services are being concentrated in a smaller number of towns, making them harder to access. And all of this is being made worse by the county’s demographics. The more rural a place is, the older its population and the faster its average age is increasing. Powys exemplifies that trend, which creates ever more demand for the council’s services and ever less money to pay for them.

For years, the amount of money Powys council has spent looking after people has been creeping ever closer to what it spends educating children. In 2023-24, the sums reached level. The next year, social care took the lead, and in 2025-26, that gap grew. Over that period, for every £100 the council spent, the school budget has remained constant at £34, but the social care budget has increased from £35, to £37, to £39. As that share creeps remorselessly upwards, something else has to give. This is the grim reality that councillors face.

Sean Davies’s family has farmed in Merthyr Cynog, at the head of the Ysgir valley north of Brecon, for five generations. His kids were educated – alongside his neighbours’ children – at a small school in the village of Cradoc. But in autumn 2020, just as a new spike in Covid cases was causing the government in Cardiff to start reimposing lockdowns in towns in the south Wales valleys, he and his wife, Becky, heard that the school was to close.

“Bang! That suddenly came out of nowhere, didn’t it?” said Davies. “They refused anything like a public meeting because everything was closed. Even then, when things started getting back to some sort of normality, a consultation landed on us with no public meetings of any kind. They pay no real attention to the consultation. I mean, it’s a laugh, a paper exercise. You ask if they’re conniving or just crap? Really, it’s a bit of both.”

It can be hard for people from outside Powys to understand why rural communities are so attached to their schools, particularly since the alternative to Cradoc was just down the hill in Brecon, which is large by Powys standards, with 8,000 inhabitants (though it would practically be counted as a village anywhere else). But the difference between urban and rural schooling is real. At my own kids’ rural primary school, lessons were interrupted if a tractor drove past because the children would run to the window to watch. Indeed, some of the boys could reliably tell you what make the tractors were, just from the sound. One teacher rode to school on her horse.

Country people are used to being patronised, and parents are often therefore reluctant to praise the nature of a rural education, not least because they’re aware of all the city facilities that they lack, as well as the inconvenience of having to drive their kids everywhere. However, there is a real value to a slower-paced education, where children learn things later, discover things for themselves, and do so in smaller groups, and that’s true from Orkney to Cumbria to Cornwall to Powys.

“You know yourself, rural kids, they’re different,” Davies said to me. “It’s just, it’s a different education, and I get the feeling sometimes people roll their eyes when you try to make a case for rural education, because it’s as if they’re automatically thinking that you’re trying to say that it’s better. But I’ve never ever said that. Just said it’s different.”

After they got the bad news, the Davieses and their neighbours mobilised, found political allies, pushed back in every way they could, but month by month, other parents took their kids out of Cradoc and the school dwindled. By the time their son was the last boy in his class, their daughter’s friends were leaving and the council voted to close the school in March 2022, they realised they had to give up. Every morning, the Davies kids are now driven half an hour to a different village school, which is – for now – still open. Every morning, they pass the abandoned buildings where they once studied.

“I don’t think people appreciate the damage it’ll do to the community. I find it very hard,” said Davies. “And cutting things doesn’t automatically mean an improvement. It’s the same like rugby players now leave Wales to go and play in England. They’re doing really well there, but they’re gone. That’s exactly what will happen in Powys. People will just look around and unless they’re involved in farming or tourism, which is under pressure as well, they won’t stay.”

This is what people in Gladestry are concerned about. It’s quite normal for locals to leave and work in England or in Cardiff in their 20s, then return to Powys once they have children of their own. But it becomes much harder to draw them back, let alone to attract other young families, if there is nowhere nearby to educate their children.

This is bad for the economy because without young adults, businesses struggle to attract employees, as do key services. When Powys county council tried to hire specialised staff in 2022 to support primary schools, it was unable to find any suitable candidates. But it’s also just bad for a community; a village needs people of all ages.

One morning in early October, a dozen or so Gladestry residents drove to Llandrindod Wells – a crumbling ex-spa town of 6,000 people that’s now better known for the periodic arrests of county lines drugs gangs than for people taking the waters – to stand outside the brick-and-glass county council offices.

The council had much on its agenda that morning, but the protesters were interested in only one item – No 15. Councillors were due to vote on whether to change the rules so that a school could be closed only with the approval of the full council, rather than just the cabinet, in a motion proposed by Gladestry’s local councillor.

These were not habitual protesters, so they didn’t have chants prepared, but they had painted placards – “Powys needs its small schools”; “Lose a school lose a community”; “Who decides? Our elected councillors” – and were stopping everyone who passed and engaging them in conversation.

These lobbying efforts were slightly shambolic, since no one knew what most councillors looked like. That meant they regularly engaged people in conversation about “item 15” only to discover their target was an ordinary council employee trying to get into the office in time for a video call. But the few councillors who did stop and chat seemed to be on side.

Item 15 did indeed pass – full council approval would be needed to close schools – but something potentially even more significant for the school’s fate emerged. The council was forced to extend its consultation period because it had left out of its original document the fact that, although the closure would save the council £43,000 in the first year, changes to the funding formula meant it would actually cost the council money thereafter. The omission reset the clock on the consultation period, which will now end in December, rather than October, pushing the whole timetable back by a couple of months.

It looks unlikely, therefore, that there will be enough time to complete the process to close the school before council elections are held in May. If this year’s Senedd voting pattern is repeated, the current Liberal Democrat-Labour coalition will lose control of the council and be replaced by either Reform UK or Plaid Cymru. Both have committed to protecting rural schools, which is great news for Gladestry, but whoever is in charge will find themselves squeezed by the same mathematics.

The council’s plan for escaping this trap involves building “all-through schools” that combine primary and secondary education on a smaller number of single sites. The conundrum is that the council needs to invest in new facilities to do this, but can’t afford to, so it’s stuck in the same doom loop of cuts year after year after year.

The obvious answer to that conundrum, according to most people in Powys, is that they should get more money from outside. Parts of Scotland with equivalently sparse populations to Powys receive more than 50% more funding per head of population as mid-Wales, whereas Powys’ funding is almost exactly at the Welsh average.

Partly this is because the government in Edinburgh appears to value the culture of the Highlands and Islands as a core part of Scottish identity, and funds them accordingly, in a way that the Welsh government simply doesn’t value Powys. But mainly it’s because Wales receives less money from Westminster per person than Scotland does, for reasons that are complex but can be boiled down to the fact that Scots have historically been a lot better at making a fuss than the Welsh.

And as Powys tries to divide up this smaller pot of money, it also has to consider the fact that Welsh schoolchildren score significantly worse in international tests than their counterparts in England or Scotland. It’s hard to justify spending what little money Powys does have on subsidies for small primary schools when investment needs to go into the county’s secondary schools, which are based in towns and urgently need improvement.

You can blame the unfortunate situation on the legacy of English colonialism, on geography, on mismanagement, or on English pensioners who buy houses here but never learn how to pronounce Pen y Fan, but the fundamental problem is the same: Powys’s population is too sparse and too old. The county certainly needs more money, but above all it needs more people. Without more young people, the county will never receive the funding it needs to provide the services its residents want, nor will it have the electoral heft to force politicians to address its concerns.

“Powys is in a bit of a world of its own,” said Alman. “It’s just forgotten about.” He was looking out of the kitchen window at Gladestry school. “It’d be an awful thing if it closed,” he said. Gladestry has produced a new rescue plan for the council to look at, which involves the school staying open while forging closer ties with a neighbouring school, alongside efforts to recruit more pupils. If next year’s newly elected councillors approve of the plan, the village can save its school for a third time.

Gladestry’s fight for its school may not have been quite as epic as the kingdom of Powys’s centuries-long struggle for survival, but it’s been going on for most of my life and is not lost yet.

The Ukraine-Russia war is escalating – and it will go global unless Europe speaks with one voice

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 08:00:10 GMT

Attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the Baltic Sea are a rebuke to western complacency. Trump is a liability, and he must be bypassed to ensure peace

Ukraine’s spectacularly successful weekend drone attack on a spanking new Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, more than 1,300 miles (2,200km) from Kyiv, is further proof, if it were needed, that the catastrophic full-scale war Vladimir Putin launched in 2022 is escalating and spreading uncontrollably.

The sinking follows a similar incident in the Baltic last week, which crippled a Russian cargo ship, and previous Ukrainian attacks on oil tankers and Russian navy ships and bases in the Black Sea region. Last week, Russia was blamed for a missile and drone strike on Nato member Poland, which Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, claimed was intentional, and for deliberately targeting western diplomatic compounds in Kyiv. While Moscow’s murderous winter bombing of Ukrainian civilians and energy infrastructure continues apace, provocative and disruptive Russian hybrid warfare operations across all of Europe, including sabotage, arson and cyber-attacks, are becoming daily occurrences.

After almost five years of continual fighting, the Ukraine war has become deadeningly familiar to those looking on from the outside who, unlike tens of thousands of Ukrainian citizens and more than 400,000 hapless Russian soldiers, are not already dead. The lamentable failure of numerous, mostly half-hearted, half-baked US efforts to negotiate a peaceful way out of the morass is no longer news. Partly because it’s so difficult and so protracted, ending the war somehow appears to many Europeans and Americans to have become less urgent, even less of a priority. That’s a dangerous mistake. The huge human, economic and geopolitical damage it has already done is nothing as to what could follow if the conflict goes truly global.

This latest, alarming string of attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the high north must finally vanquish an enervating, collective western complacency that simultaneously condemns Russian aggression, and pledges increased financial and materiel support for Kyiv, while in effect tolerating the continuation, intensification and widening of what could become an existential conflict for all concerned. European leaders say they are fully awake to the hazards. Meeting in Berlin last week, the western, pro-Ukraine “coalition of the willing” declared it was ready for direct talks with the Kremlin and was even prepared to discuss Europe’s wider post-Soviet security architecture – Putin’s longstanding, contentious demand. “Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Andy Burnham said. But that’s not the whole story.

Agreement the war should end immediately is hardly the same as taking concrete steps to make it happen. The EU – principally represented in this instance by France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, plus the leaders of Italy and Poland – has even struggled to agree with the European Commission who should be lead negotiator. Logically, it should by Kaja Kallas, the EU’s hawkish foreign policy chief. Russia claims her appointment would collapse any future talks. As ever, Europe, acting in close coordination with Kyiv, needs to speak with one voice on Ukraine; and the Kremlin cannot be allowed a veto on who does the talking if, as is proposed, a European delegation, including a UK representative, travels to Moscow in the coming days.

Just as vital if there is to be any chance of lasting diplomatic success is a clear, prior understanding between Europe and the Trump administration over red lines, what’s wanted, and what can and cannot be conceded. On this as on so many other international issues, Donald Trump is a liability who speaks without thinking, lacks strategic grasp, and shows no loyalty either to his allies or to the values of liberty, democracy, law and justice for which the US once stood. Speaking during and after last week’s trilateral Shenzhen summit with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Putin, Trump floated some vague grand bargain with Russia over Europe-wide security; again failed to object to ongoing, merciless targeting of Ukrainian civilians; and, outrageously, called the indicted war criminal Putin a “friend” whom he was proud to publicly embrace (and on whom he has eased US oil sanctions).

A full Russian withdrawal from Ukraine, Nato-backed security guarantees, reparations and an independent international investigation into human rights abuses in the occupied Donbas must be among the minimum demands backed jointly by Europe and the US in any talks. There must be no backsliding. It’s pointless trying to win over Trump personally. There are many smarter, better-informed American politicians who understand US interests. Democrats will soon control both chambers of Congress. They will oversee US government purse strings. And there are still plenty of sensible diplomats in the state department (although Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, cannot be counted among them). As leading Republicans, such as the vice-president, JD Vance, distance themselves from Trump, a gritty, concerted diplomatic offensive in Washington by Burnham, Macron, Merz and the EU commission could yet induce a more realistic, less self-defeating US policy approach – and revive the overall western policy consensus on Russia.

Putin is his own worst enemy. The Trump era represented a golden diplomatic opportunity for him that will not be repeated. Putin is in the process of squandering his chance to cut a face-saving deal over Ukraine and secure what he would see as his legacy. He seems doomed to go down fighting. And that it is what the Nato alliance, which met in emergency session on Monday to discuss the attacks on Poland, must ensure is his fate if he refuses to compromise. Retaliatory, proportionate but offensive and intrinsically hazardous Nato military actions against Russia, pushing back against Putin’s widening wars, will become inescapable if the western democracies jointly fail to get their negotiating act together. In 1914, the British foreign secretary Edward Grey warned “the lamps are going out all over Europe”. As Russia plunges Ukraine into darkness, it looks dismayingly like it’s happening again.

Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch

The Guardian Tue, 24 Nov 2026 07:00:10 GMT

These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Back in the day, when poll tax riots brought down Margaret Thatcher, the issue was that a duke paid the same flat poll tax as the dustman. But nowadays King Charles pays less council tax for Buckingham Palace than nearly half of his subjects. The palace “sits in band H and is charged £1,828 [per year] by Westminster city council, less than an average three-bedroom semi in Blackpool,” notes economist Paul Johnson.

The groundswell for reform may explain the king’s hasty announcement last week that he would now volunteer to pay more council tax. He may foresee the upcoming row about Rachel Reeves’s radical mansion tax, the “high-value council tax surcharge” arriving in April 2028, which will charge homes worth £2m or more £2,500 per year, and those worth £5m or more £7,500 per year. (But why have that cap when the purchaser of a £265m Chelsea property this year would hardly notice the extra pennies?)

It’s easy to see why Jonathan Brash, chair of the all-party group for council tax reform, leads the campaign: he is Labour MP for Hartlepool. If property taxes became proportional to property values, the north and north-east would gain hugely, while the rich in the south would lose. A huge study from the Institute for Fiscal Studies suggested a reform of the system whereby 10.1m households would gain more than £200 a year, while only 4.2m would lose more than £200 a year. The case against council tax is one of straightforward injustice. The case against stamp duty land tax is one of gross distortion, creating business-sapping stasis, deterring older people from downsizing, homeowners from moving away for better jobs and pricing young people out altogether by adding about £4,750 to the cost of buying a typical home.

An anomalous hangover from the transition from the poll tax to council tax gives a damaging 25% council tax discount to single people, with no good reason to disadvantage larger households.

With so many more winners than losers, what’s prevented every recent government from council tax reform when all politicians privately agree it’s needed? We may be about to find out whether their cowardice was justified, as complaints about the forthcoming mansion tax grow from households living in properties worth more than £2m. My local paper, the ace Camden New Journal, frequently publishes letters such as one from this week: “We’re not cash rich so why do our MPs back this unfair tax?” Jill Henry protests that in many districts in the north London borough, “a property valued at £2m is in no way a mansion”. Well, by definition, £2m is a mansion, even if it doesn’t have turrets. Prime location can make it so. There are only about 156,000 of these mansions in England, so block your ears to their noise and their rightwing media foghorns.

The trope is the little old lady with a fixed pension sitting inside the goldmine that is her lifelong home. The answer is it’s time for her to move: she’d do better somewhere cheaper to heat. If not, then she can take out an equity-release loan. Or, a reformed property tax could allow her not to pay it and its accumulated interest until she sells or dies. If she is holding out to leave it to her children and they want to avoid accumulating high interest for delaying her mansion tax charge, then let them pay her council tax bill. Harden your heart to her when she could be cruising the world on the colossal untaxed profit she has made on her home over her lifetime.

Labour MPs holding their nerve in the mansion tax storm may privately wonder if it was worth its projected £400m yield. They should ask why they don’t go the whole way while they’re at it. For all the sound and fury, why not reform all the property taxes in one go? A fair tax, directly proportionate to a home’s value, would be well on the way to creating a wealth tax – and it would be easier to collect as you can’t move a mansion to Monaco, while taxing wealth tied up in pearls, Porsches and paintings is harder.

Property tax reform would depress prices, critics complain. That’s no bad thing. We should celebrate any attempt to reduce the use of homes as a piggy bank, pension, or inheritance store. My generation, without lifting a finger, found their houses become an ever-escalating one-way bet on getting rich: during one period of economic boom my home was earning more in a day than I had when I came back from work in the evening, with all that profit going untaxed.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Look what that has done to young people. It’s long past time to abolish England’s 1991 council tax valuations and claw back from us fortunate homeowners some of our ill-gotten gains. And to build, build, build those promised council houses and new towns.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Andy Burnham’s EU deal leaves Brexit open to question

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:11:21 GMT

Stuart Finegan says the PM deserves credit for his practical steps to rebuild European relations, while Julian Roberts says the point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. Plus letters from Lindsay Bray, Helen Elliott and Nick Smith

Your article (Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy.

Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. Meanwhile, younger generations have seen opportunities to study, work, travel and collaborate across Europe reduced through no fault of their own. The benefits of closer trade links with the UK’s nearest and largest market cannot be overestimated. Yet Nigel Farage and Conservative Brexit supporters have failed to deliver the economic opportunities and global trade advantages they promised.

Andy Burnham deserves credit for acknowledging that Brexit has failed in many respects and for supporting practical steps to rebuild relations with the EU. The choice is no longer between leave and remain; it is between decline and renewal.

The country deserves leaders willing to put economic reality ahead of ideology, and this agreement is a welcome step in that direction. Stuart Finegan Lewes, East Sussex

The sight and sound of former prime ministers criticising Andy Burnham’s proposal to open a discussion on Britain’s future relationship with the EU is unedifying. It is as though they have learned nothing and forgotten nothing, not least their own responsibility for the toxic mess of Brexit. In advising Andy Burnham to “move on”, Theresa May appears to overlook her own stasis (Report, 22 November).

The point of democracy is surely the right of the people to change their minds. We accept this during the routine electoral cycle. Why can we not do so regarding our relationship with the EU? It is inconsistent to argue that the 2016 referendum was binding for all time whereas the 1975 EEC referendum was not.

Labour’s next manifesto should therefore include a commitment to explore and openly present the options, followed by discussions with the EU on the terms that might be on offer and by a referendum, conducted on the same basis as that of 2016, whether to accept those terms. Julian Roberts Leatherhead, Surrey

Your report describes Andy Burnham’s push for closer European alignment as a political gamble (Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform, 20 November. Yet by anchoring his case in the prospect of stronger GDP growth, he is simply returning to the hard-headed economic logic that has governed Britain’s relationship with Europe for more than half a century.

When Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973, the argument was never built on federalist sentiment. It sought access to a dynamic continental market to revive sluggish growth and boost exports. Two years later, in the 1975 referendum, voters overwhelmingly backed remaining for the exact same bread-and-butter reasons, just as British economic self-interest later drove the creation of the single market.

Seen through this historical lens, 2016 was not the culmination of a longstanding economic critique but a political aberration. In the runup to the Brexit referendum, rational debate over trade and living standards was hijacked by a toxic combination of Boris Johnson’s ruthless personal ambition for the Tory leadership and visceral anxieties over borders – anxieties turbocharged by Angela Merkel’s 2015 decision to open Germany’s doors to about a million Syrian refugees. Leave campaigners weaponised those images.

Britain’s European story has always been one of economic necessity; Burnham is merely picking up where we left off. Lindsay Bray Ferndown, Dorset

Among all the scenarios citing the fact that things are different now than in 2016, the most significant is not being commented on. The current 18- to 28-year-old demographic was not eligible to vote. Perhaps an opinion poll of this cohort of now eligible potential voters would tell us a lot about the direction of travel. Helen Elliott Ruishton, Somerset

Ten years ago, the UK had a referendum to decide whether to stay or leave the EU. In a once-in-a-generation vote, this country decided to leave. As a generation is generally accepted as being between 25 and 30 years, why is there now talk of rejoining? A democratic decision was made and must be respected. We voted out: out means we leave, not hover on the doorstep. Nick Smith London

A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:09:00 GMT

Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction

The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all (UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November).

The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines.

Specialist species have been hit particularly hard. The willow tit, which depends on young wet woodland, is nearing extinction. Its close relative, the marsh tit, has had a catastrophic fall in numbers. As woodlands become increasingly fragmented, their populations are left isolated and vulnerable. We know that creating larger, better-connected habitats can help these species, but too little has been done to create and protect them.

There is, however, reason for hope. The recovery of the Dartford warbler from near extinction in the 1960s shows what is possible when suitable habitat is properly protected. When governments invest in and support nature, species can recover.

We have the evidence. We understand many of the causes of decline and what needs to be done. The government must now respond to this legal failure with long-term investment and action before more of our cherished birds disappear. Emma Phipps Scientific research and impact manager, SongBird Survival

Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear

The Guardian Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:04:25 GMT

There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg

Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere. At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption. Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources. Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies. James White and Nora Söderberg Department of Technology and Society, Lund University
