An Adored Manhattan Grocery, and Seinfeld Favorite, May Close Its Doors

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Zingone Bros. is beloved on the Upper West Side. That might not be enough to keep it open.

Zingone Bros. is beloved on the Upper West Side. That might not be enough to keep it open.

After some 50 years of six-days-a-week, 12-hours-on-your-feet days, Dominick Zingone is ready to retire. Credit... Anna Connors for The New York Times

Supported by

By Katherine Rosman

Zingone Bros., the family-run market that has operated on the Upper West Side of Manhattan for 99 years, is the kind of place where longtime customers sign a receipt for a quart of milk and pay their bill at the end of the month. Where neighbors leave a spare set of keys. Where children stop on their way to school to pet Oliver, the orange tabby bodega cat.

And so earlier this month, after the West Side Rag reported that Zingone Bros. was set to close on Nov. 30, people inside the store on Columbus Avenue, between 82nd and 83rd Streets, were awash in disbelief.

Melissa Salten Rothman stopped in Thursday to pick up a few items, and thank the Zingones. She described the family as an extension of her own, and as a centerpiece of the neighborhood.

“When people would come here to visit,” she said, “my kids would say, ‘Have you taken them to the American Museum of Natural History? Have you taken them to Zingones?’”

As Ms. Rothman elegized, another customer could be heard down the aisle. “What am I going to do when I need a melon?” the woman lamented to Nicholas Zingone Sr., 91. “No one else can pick a melon like you do.”

Dominick Zingone, 66, who is Nick Sr.’s nephew, and Richie Zingone, 61, one of his sons, were working in the vegetable aisle, making sure the produce was fresh and nicely stacked. Nick Sr.’s other son, Nicholas Zingone Jr., was loading a cardboard box with Thanksgiving items — 40 Yukon Gold potatoes, two pounds of butter, four loaves of white bread — that a customer had called for. At Zingones, delivery orders still come in over the phone. (“You ring, we bring,” said Nick Jr., 54.)

It had been an emotional week. “I knew people would be sad,” Richie said, “but I didn’t know it would feel like someone had died, that it would feel like a shiva.”

New Yorkers understand that the city’s retail landscape is constantly evolving. They are sentimental yet pragmatic, prone to telling their children about the bar that was on the corner before it became a CVS and the deli that was up the block before the Pilates studio took over. This is how it goes. New York looks back as it looks forward, a modern city steeped in nostalgia.

But longtime residents of this slice of the Upper West Side not far from Central Park say this hits differently. They fear that Zingone Bros., which locals refer to simply as “Zingones,” will take with it something that can’t be replaced.

“There are certain things only time can make,” said Jerry Seinfeld, the comedian, who has lived in the neighborhood since 1976 and has shopped at the market for nearly as long.

“Zingones is one of those things,” he said. “It cannot be made by man.”

Mr. Seinfeld said Zingones was the first place he and his wife had let their children walk to by themselves when they were in elementary school.

“It’s just like home,” he said. “It just smells like home. A store that has the comfort and the familiarity of home is what makes a neighborhood a neighborhood.”

John McEnroe, the tennis legend, said in an email that he loved trudging down through the basement at Zingones to pick out a Christmas tree, making sure to duck his head on the way down. “I can’t believe they’re closing,” he said.

Zingone Bros. was opened on the Upper West Side by Domenico and Vicenzo Zingone, brothers who had immigrated from Praiano, Italy. It was 1927. Calvin Coolidge was president and the Ford Motor Company made its final Model T.

In the store’s early days, Vicenzo and Domenico shared a space with a butcher named Carl, said Andrew Alpern, 88, who lived as a child on West 82nd Street. Not much of his childhood remains, so Mr. Alpern was shocked and delighted a few years ago when, as he was traveling down Columbus Avenue on a bus, he spotted Zingone Bros., still in the same spot. “I said, ‘Holy mackerel!’” he recalled.

By the 1960s, Domenico’s sons, Nick Sr. and Ralph, had joined the family business in earnest, eventually taking over Zingones and running it with the assistance of a cousin, Angelo Zingone. When Ralph died in 1976, his wife Giuseppina Zingone, known as Josephine, began to help at the cash register, where she sat perched on a stool for nearly 50 years. She died in 2023, at 91.

The store saw its neighborhood through World War II, urban decay, urban renewal, hippies, yippies, yuppies, hip-hop, Covid and the opening and shuttering of butchers, bakers and Blockbuster Videos.

But what Zingones could not survive, the men said, was the new era of internet grocery delivery, as well as recent tariffs, the rising cost of doing business in New York and concerns about whether the fourth generation would want to run a market as a lifelong career.

Dominick is ready to retire. After some 50 years of six-days-a-week, 12-hours-on-your-feet days, he said, “I’m really drained.” Nick Sr., Nick Jr. and Richie want to keep the business going but they would need to buy out relatives — as in many multigenerational family businesses, not everyone sees eye to eye on the future — and are losing hope that they can swing it.

“The only way to stay alive,” Nick Jr. said, “is if we have a fairy godmother.”

His daughter, Ariel Zingone, 18, is worried about what her father, her uncles and her grandfather — especially — will do without Zingones. Her grandmother Evelyn Zingone died in August, and now “the store is my grandpa’s entire life,” she said. One of Richie’s daughters, Erica Zingone, 26, said she, her sisters and her cousins had grown up watching their parents give the neighborhood “the care, attention and hospitality” the store was known for. “It feels like we are losing a loved one,” she said.

The Zingone family has shown up for the community and the community has reciprocated. When Richie performs stand-up comedy, customers come out to support him. The singer David Lee Roth used to be a customer, and when Van Halen performed at Madison Square Garden decades ago, he arranged for the Zingones to have six tickets, right up by the stage.

Mary Vinci, Dominick’s sister, kept the store’s books and served as the emotional heart of the place. After she was diagnosed with cancer several years ago, J. J. Grabenstein, a customer since 2001, volunteered to help care for Oliver the cat, as Mary had done.

When Mary died from complications related to cancer in 2022, the neighborhood went into mourning. Bouquets of flowers piled up at the door of the store.

Ms. Grabenstein continues to dote on Oliver, taking him to the vet and attending to his grooming. The cat likes to “meet and greet people,” she said, adding: “He is a true Zingone.”

She said she was now making plans for Oliver to find a new home.

Zingone Bros. and Oliver were immortalized by Olivia Rodrigo, the pop star, who filmed the music video for her hit single “Stupid Song” at the store last spring. But the news of an impending closure has prompted a more in-depth look by David Koepp, a filmmaker who co-wrote the screenplay for “Jurassic Park,” and his wife, Melissa Thomas, a former news producer.

“Honey, I think we’ve got to get over there with a couple of cameras,” Mr. Koepp recalled his wife saying when they learned that Zingones’ days were numbered.

They have been recording these final days. “Half the people we interview start crying immediately,” Mr. Koepp said, “and the other half start crying without much prodding when we ask, ‘How do you feel about Zingones not being here anymore?’”

Andrew Briedis, a screenwriter who lived above Zingones with his wife for 11 years, said that the store represented the city’s still-enduring promise of being a place where immigrants could build a long-lasting family business — one that would not just be accepted by the community but might help to define it.

“When you imagine what New York is supposed to be,” he said, “you first see the skyline — and then you zero in, and Zingones perfectly exemplifies what you dream New York to be.”

When he learned the news that the store planned to close, Mr. Briedis recorded a video and posted it online. “It’s like telling me they’re going to take down the Empire State Building,” he told his followers.

Standing at the front of the store last week, Dominick, Richie and Nick Jr. huddled around a phone, watching Mr. Briedis’s video.

“I love that guy,” Dominick said, “but he used to buy so many carrots that he started to turn orange.” (Mr. Briedis was astounded that Dominick remembered his carrot obsession, which he agreed was excessive.)

He may have left the neighborhood five years ago, but a Zingone never forgets.

In the video, Mr. Briedis shared his appreciation for all that Zingones had done for him and his wife — holding a spare set of their keys, accepting their Amazon packages, offering their neighborly friendship. When he talked about Mary and Josephine, his eyes welled up.

He wasn’t the only one. By the time the video ended, all three of the Zingone men — whose grandfathers started the business together nearly a century ago — had tears rolling down their cheeks.

Katherine Rosman covers newsmakers, power players and individuals making an imprint on New York City.

U. S. Spy Agencies Suffer Breach of Some Unclassified Information

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The intrusion affecting the C. I. A. and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence comes amid heightened concerns about cybersecurity.

By Dustin VolzTyler Pager and Julian E. Barnes

Dustin Volz and Julian Barnes reported from Washington, and Tyler Pager from New York.

The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information, according to U. S. officials and other people familiar with the matter.

The intrusions affected an open-source intelligence analysis system, a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, unclassified material, the people familiar with the issues said.

It was not clear specifically what information was compromised, but classified material was not jeopardized, the people said. Information at other government agencies was also believed to have been exposed in the breach, according to two of the people, one of whom said the issue had been resolved.

Open-source intelligence can include vast troves of commercially available data sets, social media content, satellite imagery and other online material. Much of it is publicly available, but it can include information sold by data vendors that can be highly revealing, especially when combined with other tranches of data.

Spy agencies can also use the data alongside other sources of intelligence to inform analytical judgments.

It is not uncommon for federal agencies to suffer cybersecurity breaches, but several have recently detected intrusions into some of their systems, prompting heightened concern among current and former U. S. intelligence officials.

The officials and others familiar with the matter spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive security matter that had not been made public.

An official with the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there had been no disruptions to critical capabilities. The C. I. A. declined to comment.

The episode coincides with a surge of technological disruptions, including a dayslong outage last week of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network that officials and businesses said were not the result of cyberattacks. The problems have rattled the American public. U. S. officials say that in some cases, artificial intelligence is uncovering software vulnerabilities that need to be quickly patched.

In this instance, it appears that a hacker gained unauthorized access to at least one government system, though the people familiar with the matter did not say whether investigators knew who was responsible.

It is just the most recent breach of government systems to surface recently. Last week, President Trump appeared to confirm that the F. B. I.’s National Crime Information Center — a nationwide database used to swap information among local, state and federal law enforcement agencies about criminal suspects — had recently been hacked.

“I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Mr. Trump said on Saturday during a phone interview with Fox News when asked about the F. B. I. breach, which CNN had reported earlier. The F. B. I. is investigating the breach, according to people familiar with the matter.

Also last week, the U. S. Department of Agriculture discovered a cybersecurity incident that led to some of its internal applications being taken offline, according to a department employee. News of the U. S. D. A. matter was reported earlier by Nextgov, a site that focuses on federal government technology issues.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, whom Mr. Trump recently tapped as his acting cyber director, appeared on several news programs on Sunday trying to quell rising public anxieties about recent technology outages, including the national air grounding this month. Officials have said the grounding was caused by issues related to router maintenance.

Pressed on the recent hack of the F. B. I. crime database, Mr. Clayton said breaches occurred frequently and that there was no cause for alarm.

“Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time,” Mr. Clayton said on ABC’s “This Week.”

“And what we’re hearing about the F. B. I., and what I’ve talked to them about is, they have an incident. They’re dealing with it in the ordinary course.”

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees and Says He Is in Therapy

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

A day after returning to his company, Mr. Huang acknowledged that he had violated Nvidia’s code of conduct and “made some terrible mistakes.”

By Tripp Mickle and Kalley Huang

Reporting from San Francisco

A day after returning as chief executive at Nvidia, Jensen Huang apologized on Tuesday to his entire company for violating its code of conduct during an hourlong meeting that began on a somber note before transforming into a defiant airing of grievances.

“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said in his first all-hands meeting with employees since his return. Referring to his wife, he added, “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, hurt all of you.”

Mr. Huang said he is in therapy every day for 90 minutes, adding that it is “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct, some of which he wrote. He said his actions had forced the company’s board of directors to evaluate his future with the company, which led him to resign this month.

The meeting cemented Mr. Huang’s return to Nvidia after two head-spinning weeks that threw the chip-making giant into turmoil, sent tech stocks into a nosedive and threatened the tech industry’s artificial intelligence boom.

Mr. Huang resigned after revelations that he violated the company’s code of conduct. He had an affair with a customer and Chinese citizen, Alice Huang, who U. S. government officials determined was feeding information to Chinese intelligence services. He also had a relationship with a direct report at the company. The company’s board unanimously accepted his resignation.

While Wall Street has cheered Mr. Huang’s reinstatement, there are still broad questions about his conduct, and he is expected to testify in a series of potentially contentious congressional hearings in Washington next week.

During his talk with employees, Mr. Huang sought to dismiss narratives about what had happened behind the scenes to ease his return. He said he was back not because he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law” and “above the code of conduct.” Nor was he back, he said, because President Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

“That is also completely untrue,” Mr. Huang said in a livestream that was reviewed by The New York Times. He was back, he said, because Nvidia’s board “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts.” It also received assurances from the Trump administration that Mr. Huang was not a national security threat.

Tuesday’s meeting was the second in the past six days at Nvidia. Last Wednesday, Colette Kress, who served as interim chief executive, sought to reassure a rattled company by telling employees that Nvidia’s “ambition will not change.” She was joined onstage by more than a dozen of the company’s leaders, several of whom spoke about how they planned to move forward without Mr. Huang.

Mr. Huang began Tuesday’s talk by thanking Ms. Kress and the company’s leadership team, which was seated on the front row, for doing “an incredible job.”

He also praised Mr. Trump, who had encouraged the board to bring back Mr. Huang. He said Mr. Trump “really, really loves our company” and “gloats about Nvidia.”

“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Mr. Huang said.

Mr. Huang said he would be “in service of helping our president make our country successful,” but he said that did not make Nvidia a political company.

“Not even a little bit,” he said. “We are the most apolitical company.”

Mr. Huang told employees that he had returned to the company because Nvidia’s board had decided it was “in the best interest of the company and shareholders.”

He also said the board’s decision did not mean other employees could violate the code of conduct. That would not be “appropriate” or “tolerated,” he said.

“Sometimes, it’s appropriate to forgive,” he said. “Sometimes it’s not.”

Mr. Huang addressed a report by The Times about his management style, which he had described in the past as “torture you into greatness.” For years, he berated employees with insults, personal attacks and violent comments.

“I can go too far,” Mr. Huang said. “When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right.”

Mr. Huang said Nvidia’s human resources department would collect feedback about him and share it monthly with the board of directors. He said he wanted to make sure he was “able to channel my intensity in the service of making our company better.”

He also attacked criticism of the company’s organizational structure, in which he had more than 60 direct reports, while boasting that he doesn’t “believe in succession planning” because it would imply some executives were more important than others.

In his defense of Nvidia’s unusual management structure, Mr. Huang said it was “his pride and joy.” He credited it with allowing the company to move fast, innovate often and continue operating in his absence.

“This company is wired up to execute and execute and execute and deliver on financial results,” he said. He said any of the company’s top 60 executives could succeed him.

“That is the definition of an extraordinary organization, not an example of brittleness,” he said. “I will fight that all day long.”

Tripp Mickle reports for The Times on some of the world’s biggest tech companies, including Nvidia, Google and Apple. He also writes about tech industry trends like layoffs and artificial intelligence.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering the technology industry and its largest companies, including Nvidia and Apple.

The Mississippi Senate Race Wasn’t Even This Year’s Biggest Upset

The New York Times November 24, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

We found the most unlikely winners of the 2026 midterms.

By C. J. Robinson

Even amid the many surprises in this year’s Democratic rout in the midterms, Scott Colom’s win in the Mississippi Senate race — the first by a Democrat in more than 40 years — was a stunning upset. Prediction markets gave Mr. Colom a 15 percent chance of success; expert forecasters suggested even lower odds, at 2 to 4 percent.

But by those measures, the race wasn’t this year’s most unexpected result, according to a New York Times analysis.

That distinction goes to Tennessee’s Fourth House District, called on Tuesday by The Associated Press for Victoria Broderick, a Democrat.

Prediction market odds

Forecasting models put Ms. Broderick’s probability of winning at less than 1 percent, and markets were only slightly more generous. The Cook Political Report rated the race as “Solid Republican,” its strongest confidence category. In the end, Ms. Broderick won by about two-tenths of a percentage point. The Republican incumbent, Scott DesJarlais, won the seat by 43 points in 2024, though under different boundaries.

Earlier this year, Tennessee Republicans led a mid-decade effort to redraw the state’s congressional map. They primarily aimed to eliminate the state’s lone Democratic seat, in Memphis, but also redrew boundaries around Nashville, including the Fourth District. The new map added parts of Nashville and neighboring Rutherford County, increasing the district’s share of Democratic voters.

Even accounting for the new boundaries, Tennessee’s Fourth is the most Republican-leaning seat won by a Democrat this year, based on President Trump’s 2024 winning margin in the district — about 24 points.

The race is one of many big surprises from this year’s midterms, which we ranked using a combination of odds from some of the leading prediction markets and election forecasting models.

Prediction market odds

Prediction market odds

Prediction market odds

Prediction market odds

Prediction market odds

Five of the top 10 most surprising victories, by this measure, occurred in North Carolina. Roy Cooper, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, benefited from some of the largest partisan shifts among voters compared with other battleground states, according to Times Voter Trends. His big victory may have helped lift down-ballot candidates, and North Carolina’s redistricting probably backfired against Republicans.

Republicans flipped Maine’s Second District, as well as two redistricted seats in Texas and Tennessee, but in those races the Republicans were slightly favored in forecasts and prediction markets and didn’t make our upsets list. All of the most surprising wins went to Democrats. (Our analysis includes only races called by The Associated Press. The race in Minnesota’s First District, currently led by a Democrat, would make our list if the current margin held.)

“Every year we know there are going to be surprises,” said Amy Walter, publisher and editor in chief of The Cook Political Report, which uses qualitative interviews, demographic information and polling to forecast races. But, she added, “the number of them flipping this time was quite extraordinary, and speaks to how unprecedented this wave was.”

Mr. Colom said on X that his race’s initial “Solid Republican” rating — which Cook had changed to “Likely Republican” by the end of the campaign — made it “difficult to fund-raise” and was part of a pattern of neglect for contests in the South.

Modelers and prediction markets largely agreed on the projected winners for most races. In the months before the election, leading prediction markets performed no better than forecasts on average, according to a Times analysis. But prediction markets, like Kalshi and Polymarket, became more accurate in the days leading up to Nov. 3.

In several races, prediction markets moved the Democrat’s odds slightly higher shortly before the election, seemingly anticipating the possibility of an upset. Prediction market traders could consult forecasts from modelers to inform their bets, and could also react to new information, like early vote counts, closer to Election Day.

On both prediction markets and forecast models, a common misconception is that a low-probability estimate of victory, like 10 percent, means it’s almost impossible for a candidate to win. In reality, the expectation is that these underdogs will actually win 10 percent of the time.

And there weren’t that many more upsets this year than expected, said G. Elliott Morris, who helps run the polling aggregation and election forecasting website FiftyPlusOne. FiftyPlusOne’s models can estimate how many upsets may happen, and only a handful more races defied their forecasts than expected, given polling and other signals.

Some markets had relatively low trading volume, which may have made their forecasts less reliable. Texas’ Ninth District had just over $100,000 in trades, for example, according to its Polymarket page. By contrast, users traded nearly $32 million over which party would control the Senate. Less prominent races also had less information for forecasters to pull from.

In addition to data from previous elections and demographics, Cook relies on information from political insiders to determine ratings for lower-profile races like Tennessee’s Fourth, and occasionally uses internal polling from campaigns to make calls. It can move races away from “Solid” as they appear more competitive, and vice versa.

This year, two Democrats won races that Cook rated as “Solid Republican.”

“You will still wake up in the middle of the night saying, ‘Man, I wish we had moved that,’” Ms. Walter said.

About the data

The Times used race probabilities from Polymarket, Kalshi, Silver Bulletin and FiftyPlusOne one day before Election Day. Any race where at least one forecaster or market put the winner’s chances at 50 percent or less is included.

Races are ordered by an average ranking of upsets by each forecaster or market. With Polymarket, for example, Mississippi’s Senate race is considered its fourth-largest upset because it gave slightly lower probabilities to three House districts that flipped. The Mississippi race is FiftyPlusOne’s second-largest upset because it gave all other flipped races besides the Tennessee race better odds for the Democrat to win. We then averaged those rankings for each market and model, not including Cook.

Prediction market odds over time are daily averages of Kalshi and Polymarket.

Stuart A. Thompson and Evan Reynolds contributed reporting.

C. J. Robinson is a reporting fellow at The Upshot and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Trump’s Nvidia Move Heralds a New Front in Economic Intervention

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Presidents before him have bailed out companies in times of national crisis. Mr. Trump went further: He staked the fortunes of the United States on those of a favored chief executive.

By Patricia Cohen

Patricia Cohen is the global economics correspondent in London.

As great-power politics increasingly revolve around technology, trade and finance, private businesses have been thrust to the front lines of foreign policy, often unwillingly.

For many global titans and mom-and-pop shops, the growing use of tariffs and export restrictions has forced them to sacrifice their bottom lines in the interests of national security.

Then there’s what happened this week.

President Trump’s decision to personally lobby Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as chief executive despite a China-related spy scandal reversed those priorities. Mr. Trump swept aside national security concerns to revive the fortunes of a single corporation — even a single executive — that he views as critical to the American economy and stock market.

“An individual C. E. O. has just demonstrated that the interests of his company can trump U. S. national security,” said Edward Fishman, director of the geoeconomics center at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Nvidia, a Silicon Valley giant worth some $4 trillion, has been at the center of an intense global competition with China for an edge in artificial intelligence. Mr. Huang resigned this month after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who U. S. intelligence officials believed was spying for the Chinese government.

Mr. Trump said he did not view Mr. Huang as a national security threat. “I just thought he should be running the company,” he told The New York Times on Monday.

His extraordinary intervention has surprised and worried Republican lawmakers in Washington and longstanding allies.

“It shocked me, to be honest,” Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister, said on Tuesday. “⁠In ⁠free, democratic and rules-based countries, political power should refrain from interfering ⁠in the economic engagement ​of companies.”

Presidents before have pushed into the affairs of industry and even individual companies during national emergencies and wartime.

But Julian E. Zelizer, a presidential historian at Princeton University, said Mr. Trump’s intervention is “very different from how other presidents have acted.”

“It’s the stock market first,” Mr. Zelizer said. “National security seems secondary. ”

President Harry S. Truman temporarily seized control of steel mills to prevent a strike during the Korean War. After the steel companies sued, the U. S. Supreme Court struck down the president’s order as unconstitutional.

A decade later, President John F. Kennedy pressured steel companies to roll back a planned price increase. And in 2009, amid a quickening global financial crisis, President Barack Obama pushed out the chairman of General Motors as part of a multibillion-dollar bailout of the auto industry.

But Mr. Trump’s role in the boardroom decisions of Nvidia is in a different category, historians and analysts said.

“This is a whole other level,” Mr. Zelizer said. “It’s a kind of Trumpian socialism we’re seeing.”

Mr. Trump’s move doubles down on other actions he has taken in the affairs of private companies. By the end of 2025, the Trump administration had committed more than $10 billion of taxpayer money to buy up ownership shares of companies it considered essential to national security, including Intel, Westinghouse and U. S. Steel.

Mr. Trump has cultivated relationships with technology chiefs, especially Mr. Huang. In 2025, Nvidia agreed to give the federal government a cut of the revenue it generated from the sale of approved chips to China. It also said it would route deliveries of chips produced in Taiwan through the United States so the government could collect a 25 percent tariff and do security checks.

The administration’s dealings with Nvidia reflect a broader trend: the growing centrality of economic warfare.

Military conflicts, of course, continue. And nuclear weapons constitute a profound threat. But the world’s most powerful nations are relying more on their economic arsenals than their military ones.

The cooperative global order that prevailed after the fall of the Berlin Wall has crumbled, and statecraft has increasingly revolved around the tools of economic coercion. A long list of weapons have been put to greater use: tariffs, sanctions, export controls, the freezing of assets, prohibitions on financial transactions, access to loans and more.

The shift has at times pressed companies into active duty. President Joseph R. Biden Jr. barred Russia from the global financial system after it invaded Ukraine in 2022, counting on private banks rather than public offices to carry out the restrictions.

Now the sweep of policy coming out of Washington is directly affecting the bottom line of companies and banks more than it has in the previous three decades, said Josh Lipsky, senior director of the GeoEconomics Center of the Atlantic Council, a research institute.

“I think that trajectory is only going to continue,” Mr. Lipsky said.

Government restrictions on international business dealings have soared, according to a recent study that surveyed earnings calls and analyst reports from thousands of firms around the world.

China has increasingly been a target. In 2022, the Biden administration imposed sweeping limits on China’s access to semiconductor and other technology. And last week, the Trump administration pushed ahead with a new rule to restrict China’s access to advanced A. I. chips through the use of data centers outside its borders.

China, too, has sharply stepped up its use of restrictions on exports. In 2023 and 2024, China designated five Western companies as “unreliable entities” and put them on its export control list. In 2025, 76 companies, including Raytheon, Boeing and Lockheed Martin, were added.

This spring, Beijing blocked Meta’s acquisition of an A. I. start-up founded by Chinese entrepreneurs, citing rules about foreign investment and technology exports. It has also kept a tight rein on the foreign sales of critical rare earth elements, using control over their export to punish and pressure trading partners on diplomatic issues like Taiwan.

“The share of global firms that report being affected by export controls has tripled in recent years compared to the 2010s,” said Matteo Maggiori, a professor of finance at Stanford Graduate School of Business, part of the team that conducted the research.

The vast majority of cases in which political leaders have sought to pressure countries abroad, Mr. Maggiori said, involved “private sector firms that are arm’s length from the government.”

American and European companies have frequently pushed back against trade and other restrictions imposed by their democratically elected governments that they viewed as harmful.

By contrast, authoritarian governments in China and Russia have much tighter control of the market and businesses. That grip can be an advantage when a government wants to deploy economic tools to achieve foreign policy goals, Mr. Fishman at the Council on Foreign Relations noted.

When China imposes export controls, “it’s almost more like military power,” he said. “I do think there’s a real question around whether our distinctly American model of free market capitalism is well suited to the current age of geoeconomics.”

At the same time, he added, that model has produced extraordinary innovation, which has given the United States a strategic edge.

Mr. Trump’s intervention goes against that tradition. Mr. Wadephul, the German foreign minister, cited the Nvidia news in his speech before the Berlin Foreign Policy Forum on Tuesday. He warned against political leaders meddling so intimately in the affairs of private companies in democratic countries.

“I do have some doubts whether this is a very good model ⁠for the future,” he said.

Tatiana Firsova contributed reporting from Berlin.

Patricia Cohen writes about global economics for The Times and is based in London.

Detonation in Iowa Is on Track for Wednesday, but Weather Adds to Risks

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Planned Explosion in Iowa

Advertisement

Supported by

Freezing temperatures threaten to make the degrading explosives even more unstable, while winds could carry a toxic lead plume up to 100 miles away.

By Quinn Glabicki and Hiroko Tabuchi

Quinn Glabicki reported from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown and Hiroko Tabuchi from New York City.

As worries mounted over a planned detonation of toxic materials in Iowa, government and military officials sought to reassure people on Tuesday that the explosion would be handled safely and said that residents around the city of Middletown may be evacuated.

An alert from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, issued just before 8:30 local time, said residents within five miles southwest of the plant could be evacuated and warned residents within 20 miles to stay indoors to avoid dust, noise and vibrations.

The Army plans to detonate a cache of dangerously degrading explosive materials at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa at 9 a. m. local time on Wednesday.

An interagency team “has been working around the clock” to “protect the health and safety of the citizens of this region,” Adam R. Telle, acting secretary of the Army, said in a briefing at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant.

Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, head of Army Sustainment Command, speaking at the same briefing, said the goal of the operation was “zero release of lead particulate into the atmosphere.”

The explosion, which had previously been delayed three times, threatens to launch a cloud of toxic lead dust over homes and farmland and has triggered widespread confusion and alarm among residents, farmers and local elected officials.

Temperatures dropped on Tuesday morning and frost dusted the fields surrounding the facility. The Army has warned that freezing temperatures threaten to make the lead azide increasingly unstable and may cause it to explode spontaneously. The Army did not say where residents would be evacuated to.

“We understand your frustration,” Mr. Telle said. “We’ve taken every viable solution and considered it.”

“Now, we’ve got to go execute over the next 24 hours,” he said.

Still, new details pointed to concerns about the condition of the explosives and the state in which they have been stored.

The New York Times

The Army was working to flood the tops of storage bunkers with fire-suppressing foam, Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the U. S. Army’s 71st Ordnance Group, said at the briefing. “They’re approximately 80 years old, and they’re deteriorating,” he said. “We’ve observed cracks in the concrete.”

That meant there was “a good possibility” that the tops of the bunkers would blow during the detonation, he said. To mitigate that, the Army last night added a containment screen to trap lead. Two feet of aqueous foam, a fire suppression agent, would go on top of that, he said.

The planned operation comes after a federal court late Monday rejected a request for an emergency stay from several environmental groups.

The forecast for colder weather in Iowa has made the task more urgent, because freezing temperatures could fracture the unstable crystals of lead azide inside the barrels, potentially triggering an uncontrolled explosion.

Maps released by the Army this morning showed that the plume from the detonation would travel southwest from the plant, and potentially as far as 100 miles into northeast Missouri. The plume models showed that lead could be deposited over as many as 148 square miles. The government has also deployed weather balloons to gauge conditions over the area, said Andy Nelson, a director at the Army’s Construction Engineering Research Laboratory.

The Environmental Protection Agency said it had dispatched sampling teams that were preparing to track the plume. Richard Fordyce, under secretary at the Department of Agriculture, said there were approximately 350 farms that could be affected based on the plume’s anticipated direction.

Scott Dance contributed reporting from Washington.

Quinn Glabicki is a climate reporter for The New York Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

Democrat Flips Tennessee House Seat in One of Biggest 2026 Upsets

The New York Times November 24, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Democrats’ midterm rout kept expanding in the House after a tech support worker ousted an eight-term Republican without having aired a single TV ad.

By John Yoon and Emily Cochrane

Democrats picked up their 259th seat in the House on Tuesday, as their victory in a sprawling district in Tennessee gave them their largest majority in three decades.

Victoria Broderick, a progressive tech support worker who ran for the House as a Democrat, narrowly defeated Representative Scott DesJarlais, according to The Associated Press, unseating an eight-term Republican in one of the biggest upsets this cycle.

Her victory in Tennessee’s Fourth Congressional District will give the Democrats their biggest majority since the early 1990s, when the party held 267 seats. In the largest House majority on record, Democrats won 334 seats in 1936. Republicans won their largest House majority, 302 seats, in 1920.

“Whether you voted for me or not, I want you to know that I will be your representative,” Ms. Broderick said in a statement Tuesday. “I look forward to listening and doing the work you’ve entrusted me to do.”

A few House races were not yet called as of Tuesday, including Minnesota’s First District, which will advance to a recount on Nov. 30, and Louisiana’s Fifth and Sixth Districts, where runoff elections are scheduled in December. In all three districts, which President Trump won, Democrats were leading overall by a slim margin.

Ms. Broderick’s victory was one of the most striking upsets by Democrats in the midterms in part because many election forecasters had rated her race as solidly Republican. Mr. Trump had won the Fourth District by 24 points in 2024, making it the constituency most strongly aligned with Mr. Trump that Democrats have taken so far. And Mr. DesJarlais defeated Ms. Broderick by 43 points just two years ago.

She had also been outspent by a vast margin. Her campaign spent just over $90,000, compared with $508,000 spent by Mr. DesJarlais, according to Federal Election Commission data. Her campaign had no record of airing a television ad.

“I just sat there in just disbelief,” Ms. Broderick said in an interview published the week after Election Day, when she led Mr. DesJarlais by fewer than 300 votes. “It was surreal.”

Ms. Broderick became the only Democrat in Tennessee’s new congressional delegation. Republicans had carved up the state’s congressional map after a Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965, in an effort to sweep all nine House districts, including a reliably Democratic one that had included Memphis. The new boundaries added part of Nashville and neighboring Rutherford County to a district that runs to the southern edge of the state, making it lean less Republican than before.

Before the race was formally called, Mr. DesJarlais said in a statement on Nov. 16 that he had conceded to Ms. Broderick. “All of us hope that the new Member of Congress feels the same level of awe and gratitude for this tremendous undertaking that I felt every day I had the privilege of serving,” he wrote.

Ms. Broderick, 34, was born in Brandon, Fla., and lived in several places in the South, including in San Antonio and Atlanta, before her family moved to Tennessee in 2007, she said in an interview. She said she was involved with the Democratic Party in high school, but her experience of a miscarriage in 2021 helped deepen her political activism.

The failure of her intrauterine device, or IUD, led her to discover that she was pregnant, she said. Ms. Broderick had to navigate the medical care system, and then miscarried, which she described as an education in the physical challenges of a pregnancy.

About a month later, she said, she became pregnant again. While she was on maternity leave after having her baby, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. That decision, she said, compelled her to act.

“I can’t stand by anymore,” she recalled thinking. “I have to do more.”

She began talking about politics on TikTok and became a chairwoman of the Lincoln County Democratic Party. In 2024, she ran for Congress.

She said throughout her recent campaign that she supported abortion rights, along with progressive policies like Medicare for all, a proposal for universal government-funded health insurance. She also identifies as a member of the L. G. B. T. Q. community.

She said that her campaign, which also focused on affordability and reducing inequality, was informed by her experience in the service industry.

“This wasn’t a right or left fight for me,” she said. “This was a bottom versus top.”

Ms. Broderick defeated Mr. DesJarlais by less than one point, or about 270 votes out of more than 195,000 cast.

“We did not have the political machine behind us,” she wrote on social media on Nov. 4, the day after Election Day. “We didn’t have corporate PAC money, we didn’t have powerful insiders. We had you, the people.”

That day, Ms. Broderick said, she told her boss she needed the day off because she might have been elected to Congress. The next day, she wrote in a statement: “This win is a testament to the fact that working class people, people just like you, have a place in deciding your today and your tomorrow.”

John Yoon is a Times political reporter based in New York.

Emily Cochrane is a national reporter for The Times covering the American South, based in Nashville.

Smithsonian Boss Defends Autonomy After Report of Trump Overhaul Plan

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Lonnie Bunch wrote a letter intended to calm his staff after an outline of major personnel and programming changes was seen on a White House aide’s computer.

By Robin Pogrebin

The secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, Lonnie G. Bunch III, reasserted its independence in a letter to his staff on Tuesday in response to a report that a Trump aide had been spotted with a document detailing a major overhaul.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Mr. Bunch wrote. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

The outline was photographed on a laptop the aide was using on the Washington Metro. It laid out plans to fire Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of spreading “radical activist ideology.”

Other top administrators and curators would also be dismissed, according to the memo, and a new permanent exhibition called “The Riches of Our Western Civilizational Inheritance” would be established. Among a raft of other proposed changes, the plan included erecting a huge statue of George Washington outside the history museum, a request that President Trump made online in September.

ProPublica on Monday identified the staff member whose computer held the plan as an associate policy adviser with the White House’s Domestic Policy Council. In July, that group released a report criticizing the Smithsonian for “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”

The White House has not responded to requests for comment on whether such a plan is under active consideration. It would face a number of hurdles, including that the Smithsonian has long operated as independent of the executive branch, though most of its $1 billion annual budget comes from the federal government.

The institution reasserted its autonomy this year when President Trump tried to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery over what he described as partisan bias. But the director ultimately decided to resign.

The Smithsonian, which includes 21 museums and the National Zoo, is governed by a bipartisan 17-member Board of Regents, made of nine citizen trustees, six members of Congress (split between the parties), Vice President JD Vance and the chief justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr. Amid the turmoil, six of the citizen regents seats have gone vacant without any replacement names being sent for appointment to Congress. But Mr. Bunch would appear to currently have the support of a majority of the remaining 11 regents.

Representative Chellie Pingree, the ranking member of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies, which funds the Smithsonian, reacted strongly to the leaked memo in a letter sent Tuesday to Roger W. Ferguson Jr., the chairman of the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents.

“I intend to investigate these matters in the 120th Congress and vigorously defend the Smithsonian’s independence,” Ms. Pingree wrote. “This reporting is extremely concerning, but not surprising given this administration’s previous attempts to illegally impound Smithsonian Institution-appropriated funding, use federal agencies to spread misinformation about the Smithsonian, and release a demonstrably false report accusing the Smithsonian Institution of systemic bias in its curatorial decisions.”

Although the Trump administration has argued for substantial changes at the Smithsonian, and has closely audited its content and operations, most of these efforts have been designed to draw public attention to what the White House has characterized as an inadequate and biased presentation of American history.

In July, for example, the White House ordered that $84,000 in signage be posted outside the history museum to warn against what it called “inaccurate information.” But the signs have yet to be installed.

While the White House has alluded to withholding funds to the Smithsonian, the Republican-led Congress rejected the president’s proposed 12 percent budget cuts in the 2026 fiscal year.

The Trump administration has at times targeted Mr. Bunch himself, with a presidential aide calling him a “rabid partisan,” liar and failure and some conservatives calling for the secretary’s ouster. But Mr. Bunch, who announced in September that he would step down at the end of the year, has managed to navigate such attacks while continuing to assert the Smithsonian’s autonomy.

In his letter on Tuesday, Mr. Bunch addressed the pressure the institution has been under because of the Trump administration’s reviews of its operations.

“As I have said before,” he wrote, “we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

Mr. Trump has spoken of his interest in appointing citizen regents who would align with his own agenda for the Smithsonian. But, in a break with tradition, none of the replacement candidates selected by the regents have been forwarded to Congress, possibly because they would be unlikely to win support from a Republican-led House or Senate. The regents have not publicly discussed the process.

Democrats will take over Congress in January. But as president, Mr. Trump would still be able to veto any proposed replacements.

Julia Jacobs contributed reporting.

Robin Pogrebin, who has been a reporter for The Times for more than 30 years, covers arts and culture.

The New York Times November 24, 2026

Turmoil at Nvidia

Shares have veered wildly for days, pushed and pulled by the drama at Nvidia and the rise and fall of Anthropic’s stock after its blockbuster public offering.

How the tech-heavy index in the United States is trading

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Aruni Soni and Jason Karaian

Stock markets in the United States slipped on Tuesday as technology shares tied to the artificial intelligence industry erased some of their heady rally the day before. Shares of Nvidia and Anthropic, both seen as barometers of the sustainability of the A. I. boom, traded sharply lower.

Investors have been buffeted by wrenching volatility in recent sessions, as tech stocks in particular have veered up and down, recording both their biggest daily rise and fall in more than a year. This pattern has extended into another day, with major indexes turning down.

The S&P 500 fell around 0.5 percent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite posted a decline of more than 1 percent, dragged down by Nvidia and other tech stocks. Both moves only partially reversed the big gains at the start of the week.

Nvidia, which rocketed more than 30 percent on Monday after the reinstatement of the chip maker’s former chief executive, Jensen Huang, fell around 8 percent on Tuesday. Anthropic, the A. I. giant that broke records in its initial public offering last week, tumbled nearly 8 percent on Tuesday, sliding below its I. P. O. price for the first time since its market debut.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The hangover from Monday’s euphoric rally left many analysts wondering what to make of the return of Mr. Huang to Nvidia, which followed an extraordinary intervention by President Trump and came even though its board of directors had declared that the company founder would not be returning. Less than two weeks ago, Mr. Huang had resigned after revelations of an affair with a woman U. S. officials believe was spying for China and another with a subordinate.

“The on-again-off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” analysts at Bernstein wrote in a report. The recent turn of events “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions,” they added. Mr. Huang’s record of keeping “questionable company on occasion” was also troubling for the market watchers who, nonetheless, were “happy to have Jensen back.”

The political intrigue behind Mr. Huang’s swift fall and sudden return weighed on analysts from Raymond James, who were unsure how the “internal struggle between national security hawks and more business-friendly factions” will play out within the Trump administration. “Recent developments suggest the political winds may be shifting, with commercial interests regaining influence, but the underlying tensions are far from resolved,” they wrote.

Notes: Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The slide in Anthropic’s high-profile shares also suggests wariness about the prospects for companies at the forefront of the A. I. boom. Fears about the sustainability of the rapid build-out of data centers and related infrastructure were already weighing on tech stocks before the turmoil at Nvidia.

“That financial markets moved on the employment prospects of one individual suggests either equity valuation models or current pricing might need to examined,” noted Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management.

The Nasdaq remains roughly 15 percent below its peak in early October. Nvidia’s shares, even after Monday’s rally, which added roughly $1 trillion to its market value, are still down for the year.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Jason Karaian is a deputy business editor at The Times, based in London.

OpinionGuest Essay
