Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Here is the standout fiction and nonfiction of the year, chosen by the staff of The New York Times Book Review.

Credit... Derek Brahney

Supported by

It seems like such a big number, 100 books, doesn’t it? Yet every fall, the Book Review’s editors struggle mightily to winnow our list of the year’s standout fiction and nonfiction to that tidy sum, and all of us inevitably have favorites that didn’t make the cut. So please, take this list in the spirit it’s intended: as a goad and a tip sheet, an earnest conversation with your nerdiest friend and a good place to find holiday treats for yourself or your loved ones.

As you browse, you can save the books you’ve read or want to read. By the time you reach the end, you’ll have a personalized reading list to share. (Not sure where to start? We broke the list down in this guide.)

Family saga

The third novel in Lee’s planned quartet about the Korean diaspora revolves around a hagwon, or cram school, in Southern California between 1992 and 2007. Set against the backdrop of the Asian financial crisis and early social media, and skillfully eliding the narrative challenges of 9/11, the Great Recession and iPhones, “American Hagwon” has the wonderful muchness of a 19th-century novel.

For fans of “Homegoing,” by Yaa Gyasi, and “The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny,” by Kiran Desai.

Save to your reading list:

Mystery

This slow-burn mystery — which doubles as a moving coming-of-age tale — is set in a vividly rendered working-class Glasgow neighborhood where Janey Devine, 12, has discovered a corpse. The police think Janey saw something at the crime scene that she’s hiding, and so does her father, a dangerous gangster.

For fans of “Young Mungo,” by Douglas Stuart.

Save to your reading list:

historical fiction

This historical saga unites an unlikely group of spinsters, sex workers and orphans in Depression-era Mississippi for a rollicking and wrenching story of economic hardship and injustice.

For fans of “Demon Copperhead,” by Barbara Kingsolver, and “The Four Winds,” by Kristin Hannah.

Save to your reading list:

Fantasy

Lewis’s wild, heretical epic follows two heroes on divine quests: Yara, a nonbinary embroidery artist with O. C. D., and Adrena, the daughter of a famous prophet. With visceral detail, the novel’s cheeky voice shatters the fourth wall into a million sparkly smithereens.

For fans of “Angel Down,” by Daniel Kraus.

Save to your reading list:

Historical Fiction

In exploring how history accumulates in layers, shaping our consideration of both past and present, Mora’s novel — translated by Rahul Bery — takes us to early-19th-century Prussia, where a freeholder keeps finding perfectly preserved corpses of soldiers on his land. Some appear to be Napoleonic, some Roman. None are decomposing, giving his farm the look of a permanent battlefield.

For fans of “Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead,” by Olga Tokarczuk.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

Mahajan follows the descendants of an Indian politician in this sweeping tale of political machinations, family drama, betrayal and social transformation. Among the scions is Laxman Chopra — business flop, cheerful sociopath, rapist, avoider of blame — who succeeds with terrifying ease in the world of politics.

For fans of “City on Fire,” by Garth Risk Hallberg.

Save to your reading list:

Heist novel

The final installment of Whitehead’s Harlem crime trilogy finds the furniture salesman and sometime crook Ray Carney reckoning with 1980s New York, where excess and scarcity alike weigh on his neighborhood. “Whitehead cracks the city open like a crab and pulls out the meat,” our critic Dwight Garner wrote.

For fans of “Blacktop Wasteland,” by S. A. Cosby, and “The Hot Rock,” by Donald E. Westlake.

Save to your reading list:

Literary fiction

A violent mob attacks a group of eight gay men in Kingston, Jamaica, leaving one dead and the rest scarred. With an unflinching eye for detail, James follows the men as they recover and deal with the violence in their own ways. “Why not just say it?” our critic Dwight Garner wrote. “James has written a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far.”

For fans of “A Little Life,” by Hanya Yanagihara.

Save to your reading list:

science fiction

Unferth’s stellar novel is part cosmic comedy and part dirge to our dying world. Behind its stream of delightful surprises, the novel is concerned with larger questions of humanity and our inhumanity to the natural world. How do we reckon with the damage we’ve wrought?

For fans of “The Leftovers,” by Tom Perrotta.

Save to your reading list:

historical fiction

Inspired by Tergit’s family, this account of the rise and fall of a German Jewish clan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries — translated by Sophie Duvernoy — has an addictive immediacy that makes it hard to put down.

For fans of “Kantika,” by Elizabeth Graver, and “This Strange Eventful History,” by Claire Messud.

Save to your reading list:

Science fiction

In this eerie Booker Prize winner — set after a disaster has changed the world — a British beachcomber scouring the coastline comes upon a strange, shape-shifting entity with mystical and destructive powers.

For fans of “Point Omega,” by Don DeLillo.

Save to your reading list:

LITERARY FICTION

This slender, wrenching novel tells the classic tale of a war veteran struggling to make his way home. Except in “Etna,” the veteran is a combat dog with powers of empathy and wisdom, who can speak to other animals (and some people). His journey is experienced almost completely at ground level, through his eyes, ears and — most especially — his exquisitely sensitive nose.

For fans of “The Eyes & the Impossible,” by Dave Eggers.

Save to your reading list:

Romance

A pop star leaves the spotlight behind for life as a college student, hoping to find some semblance of normalcy — with the help of her recently divorced professor. The age gap and teacher/student tropes are two of the romance genre’s biggest flash points: It takes a bold writer to pull both off with such nuance and charm.

For fans of “Love, Theoretically,” by Ali Hazelwood.

Save to your reading list:

historical fiction

On an island off the coast of Ireland in 1847, a naturalist is documenting the behavior of a small colony of great auks. It is a world of ambergris, gruel, gizzards, guano and grog, and Walls pulls off the considerable feat of engaging the reader with the fate of flightless alcids.

For fans of “The Signature of All Things,” by Elizabeth Gilbert, and “Euphoria,” by Lily King.

Save to your reading list:

LITERARY FICTION

A teenage girl, the beautiful rebel in a prosperous Afghan American family, is found dead. Was it suicide, an accident, an honor killing? Sabit’s novel unfurls that mystery through alternating narrators whose testimony offers a polyphonic view on adolescence, immigration and the strictures of embodying a “model minority.”

For fans of “A Thousand Splendid Suns,” by Khaled Hosseini, and “The Appeal,” by Janice Hallett.

Save to your reading list:

mystery

After years as a narcotics detective, Callie Hauser has returned home to a small town in the Pine Barrens as its police chief — and the first person she arrests is her own mother. Following this showstopping opener, Mullen unspools a narrative of corkscrew complexity involving a decades-old cold case and even older family secrets.

For fans of “Long Bright River,” by Liz Moore, and “Dirt Creek,” by Hayley Scrivenor.

Save to your reading list:

Literary fiction

Suzanna, 8, shuttles between two worlds: the prison where her mother is serving a life sentence for her role in a bank robbery, and the New York City apartment where her imperious grandmother, a former communist activist, is raising her. It’s an acute portrait of a child caught between divided loyalties.

For fans of “White Oleander,” by Janet Fitch, and “My Phantoms,” by Gwendoline Riley.

Save to your reading list:

SHORT STORIES

Nunez won the National Book Award in 2018 for her novel “The Friend.” Now she’s produced her first story collection, which our critic Dwight Garner loved: Nunez, he wrote, “is one of American fiction’s most crisp and realized voices.”

For fans of “Brawler,” by Lauren Groff.

Save to your reading list:

Literary fiction

John-Calum Macleod, a recent art school graduate, returns to his family home in Scotland’s Hebrides Islands to care for his ailing grandmother — and learns the bigger task will be facing family secrets and a father at odds with his son’s queer, liberal transformation.

For fans of “The Sense of an Ending,” by Julian Barnes, and “Mothers and Sons,” by Adam Haslett.

Save to your reading list:

Romance

Kumar’s Scottish road trip romance combines a seductive “one-night stand leads to love” story with sensitive explorations of grief, guilt and estrangement. As Jacob and Neelu drive around the countryside with her father, who is pursuing his runaway bride, the shared crisis builds to a marvelous catharsis.

For fans of “These Summer Storms,” by Sarah MacLean.

Save to your reading list:

Thriller

In the final volume of French’s detective series starring Cal Hooper, a young woman’s drowning brings to light the ugliest secrets of a small town in rural Ireland. Longstanding feuds and rivalries implicate nearly everyone in the search for the truth behind the girl’s death.

For fans of “The Dry,” by Jane Harper.

Save to your reading list:

poetry

Graham, a Pulitzer-winning poet who participated in the 1968 student uprisings in Paris, writes from the dust cloud left by the collapse of the 20th century’s progressive hopes. Her lines arrive in clipped, em-dash-laden bursts that can hardly believe these utopian dreams have buckled.

For fans of “The Octopus Museum,” by Brenda Shaughnessy.

Save to your reading list:

historical fiction

Jones’s latest novel immerses the reader in the tale of Niecy and Annie, two motherless girls in Jim Crow Louisiana who grow up as “cradle friends,” so close they could be sisters. Though their lives take very different paths, they remain tight, and their stories deepen together.

For fans of “The Vanishing Half,” by Brit Bennett, and “My Brilliant Friend,” by Elena Ferrante.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

This sweeping, sensational family saga — translated by Jamie Bulloch — follows a blue-blooded Hungarian family through the highs and lows of the 20th century, from imperial grandeur through two world wars and an anti-communist revolution.

For fans of “The Tsar of Love and Techno,” by Anthony Marra.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

A novel stacked with deadpan wit and wordplay, “Lost Lambs” centers on the flailing Flynn family: a mother dabbling in polyamory, a deeply depressed dad and their three precocious adolescent daughters — one of whom may have cracked the case of a local billionaire’s financial shenanigans.

For fans of “The Bee Sting,” by Paul Murray, and “The Family Fang,” by Kevin Wilson.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

A travel writer named Leonie freaks out when her boyfriend, Max, a literary translator working on a collection of Maltese poetry, goes radio silent after departing for the Mediterranean. But she doesn’t really want to learn the truth — of what’s going on between him and the sexy poet he’s translating, or of her own artistic ambitions.

For fans of “A Separation,” by Katie Kitamura.

Save to your reading list:

historical fiction

A Booker finalist, this novel follows a curator who specializes in historical re-enactments. Working in a 750-year-old British palace, she finds herself drawn to one medieval king in particular — and then, almost as if a portal opens, we find ourselves back in time with him.

For fans of “What We Can Know,” by Ian McEwan, and “Trust,” by Hernan Diaz.

Save to your reading list:

HISTORICAL fiction

This stunning novel animates two real-life classical musicians at the turn of the 19th century: John Field, a piano prodigy in Dublin, and Adelaide Percheron, an orphan in Pondicherry, French India, who determines to excel at the pianoforte. Li’s saga merges their unlikely paths across European capitals at the peak of empire.

For fans of “An Equal Music,” by Vikram Seth, and “The Time of Our Singing,” by Richard Powers.

Save to your reading list:

speculative fiction

This daring, twisty novel about a Black cop takes on police brutality, racist conspiracies and much more — it’s an athletic book for nerds who pump out supersets with “Infinite Jest” and “House of Leaves,” then wind down with Percival Everett.

For fans of “The Sellout,” by Paul Beatty.

Save to your reading list:

HORROR

Jones’s latest — a coming-of-age tale, a fabulist possession novel and a revenge epic rolled into one — centers on a young Blackfeet man on an illicit road trip to recover the bones of a boy who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania.

For fans of “The Reformatory,” by Tananarive Due.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

A former piano prodigy receives an unexpected call from the man who derailed her ambitions years earlier, and must decide whether to open her life to him once again. It’s a lush and wrenching narrative about the paths not taken, the ingenuity of music and human decency. (There are some impressive sex scenes, too.)

For fans of “Heart the Lover,” by Lily King, and “Tom Lake,” by Ann Patchett.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

An interminable delay at LAX is the backdrop of Maksik’s eerie, elegant new novel, which follows a father and his adult daughter waiting for a flight to Paris. The situation is both highly inconvenient and seemingly dire — phones aren’t working, and the sky has turned yellow. As our heroes look for an escape, the novel presses against the limits of the form.

For fans of “Leave the World Behind,” by Rumaan Alam, and “Station Eleven,” by Emily St. John Mandel.

Save to your reading list:

LITERARY FICTION

Akhtar’s third novel is at once campus satire, autofiction and page-turning drama about a playwright and novelist named Ayad. A pickup truck nearly kills him while he’s riding his bike, and when he comes out of a postoperative coma he is subtly, but utterly, changed.

Save to your reading list:

For fans of “Trust Exercise,” by Susan Choi.

literary fiction

In this luminous novel of isolation and yearning beneath the stars, translated by Caroline Waight, an astrophysics professor craving solitude moves to the sparsely populated Danish countryside — only to discover it’s harder to get away from other people than she thought.

For fans of “The Easy Life,” by Marguerite Duras, and “The Fell,” by Sarah Moss.

Save to your reading list:

SPECULATIVE fiction

The narrator of this Kafkaesque novel discovers that her newly remodeled bathroom is actually a portal to a prison cell in Turkey, the country she and her family left behind for a new life in Italy. While caring for her ailing father, she tries to get to the bottom of this mystery but winds up facing even thornier questions.

For fans of “Martyr!,” by Kaveh Akbar.

Save to your reading list:

ROMANCE

While the carriages and Rolodexes of Sebastian’s historical romances may have been replaced by hot rods and cellphones, her trademarks remain in this tale of TV co-stars: a tender grumpy-sunshine slow burn, queer joy and oodles of yearning (plus an emotional support dachshund).

For fans of “Fan Service,” by Rosie Danan.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

In the Irish Midlands in the 1980s, Roísin and Red strike up an unlikely friendship — she a deeply unpopular loner at high school, he a charismatic teenage boy with an air of danger and troubles of his own. From a filthy squat in London, their paths begin to diverge, resulting in an exceptional portrait of adolescent love, heartbreak and regret.

For fans of “Normal People,” by Sally Rooney; “The Happy Couple,” by Naoise Dolan; and “The Rachel Incident,” by Caroline O’Donoghue.

Save to your reading list:

science fiction

Kim reimagines the politics and dilemmas of immigration through a story about scheming clones, in which crossing an international border creates a version of yourself that stays behind to keep living your old life.

For fans of “Exit West,” by Mohsin Hamid.

Save to your reading list:

poetry

Levis died at 49, in 1996; this collection gathers all of his work in one volume. His poems were a staggering achievement of style entwined with worldview, humane and attentive and complex in their philosophy.

For fans of “Half-Light,” by Frank Bidart, and “Dunce,” by Mary Ruefle.

Save to your reading list:

Literary fiction

Cline’s new novel gets inside the head of a stoic businessman with dementia who is flying to Switzerland to end his life — but not before confronting the boarding-school roommate who has held an outsize place in his psyche. Our critic Alexandra Jacobs wrote that “‘Switzy’ does so much so very well; Cline collates beautifully the absurd detritus of modernity.”

For fans of “Flesh,” by David Szalay, and “Cosmopolis,” by Don DeLillo.

Save to your reading list:

LITERARY FICTION

What led to 9/11? Vollmann’s 3,000-page opus, spread over four volumes, considers decades of intelligence endeavors — both well-intentioned and malicious, prudent and disastrous — by the C. I. A., from the Cold War and Vietnam to the interminable conflicts in the Middle East. Our guide is the fictional Elliott Stevens, who helps put a human face on a fraught history.

For fans of “Tree of Smoke,” by Denis Johnson, and “Harlot’s Ghost,” by Norman Mailer.

Save to your reading list:

coming-of-age novel

Kuang, the author of wildly successful fantasy novels, here turns her interest in language and empire to the realistic story of an American student adrift in Taiwan amid everyday dramas of roommates and midterms and sisters and sex. She pulls it off so well that if you didn’t know better, it would be hard to imagine her writing in any other register.

For fans of “The Idiot,” by Elif Batuman.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

This novel has at its center the workings of an old and teeming Pakistani farm, where castes and ambitions collide. Mueenuddin’s exacting sense of social hierarchy finds multiple meanings in a glance, a touch, a vocal inflection, a phone call not placed.

For fans of “The White Tiger,” by Aravind Adiga.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

A journalist’s nightmare — a smartphone on the fritz — is the catalyst for this slender meditation on artistic legacy. As talky and thinky as a memory play, “Transcription” is about how technology can sustain as well as stultify life.

For fans of “Audition,” by Katie Kitamura, and “All Our Yesterdays,” by Natalia Ginzburg.

Save to your reading list:

Fantasy

Following estranged friends who find themselves at the Temple School of Thaumaturgy, this witty novel reimagines the classic “school for magic” tale. Part action adventure, part tender second-chance romance, it is a moving meditation on friendship and trust, class and power.

For fans of “Ninth House,” by Leigh Bardugo.

Save to your reading list:

thriller

In the grimy underbelly of Los Angeles, three unlikely people — a livestreaming influencer, a concierge to the fantastically rich and a lawyer who’s just been drafted to defend a pedophile producer — join forces to investigate a serial killer. “‘A Violent Masterpiece’ reads like pure rage cooled into crystalline prose, each sentence a thrilling indictment of the corruption we live in,” our columnist Sarah Weinman wrote.

For fans of “Queenpin,” by Megan Abbott.

Save to your reading list:

poetry

Bennett’s fourth poetry collection moves from loosely autobiographical poems into an expansive celebration of Black culture across the 250 years of America’s existence. Bennett combines structural elegance with taut rhythms harking back to his days in the New York slam poetry scene.

For fans of “Best Barbarian,” by Roger Reeves, and “Wade in the Water,” by Tracy K. Smith.

Save to your reading list:

Fantasy

Leena is a young refugee with a dangerous secret: She can see ghosts. Forced into a bargain with an enigmatic Mafioso, she finds herself on a darkly enchanting quest, grappling with evils both supernatural (demons, possession) and horrifyingly real (imperialism, the prison-industrial complex).

For fans of “The Familiar,” by Leigh Bardugo, and “Uprooted,” by Naomi Novik.

Save to your reading list:

literary fiction

Patchett’s 10th novel is a modern family’s platonic love story, beginning with a chance reconnection between a middle-aged woman and her former stepfather. Is there a place in serious literature for kind, happy characters and kind, happy stories? This intimate and entertaining novel makes the strong case that there is.

For fans of “My Name Is Lucy Barton,” by Elizabeth Strout, and “The Latecomer,” by Jean Hanff Korelitz.

Save to your reading list:

thriller

To her millions of followers on social media, Natalie is living the American dream: Pregnant with her sixth child, she purports to spend all day on her Idaho farm frolicking with her perfect kids, cowboy husband and flock of chickens. The truth is, of course, much darker, and this debut novel takes us one surreal step further to illustrate the deep chasm between our digital selves and our real ones.

For fans of “Yellowface,” by R. F. Kuang.

Save to your reading list:

history

Early in this chronicle of the “war on terror,” the reader is likely to conclude that the groups of American officials who have presided over the past two and a half decades of conflict in the Middle East consist of idiots, fools or knaves. The further one progresses into this meticulously researched book, the more this assessment seems confirmed.

For fans of “The Looming Tower: Al-Qaeda and the Road to 9/11,” by Lawrence Wright.

Save to your reading list:

Biography

Dishy, disturbing and deeply reported, this biography of Roy Cohn presents the notorious lawyer and fixer as central to understanding today’s political culture. Cohn died in 1986, but his morally dubious influence stretched from the McCarthy hearings to the Mafia, the judiciary, the Catholic Church and, notably, Donald Trump.

For fans of “G-Man: J. Edgar Hoover and the Making of the American Century,” by Beverly Gage.

Save to your reading list:

biography

The veteran literary biographer’s latest subject is the English novelist and art historian who wrote her first novel, “A Start in Life,” at 53, and went on to win the Booker Prize for “Hotel du Lac” in 1984. Lee argues that Brookner’s lonely, solemn characters made it easy to overlook the author’s vivacious social life, her rebellious spirit, her penchant for drama.

For fans of “Electric Spark: The Enigma of Muriel Spark,” by Frances Wilson.

Save to your reading list:

history

What might the 1984 assassination of Malcolm Kerr, the widely respected president of the American University of Beirut, tell us about Lebanese politics today? Ghattas has covered the Middle East for years, and offers a cleareyed account of the region’s internecine loyalties and proxies.

For fans of “Lawrence in Arabia: War, Deceit, Imperial Folly and the Making of the Modern Middle East,” by Scott Anderson.

Save to your reading list:

science

As she did in her previous book, “Nuclear War,” Jacobsen stages a sort of terrifying thought experiment: What would happen if some of the world’s deadly weaponized pathogens were to escape from the military research labs where they are stored? The answer (goodbye, civilization) is gripping, and bleak.

For fans of “The Fate of the Earth,” by Jonathan Schell.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

Blending investigative journalism and family history, Cooper — who comes from a long line of Black cops — probes the history and paradoxes of race and policing, to understand his parents and the system they served.

For fans of “America on Fire: The Untold History of Police Violence and Black Rebellion Since the 1960s,” by Elizabeth Hinton.

Save to your reading list:

BIOGRAPHY

Readers who picture Alfred, Lord Tennyson, as a bearded Victorian eminence will discover a new person here. Holmes shows us a young man coming of age in a moment of revolutionary scientific discovery and religious upheaval, questioning everything and finding the voice that would become his enduring poetic legacy.

For fans of “Dark Renaissance: The Dangerous Times and Fatal Genius of Shakespeare’s Greatest Rival,” by Stephen Greenblatt.

Save to your reading list:

investigation

Colloff, a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine and a reporter for ProPublica, digs into the story of Paul Skalnik, an unrepentant con man who served a total of 30 years in prison. While incarcerated he ran what may have been his biggest con of all: supplying alleged “confessions” by fellow inmates in return for clemency for himself.

For fans of “I’ll Be Gone in the Dark: One Woman’s Obsessive Search for the Golden State Killer,” by Michelle McNamara.

Save to your reading list:

classics

Thanks to her best-selling translation of the “Odyssey,” Wilson may be the world’s most famous living classicist. In these accessible, opinionated essays she ranges from the challenges of translating Roman comedy to the commingling of misogyny and desire in the figure of Helen of Troy.

For fans of “Talking Classics: The Shock of the Old,” by Mary Beard.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

At 3, Dohrn knew how to spot an undercover cop and lose a tail, crucial skills for a kid living on the run — the son of two leaders of the militant leftist group the Weather Underground. This intimate memoir probes the ideals that drove his parents to embrace violence and the emotional fallout for their family.

For fans of “Don’t Let’s Go to the Dogs Tonight: An African Childhood,” by Alexandra Fuller.

Save to your reading list:

cultural history

“Darkology” explores blackface performance and asks how minstrelsy came to be accepted as lighthearted entertainment well into the 20th century. “Amateur minstrelsy was no sideshow,” writes Barnes. “It was at the dark and ever-present center of modern American life.”

For fans of “Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents,” by Isabel Wilkerson.

Save to your reading list:

History

This chronicle of Syria’s 14-year civil war tells the story of a revolution through the experiences of six dissidents and agitators who fought against tyranny in the city of Manbij. Gopal’s epic story immerses readers in the group’s lives as they struggle to advance the democratic experiment.

For fans of “Behind the Beautiful Forevers: Life, Death, and Hope in a Mumbai Undercity,” by Katherine Boo.

Save to your reading list:

Memoir

Perry, a best-selling novelist, has written an ode to her father-in-law, who died nine days after receiving a cancer diagnosis. She doesn’t skimp on the unpleasant physical symptoms, the maddening search for care, the bureaucracy or the private kindnesses, and the result is a masterpiece.

For fans of “When Breath Becomes Air,” by Paul Kalanithi.

Save to your reading list:

fashion

In this illuminating study, Strasdin reconstitutes the lives and labors of the “many hands” that, since the age of Queen Elizabeth II’s great-great-grandmother, Queen Victoria, have shaped the sartorial contours of the British monarchy.

For fans of “Queen of Fashion: What Marie Antoinette Wore to the Revolution,” by Caroline Weber.

Save to your reading list:

history

In this rich, vibrant, compelling history of her hometown, a New York Times journalist makes the case that El Paso is the heart not only of Texas, but of the American experience. The city is Spanish and Mexican, Indigenous and mestizo, Anglo and Arab, Chinese and German, white and Black; in Ulloa’s estimation, it’s as important as Ellis Island.

For fans of “The Warmth of Other Suns: The Epic Story of America’s Great Migration,” by Isabel Wilkerson.

Save to your reading list:

true crime

By now, many Americans know the sordid saga of Alex Murdaugh, the high-flying South Carolina lawyer convicted of killing his wife and son and committing a host of financial crimes. (The murder conviction was overturned earlier this year.) Lasdun, who covered the case for The New Yorker, brings literary polish to a quest to understand the inexplicable.

For fans of “Say Nothing: A True Story of Murder and Memory in Northern Ireland,” by Patrick Radden Keefe.

Save to your reading list:

History

When did white rage become normalized? This is the question that drew Thompson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian, to the Bernie Goetz case, which in her deeply researched account becomes a through line to the present: the event that first gave legal cover to white vigilantism.

For fans of “Reaganland: America’s Right Turn, 1976-1980,” by Rick Perlstein, and “When the Clock Broke: Con Men, Conspiracists, and How America Cracked Up in the Early 1990s,” by John Ganz.

Save to your reading list:

group biography

Part intellectual memoir and part group biography, this sprightly book by a senior editor for the Book Review traces her undergraduate infatuation with the postmodern philosophy promulgated by a cadre of influential French thinkers including Michel Foucault and Jacques Derrida, and makes a case for their continued relevance.

For fans of “At the Existentialist Café: Freedom, Being, and Apricot Cocktails,” by Sarah Bakewell, and “The Club: Johnson, Boswell, and the Friends Who Shaped an Age,” by Leo Damrosch.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

In this fierce, grueling, cold-water plunge of a memoir — about helping a loved one with PTSD — Eubanks applies equal scrutiny to her partner’s suffering and her own impatience and peevishness. In places where other memoirists might fade to black, she turns on her headlamp. The effect is profoundly moving.

For fans of “Can’t We Talk About Something More Pleasant?,” by Roz Chast.

Save to your reading list:

EXPOSÉ

Baker arrived at Stanford in 2022 as a bright-eyed freshman. He finished that year having taken down the university president, and having become jaded by a system where faux idealism often obscures corruption and greed. His book is a scorching portrait of a university infiltrated by venture capital and tech firms, and of a dweebocracy that “sets the agenda for the planet.”

For fans of “Liar’s Poker: Rising Through the Wreckage on Wall Street,” by Michael Lewis, and “Den of Thieves,” by James Stewart.

Save to your reading list:

biography

Maria Edgeworth was famous in the early 19th century as an accomplished writer and thinker in the nascent field of political economy. Using her rise and fall as a lens, Smialek — a reporter at The New York Times — asks what was lost when women were pushed aside and economics was transformed from an accessible, widely debated set of concerns to the more narrow academic discipline it has become today.

For fans of “George Eliot: The Last Victorian,” by Kathryn Hughes, and “The Bluestockings: A History of the First Women’s Movement,” by Susannah Gibson.

Save to your reading list:

current events

An Israeli-born scholar of the Holocaust, Bartov traces how Israel — founded as a refuge from intolerance — has elevated ethnonationalism to a “state ideology.” In clear, sober, deliberate prose, he attempts to chart what has happened to the country where he was born.

For fans of “One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This,” by Omar El Akkad.

Save to your reading list:

Memoir

The Cuban Revolution severed Ferrer’s family, sending her as an infant to New York with her mother and leaving her 9-year-old half brother behind. The aftershocks of separation reverberate through this memoir as Ferrer, a Pulitzer-winning historian, sifts through letters and archives to tell the entwined stories of family and country.

For fans of “Men We Reaped,” by Jesmyn Ward.

Save to your reading list:

history

A new history of North Korea argues that the enigmatic, unexpectedly enduring Kim family dynasty owes its iron grip on power, at least in part, to its founder’s immersion in the zealous Christianity of late-19th-century American missionaries.

For fans of “Nothing to Envy: Ordinary Lives in North Korea,” by Barbara Demick, and “The Orphan Master’s Son,” by Adam Johnson.

Save to your reading list:

tech

In this wry and readable new book, Wikipedia emerges as “an escapee from a parallel universe, a refugee of the internet as it should have been, instead of the internet as it is.” Cooke, a journalist, zeros in on the all-too-human dimension of the website’s history, the tragic, pedantic and comic episodes that help explain its staying power in an age of A. I. slop.

For fans of “Index, A History of the,” by Dennis Duncan.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

This brash, appealing memoir from New York City’s first female chief lifeguard is both a sunny coming-of-age story and an exposé of corruption, understaffing and danger at Rockaway Beach. Fash is great company.

For fans of “West With the Night,” by Beryl Markham.

Save to your reading list:

true crime

Keefe’s book opens with a young man plunging to his death from a balcony overlooking the Thames and retraces, through immersive reporting, how he got there. This portrait of an ambitious London teenager consumed by a desire for wealth is embedded within a panoramic account of an urban underworld awash in violence, corruption and greed.

For fans of “Devil in the White City: Murder, Magic and Madness at the Fair That Changed America,” by Erik Larson.

Save to your reading list:

music

This unconventional history examines how the police, courts and penitentiaries have shaped the nation’s musical culture through profiles of five artists: Lead Belly, Elmo Hope, Johnny Cash, Ike White and Tupac Shakur. Taking its title from a Lead Belly song, it’s a fog-piercing down-bound train of a book.

For fans of “Alan Lomax: The Man Who Recorded the World,” by John Szwed.

Save to your reading list:

current events

This bracing book is structured around a simple proposition: In order to understand our current moment, we need to understand Elon Musk — the tech billionaire who has accumulated so much wealth that he is shaping the world according to his abiding preoccupations.

For fans of “The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State,” by Jill Lepore.

Save to your reading list:

history

Russia’s dramatic cultural, sociological and political shifts have shaped world history. Through it all, its vast forests — still around one-fifth of the world’s woodlands — have borne witness. In this biography of a place through its trees, Pinkham studies not merely Russia’s ecological history and future, but the nation’s beating heart.

For fans of “The Brother Gardeners: Botany, Empire and the Birth of an Obsession,” by Andrea Wulf.

Save to your reading list:

LITERARY CRITICISM

The first clue that this revelatory study of Toni Morrison’s work is not your usual academic exercise is the opening essay: “On Difficulty,” a defense by Serpell — herself an accomplished novelist and scholar — of her subject’s barbed intelligence, contrarian politics and exacting attention to Black aesthetics.

For fans of “White Girls,” by Hilton Als, and “Cultural Amnesia,” by Clive James.

Save to your reading list:

tech

Véliz shows how Big Tech has accrued enormous amounts of wealth and power by promising insight into the future through the use of generative A. I. These modern oracles claim to make us safer, but, she argues, they are doing precisely the opposite.

For fans of “Bottoms Up and the Devil Laughs: A Journey Through the Deep State,” by Kerry Howley, and “Empire of A. I.: Dreams and Nightmares in Sam Altman’s OpenAI,” by Karen Hao.

Save to your reading list:

history

An author of thrilling spy histories par excellence, Macintyre takes readers into post-revolutionary Iran, where a Russian agent, unable to perform in the bedroom, turns to British intelligence for a cure. The consequences are deadly.

For fans of “The Billion Dollar Spy: A True Story of Cold War Espionage and Betrayal,” by David E. Hoffman.

Save to your reading list:

politics

A riveting and richly textured narrative of the first 14 months of Donald Trump’s second term, by journalists at The New York Times. Haberman and Swan have spent more than a decade covering Trump’s political career, and the events they portray are well known; what the authors add are vivid details that make them feel actual. They wrest reality itself back from the distorted world of entertainment, illusion, fantasy and denial that Trump has generated around himself.

For fans of “American Carnage: On the Front Lines of the Republican Civil War and the Rise of President Trump,” by Tim Alberta.

Save to your reading list:

history

Immortalized as children in Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s 1881 portrait “The Pink and the Blue,” Alice and Elisabeth Cahen d’Anvers, the daughters of a wealthy Jewish family, would go on to live lives that were anything but idyllic. By examining their fates, Ostler presents a vivid picture of life for French Jews.

For fans of “What the Ermine Saw: The Extraordinary Journey of Leonardo da Vinci’s Most Mysterious Portrait,” by Eden Collinsworth, and “The Lost Painting: The Quest for a Caravaggio Masterpiece,” by Jonathan Harr.

Save to your reading list:

History

This timely, engaging chronicle of the escalating violence that plagued the Middle East from the late 1960s through the early ’80s explores how leftist militants gave way to Islamist ones.

For fans of “Black Wave: Saudi Arabia, Iran, and the Forty-Year Rivalry That Unraveled Culture, Religion, and Collective Memory in the Middle East,” by Kim Ghattas.

Save to your reading list:

history

A lyric fusion of biography, ghost story, memoir and poetry, this melancholy book conjures fuller lives for women found in the real-life casebooks of a defunct asylum in Cork, Ireland. The chorus of these patient voices coalesces around the doctor who cared for them: Dr. Lucia Strangman, the first female psychiatrist in Ireland’s mental health system.

For fans of “Stone Yard Devotional,” by Charlotte Wood, and “Small Things Like These,” by Claire Keegan.

Save to your reading list:

science

Tracey ventures across continents and millenniums to study an incredible natural phenomenon: salt lakes, nearly all of which are in danger of disappearing. Moving from the Aral Sea to the Great Salt Lake in Utah, she exposes some of the most uncanny and unknown parts of our world.

For fans of “The Garden Against Time: In Search of a Common Paradise,” by Olivia Laing.

Save to your reading list:

history

In this cleareyed history, Ali — a reporter and a contributing writer for The New York Times Magazine — examines how the United States’ response to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks shaped the lives of Muslim Americans, who were vilified and targeted by both law enforcement and their own neighbors. Through the stories of four families, Ali details what it is to survive state persecution.

For fans of “Everyone Who Is Gone Is Here: The United States, Central America, and the Making of a Crisis,” by Jonathan Blitzer.

Save to your reading list:

history

Corera’s real-life thriller tells the story of a K. G. B. archivist turned dissident who used his access to classified documents to expose state secrets. While the race to extricate him from the Soviet Union is exciting, it’s Corera’s treatment of his internal journey that really raises the stakes.

For fans of “The Man Without a Face: The Unlikely Rise of Vladimir Putin,” by M. Gessen.

Save to your reading list:

HISTORY

This chronicle of Berlin during the Third Reich traces the strategies that citizens used to get by under authoritarianism. Through letters, journals and memoirs, Buruma brings us Berliners who did their best to keep their heads down, conform or compromise when the Nazis took over.

For fans of “Cold Crematorium: Reporting From the Land of Auschwitz,” by József Debreczeni.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

In 2023, Burden went viral with an essay entitled “Was I Married to a Stranger?” Here, she explores the full heart-shock of that episode — the sudden disintegration of a long marriage and shared life that included three children.

For fans of “Splinters: Another Kind of Love Story,” by Leslie Jamison.

Save to your reading list:

history

In this rich study of the Blow plantation in Virginia, the Pulitzer-winning historian Taylor separates tradition from the truth, attending carefully to the mix of high-minded sympathy and chilling cruelty that churned inside American slave owners.

For fans of “Master Slave Husband Wife: An Epic Journey From Slavery to Freedom,” by Ilyon Woo.

Save to your reading list:

Memoir

“It’s been a long time since I’ve read so good and rowdy a memoir about blue-collar work,” our critic Dwight Garner wrote of this slim, raffish book about hauling trash in Montreal. Paré-Poupart sings a Whitmanesque song of the reeking underdog: “I love the chaos of the garbage truck,” he writes, “for its own sake.”

For fans of “Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly,” by Anthony Bourdain, and “Smoke Gets in Your Eyes: And Other Lessons From the Crematory,” by Caitlin Doughty.

Save to your reading list:

biography

George Forster sounds almost too good to be true: a brilliant naturalist who sailed on Capt. James Cook’s second voyage, treated the Indigenous peoples he met as equals and became one of the first Europeans to promote universal human rights. Wulf combines her enthusiasm for exploration and the natural world with her admiration for a now mostly forgotten champion of Enlightenment ideals.

For fans of “The Wide Wide Sea: Imperial Ambition, First Contact and the Fateful Final Voyage of Captain James Cook,” by Hampton Sides.

Save to your reading list:

Science

Kolker, a contributing writer for The New York Times Magazine, brings his signature brand of narrative reportage to the story of a large Pennsylvania clan in which the children each have a 50 percent chance of developing a rare form of early-onset dementia. His explanations of complex neuroscience are lucid; his descriptions of the family’s experience deeply compassionate. What does it mean, he asks, to know your biological fate?

For fans of “The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks,” by Rebecca Skloot, and “The Best Minds: A Story of Friendship, Madness, and the Tragedy of Good Intentions,” by Jonathan Rosen.

Save to your reading list:

art

In Britain, bohemians had Bloomsbury. In France, they had the Hôtel Vaste Horizon, a bougainvillea-draped pension on the Côte d’Azur. Drawing on letters, memoirs, artworks and photos, Thomasson captures the creative and sexual ferment of the free spirits — including Pablo Picasso, Dora Maar and Man Ray — who took over the hotel in the summer of 1937, as war loomed.

For fans of “The Hare With the Amber Eyes: A Hidden Inheritance,” by Edmund de Waal.

Save to your reading list:

History

In this clarifying and richly insightful history of the whiplash experienced by Black Americans, and especially soldiers, in the Vietnam era, Haygood wings his way from the bloody battlefields of Southeast Asia to the American streets where civil rights protesters were met with violence.

For fans of “Stony the Road: Reconstruction, White Supremacy, and the Rise of Jim Crow,” by Henry Louis Gates, and “Half American: The Epic Story of African Americans Fighting World War II at Home and Abroad,” by Matthew Delmont.

Save to your reading list:

memoir

In her 20s, O’Gieblyn broke with the evangelical church and entered treatment for drug and alcohol addiction. After more than a decade of sobriety, she relapsed into alcoholism — shortly after trying and failing to convert to Catholicism. Here she connects her relationship with institutional religion to her relationship with alcohol; both were sources of “intoxication.”

For fans of “The Copenhagen Trilogy,” by Tove Ditlevsen.

Save to your reading list:

essays

Growing out of Aviv’s articles for The New Yorker, where she is a staff writer, these essays offer a piercing look at the fraught bond between mothers and daughters, with the same appreciation for emotional complexity that characterized her debut, “Strangers to Ourselves.”

For fans of “The Empathy Exams,” by Leslie Jamison, and “Fierce Attachments,” by Vivian Gornick.

Save to your reading list:

We read a lot of new books here at the Book Review — among us, between 1500 and 2000 every year. And I’m always amazed at how hard it is to whittle down our favorites to just 100. Every single one of us has books we’re passionate about that don’t make the final list. Tell me: What are the books, published in 2026, that you love most?

Thoroughly enjoyed reading Fruit Fly and Black Bag which are not on the list. And ofc John of John and The Disappearers which are. Excited to see what makes it to your Top 10

I loved "Land" by Maggie O'Farrell. It's magical without being overly magical. It's real life with a touch of fantasy. My favorite book of the year.

How Flowers Made our World (David George Haskell) -- an extraordinary exploration of biological and cultural creativityThe Glorians (Terry Tempest Williams) -- deep reflections on our relationships with one another and with the more than human worldA World Appears (Michael Pollan) -- lively investigation of the mysteries of consciousness

Keep track of what you want to read, what you have read and what you liked, and share your picks with your friends.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

More than half a billion people globally suffer from some form of back pain. And the numbers are only growing, with no reliable solution in sight.

Credit... Stephan Dybus

Supported by

By Matthew Shaer

Matthew Shaer spoke with dozens of experts and read more than a hundred papers on back pain.

The average adult spine measures approximately 18 inches — slightly more in the mornings, when the intervertebral disks are still ripe with fluid, and slightly less after a long day of standing, when they are maximally compressed. Like any enduring piece of technology, it is deceptively sophisticated in design. Up top, closest to the skull, is the so-called Atlas bone and the six additional cervical vertebrae that support our head and shoulders. Next comes the thoracic region, after the ancient Greek word for breastplate and so named for its role as anchor to the ribs. Last in line are the lumbar, or lower back, which keeps us upright, and the fused bones of the sacrum and coccyx.

As the spinal surgeon Christopher Bono explained to me during a visit to his office at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the resulting shape — the product of millions of years of evolution — quite literally made us who we are today. Without full vertebral articulation, we couldn’t turn to greet a friend or bend down to pick up an Amazon box; without a slight spinal curve near our hips, we wouldn’t be able to stay balanced on two feet. But there was a trade-off involved.

“Bipedalism,” Bono said, “meant all the movement and stress and shear of life was now loading the lower back.” He picked up a plastic scale model of the human spine and tapped his fingers against the two vertebrae at the base of the lumbar: L4 and L5. “It loaded these big knobby blocks of bone, and it loaded the adjacent joints, and it loaded anything that moved between them,” he said. “And that pressure makes the area exceptionally prone to degeneration.”

Bono, who is 55, has three main gigs. He is the executive vice chairman of orthopedic surgery at Massachusetts General. He is a professor at Harvard Medical School. And he is the editor in chief of The Spine Journal, one of two leading journals devoted to the topic (the other is Spine). I’d arranged to meet with him because it’s possible that no one knows as much about the back and its various afflictions — and also because earlier in the year, The Spine Journal, under his watch, published a remarkable (if onerously titled) article, “Development of an Internationally Agreed National Minimum Dataset for Low Back Pain: A Modified Delphi Study,” which focused largely on efforts to standardize diagnostic procedures across the field. But it was a statistic in the opening line that had stuck in my mind and sent me tunneling through a few thousand pages of associated academic research: “Low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide.”

The statement, it turned out, was both undeniably correct — only migraines come close — and somehow, given the actual scope of the issue, not nearly emphatic enough. According to a 2023 study in The Lancet Rheumatology, an astonishing 619 million people suffer from some form of low-back pain, a 60 percent increase from 1990; by 2050, the study’s authors predict, the total number of sufferers will hit 843 million, or more than the entire population of Europe.

In the last few years, spikes in diagnoses have been recorded in nearly every part of the world, from Latin America to Asia and Africa, where, The Lancet noted, “social support systems and health care systems are often underresourced and overburdened.” As is the case with many diseases, “the burden falls most heavily on socioeconomically disadvantaged” groups. The less access you have to good medical care, the better your odds of developing back pain become.

But appropriately enough for an issue that researchers say has reached epidemic status, no one is truly exempt, no matter where we live or how much we make. In August, the journal Medicine published an analysis of three decades of back-pain data and found that in the United States, the largest concentrations of sufferers were in Kentucky, with Wyoming and Iowa not far behind — probably, the paper’s authors speculate, because so many residents of those states work in physically demanding professions like agriculture, manufacturing and mining. Similarly, age seemed to correlate with the onset of symptoms, giving credence to the idea that the rise in back pain is an unavoidable byproduct of our ever-increasing life spans.

But other studies have shown that back pain can as easily be brought on by white-collar stressors — too much time in a desk chair, for instance — and that in the United States, more than a quarter of people between the ages 18 and 29 suffer from back pain. In fact, if you are reading this article and you don’t have firsthand experience with a bad back, count yourself lucky. Or just wait: The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, a federal research agency, has estimated that a full 80 percent of adults can expect to weather a spell of low-back pain at some point in their lives.

It would be one thing, of course, if a fix was within reach. But for most of us, it is not. Americans now pour about $100 billion annually into various back-pain treatments — more than we devote to any other single malady, including cancer. (Crucially, this figure does not account for lost productivity and disability payments, or the additional billions wasted on so-called complementary solutions like emphatically non-F. D. A.-approved braces and muscle-zapping gadgets.) And every year, the number of sufferers ticks steadily upward anyway.

“Overall,” researchers at Stanford have written, “we are spending more and getting much less.” Partly, this is a testament to the complexity of the back and the delicate web of muscles and tendons and nerve endings it contains. And partly it’s because in 2026, two centuries after scientists began seriously investigating the origins of the condition, we are only now beginning to understand how back pain actually works — and why it so confoundingly hard to address.

“The reality is,” Bono told me, “everyone wants that holy grail, that magic bullet. But while the science is improving, while we’ve made great strides, a lot of the conversations I have now involve the idea that a magic bullet isn’t coming anytime soon. It’s saying, Listen, if there is a cure, quote-un-quote, it’s probably going to look a lot different than you may be expecting.”

For most of medical history, and dismayingly far into the modern era, back pain was viewed almost exclusively as a mechanical issue. It originated in the vertebrae and could be caused by disease, trauma or genetic aberration, such as a misaligned spine; as with any other broken bone, you treated it by locating the site of the injury and immobilizing the area to encourage healing. (If that failed, you could always call in the leeches, or beat your patient repeatedly on the legs with reeds, or coat her body in layers of toxin, thus purging any residual “ill humors.”)

“It is only by removing pressure, and avoiding motion, that the nerves and muscles can be allowed to recover their powers,” the pioneering British physician Thomas Brown wrote in an 1828 tract called “On Irritation of the Spinal Nerves.” When said irritation was severe, Brown continued, the “recumbent posture is absolutely necessary” — and the longer the patient stayed in bed, the better.

A few decades later, as the rigors of the industrial age inspired an unprecedented wave of crippling back pain, a different British Thomas — Hugh Owen Thomas — developed a splint that immobilized the inflamed joints of children; in New York, the surgeon Lewis Albert Sayre experimented with wrapping patients’ torsos in casts, secured with layer upon layer of plaster of Paris. Not be outdone, Richard Davy, a London surgeon, devised a system of pulleys and straps that could be used to alleviate pressure on the vertebrae by stretching out the sufferer like a Gumby doll.

Rarely did a patient emerge from these sorts of treatments with any meaningful reduction in symptoms; many got worse. Indeed, as the surgeons David B. Allan and Gordon Waddell argue in their landmark 1989 history of back pain and its treatments, what was really being inaugurated in those years was not a glide path to a cure for back pain but a century-plus of disastrous missteps and unforeseen side effects. “Iatrogenic,” they call it — a term for an injury caused by a doctor in the course of treatment. Early forms of back surgery, involving the slicing of tendons and the fusing of vertebrae, were frequently botched, leading to widespread infection or paralysis; bed rest — far from speeding recovery — often seemed to prolong it.

And yet to Allan and Waddell, no single intervention would prove as lastingly destructive as intervertebral disk surgery. Introduced in the 1930s by the Boston surgeons William Mixter and Joseph Barr, the treatment was predicated on the belief that most patients’ issues were related to the presence of lesioned or damaged — herniated, in the modern parlance — disks. Shave down the vertebrae to allow for decompression (a procedure known as a laminectomy) or remove the herniation (a diskectomy), the doctors contended, and the pain would be erased.

As it happens, Mixter and Barr were not wrong about the potential efficacy of the approach, hence the enduring popularity of laminectomies and diskectomies today. If a patient’s back ailment can definitively be traced to herniation, an operation may reduce the pain. The problem, which scientists wouldn’t grasp until much later, is that not all back pain is a result of herniation. Not even most of it is: Modern research has shown that 90 percent of diagnoses fall under the heading of “nonspecific” — meaning, in essence, that the pain cannot be traced to a recognizable injury or defect and almost certainly won’t respond to surgery.

But Mixter and Barr handed the medical establishment the equivalent of a hammer, and suddenly everything looked an awful lot like a nail. “Intervertebral Disk Lesions Are the Most Common Cause of Low Back Pain With or Without Sciatica,” reads the title of a representative (and in retrospect, wildly irresponsible) paper from 1945. Outcomes, generally speaking, were better than they’d been in the days of torso casts. But inevitably, an untold number of back-pain sufferers who did not need surgery were sent to the operating theater, and a not-insignificant portion emerged with “at least one major complication,” as a 1989 study on lumbar laminectomies put it. Soon a new condition entered the medical lexicon: failed back surgery syndrome, which was characterized by motor weakness, reduced mobility and currents of intense pain.

The commercial rollout of the M. R. I. in the 1980s seemed to pave the way for a more careful approach to surgery, and in a lot of ways, Bono told me in Boston, it was “game changer.” But, he added, “it inspired some wild goose chases.” He wheeled his chair over to his desktop and brought up a recent patient scan. I spotted several dark blotches in the man’s lumbar, which I knew to be indicators of possible herniation. Noticing my reaction, Bono nodded. “Now, 30 or 40 years ago, we’d be thinking what you’re thinking,” he said. “Like, That disk bulge could be a pain generator. And, Oh, definitely a pain generator there. And, Wow, that’s stenosis,” a narrowing of the spinal canal that could result in nerve compression. “And we’d send him off for surgery, certain we’d settled on the issue. And the guy would be right back in the office a couple of months later, still in pain.”

The reason, it transpired, was that the M. R. I., in effect, was too good at its job. It revealed “more and smaller abnormalities” than any previous technology, the physician and researcher Richard A. Deyo wrote in a groundbreaking 1994 paper. And yet those abnormalities were often not the cause of the patient’s symptoms: One study showed that 64 percent of pain-free people have the sort of structural issues that would show up on an M. R. I. scan. Deyo correctly intuited that a bad back could be traced to an array of factors, psychological as well as physical. Anxiety could be masquerading as back pain; an injury might appear to be in the vertebrae when really it was being caused by a tendon strain or simple muscle fatigue.

It took a couple of decades for Deyo’s peers to come around. From 1996 to 2004, the United States recorded a 14 percent increase in the number of diskectomies; from 1990 to 2001, the rate of lumbar fusion operations grew by 220 percent. As Bono told me — and plenty of contemporary studies confirmed — surgeons were highly incentivized to recommend an operation. They still are. “You’d very much like to believe that every time — or the majority of times, anyway — a surgery is done, it is done because that doctor wants to help that patient’s symptoms,” Bono said. “But that’s not always true. What you can say is that there is a financial incentive for any surgeon to do an operation in our current health care system, unless they work at a place that’s 100 percent salaried and their salary is independent of how much they do. That’s just the truth.”

It wasn’t until the mid-2000s that the number of back surgeries in the United States finally began to flatten and then subside — only to be replaced by another apparently groundbreaking treatment. “There can be life with relief,” proclaimed a 2003 ad for OxyContin, an opioid manufactured by Purdue Pharma, which was later accused of lavishing gifts on physicians for their help promoting the drug. A 2007 study showed that almost half of back- or neck-pain sufferers in the United States had been prescribed narcotics for their condition, despite studies demonstrating that prolonged opioid use steadily altered the pathways in the nervous system, actually enhancing a patient’s sensitivity to pain.

That same year, the American College of Physicians and the American Pain Society released a new set of guidelines on treating low-back pain, signifying the beginning of the end to what has come to be known as the dynasty of the disk. Like Deyo, the authors of the guidelines framed back pain as a composite ailment that required a correspondingly composite approach. Yes, they agreed, when it came to extreme herniation, diskectomy or epidural steroids should be on the table. But nonspecific back pain was different. Doctors were advised to consider the low back in its entirety: the tendons and muscles, the vast web of fascia and stabilizing ligaments and the nerves that ferry pain signals up to the brain.

To that end, over-the-counter painkillers were recommended as a “first-line medication,” to be followed — or supplemented — by stretching, spinal manipulation and a regimen of physical therapy. Diskectomies for nonspecific back pain were out; yoga and acupuncture were in, as was massage. And for the brain, there was always cognitive behavioral therapy, a kind of hybrid of physical and traditional talk therapy in which patients learn to overcome their fear of the pain that has kept them in bed or on the couch. If these methods failed and there was evidence of radiculopathy, or damage to the nerve endings, steroidal injections were an option.

In June, some 20 years after the publication of the guidelines, one of their primary architects, Roger Chou, a professor of medicine based in Oregon, helped write a review of 21 years of clinical data on low-back-pain treatments for The Journal of the American Medical Association. In all, he and his colleagues examined 108 studies and concluded that for nonspecific low-back pain, noninvasive techniques, writ large, can both reduce pain and improve function. Medically, scientifically, this should count as major progress: confirmation, in one of the world’s most prestigious medical journals, that we should no longer be trying to cut our way out of the problem.

But to the average patient, it may not feel like it. Surgery at least gave the illusion of action — of a path to a cure. What has replaced it is a dizzying array of potential fixes, some of which seem reductively obvious (exercise more!) and some of which are new and relatively untested. It’s hard to know what, if anything, will work — necessitating a long process of trial and error that might lead to relief. Then again, it might not.

About 15 years ago, Tatyana Baranovsky, a 41-year-old pharmaceutical director in New York, developed a needling, sharp pain in her back, which seemed to worsen the more she arched it. A longtime athlete, Baranovsky wanted a treatment that wouldn’t interrupt her training. After completing close to a dozen sessions with a chiropractor, she realized that she was “spending a lot of money in co-pays and not getting relief.” Later, she went to an acupuncturist. “And the acupuncturist was excellent,” Baranovsky said. “She fixed a lot of other aches and pains I’d been having. She just didn’t fix my back.” Strolling around New York, she would often find her low back tightening up, and she’d have to stop and hinge at the waist to unstick it. Soon the pain had migrated to a new section of her lumbar, slightly off-center from her spine.

“So I reached out to my physician and asked for help, and he gave me three names” of back specialists, she recalled. “I took the first available appointment, but it still meant a two-month wait.” Dissatisfied, she tried another, and another. “And I got a load of responses. One said my glutes were too weak.” Another opined that she had inflammation near the sacrum. “You feel a bit like a hamster,” she went on. “You’re trying to chase that diagnosis, but you’re running in place.” Her pain continues to this day, and she recently had another M. R. I., her third.

Ethan Blumen, a 62-year-old writer and editor who came down with low-back pain this year, told me that he initially tried to soldier through the condition — he’d had a sore back before and assumed this bout would eventually subside, too. When it didn’t, he reached out to his doctor to discuss what sort of treatment might be appropriate. “If you’re lucky,” he told me, “something sticks. If you’re not, there’s more pain, more powerlessness, more doctor’s visits. Lots and lots of doctor’s visits.” He remembered, early in his treatment, receiving a steroidal epidural on one side of his back. “And that did the job for a couple of weeks,” Blumen told me. “But the pain moved to the other side of my body. I got an epidural there, too, and it was completely ineffective. I felt like I was going nuts.”

James Swift, a college student in Pittsburgh, said, “It’s a weird and unnerving feeling to be told, ‘We don’t really know what’s causing the problem, and there are a lot of approaches that could work.’ ” A few years ago, Swift underwent an M. R. I., which couldn’t conclusively point to a single cause of his chronic back pain. “It’s not a matter of a doctor saying, ‘This is the problem, right here, and this is precisely what we’re going to do to address it,’” he told me. “You can get lost, or end up losing hope entirely.”

His experience is alarmingly common, as the briefest of clicks through the dizzying number of forums and websites devoted to back pain will confirm. On YouTube, uncertified experts offer up “instant fix” tips on eradicating lumbar soreness with natural home remedies and spine massagers; on a subreddit called r/backpain, users gather to solicit recommendations from fellow sufferers or to vent their frustrations. “I just feel like every medical professional I’ve talked to over the years has never actually experienced chronic back pain, and if they have they are doing a great impression of someone that hasn’t,” one Redditor wrote recently. “I’m not sure who else identifies with this, but I have NO IDEA what causes pain. Nothing feels black and white. Lack of activity causes pain. Too much activity causes pain. Too much rest causes pain.” The Redditor described seeing a physical therapist, who assigned a daily exercise regimen that included lifting weights. But three days into the new routine, the post continued, “I sneeze and my back completely tweaks out in a bad way which tends to happen when I introduce anything new. And this is always how it goes.”

In a sense, says David Brody, a Colorado internist with decades of experience treating back pain, the frustration felt by many with nonspecific back pain is a direct product of the labyrinthine — and disconnected — American health care system. “A lot of back pain is managed in primary care,” he told me. “And general practitioners are very good at prescribing medicine, but we are not always good at teasing out the causes and contributors.” That’s assuming, of course, that a patient has health insurance at all; many don’t, leaving millions of back-pain sufferers to seek treatment at emergency rooms. “To me,” Brody said, “it’s a great example of our inability to deal with really complicated conditions.”

No wonder, then, that many people end up turning to the rapidly expanding gray market in questionable cures. “I remember spending hours going down the rabbit holes of whatever website, whatever blog I found, and checking out whatever weird things they were recommending,” says Toby Lawhon, a back-pain sufferer from Atlanta. “At one point, I ordered some strange Chinese supplements off Amazon, which probably were sugar pills. The list was long. I just needed something — anything — to work.” He went on, “Where the science isn’t clear-cut, where we’re still figuring things out, it’s the perfect terrain for nefarious actors to break in.”

It’s also part and parcel of a culture that encourages patients to believe that there will be an easy and fast cure, providing they search hard enough. In 2026, we’ve solved balding and obesity; why not back pain? “People of my age,” Baranovsky told me, “we’re taught that if we want an answer to something, we can Google it, and we can figure out how to fix it. We’re spoiled that way.” She went on: “But when a doctor says, ‘Well, look, all I know is that you don’t have the kind of condition I can operate on, and back pain is really complicated,’ you realize the instant fix isn’t going to happen. And so the onus falls back on you to navigate this confusing landscape, ideally with a good physician at your side, but always with you playing advocate for yourself.”

And if you make it a point to stay current on the latest scientific literature, there will always be a new cause for hope. In the past half decade alone, scientists have promoted the potential of electrical implants that stimulate the muscles of the back and stem-cell injections that foster the regrowth of depleted vertebral tissue. Some clinics offer a minimally invasive outpatient treatment called BVNA, which uses a radio-frequency probe to heat the nerves in the spine — interrupting the transmission of pain signals — and has shown promise in early studies. For industrial workers, there’s the option of an exosuit called the SafeLift, which supplements the natural action of the back and alleviates spinal compression and muscle strain. (Picture the prosthetics from “Edge of Tomorrow,” and you’re halfway there.)

Swift told me that after a cortisone shot failed to alleviate his chronic back pain, he studied up on similarly newfangled technology — being bedbound for weeks, it wasn’t like he had anything else to do. But eventually, he decided to take matters into his own hands and create his own rehabilitation regimen. He walked slow circles around his apartment, working his way up to body-weight exercises. “I was training myself to understand that it was possible,” he told me. “And I felt that surge of positivity, which I carried forward in other exercises.” As word spread around campus about his progress, he started helping other sufferers overcome their own chronic pain. Later, he wrote a paper on the training protocol he designed and had it published in a peer-reviewed journal.

“For me, it was a matter of adjusting my thinking,” Blumen agrees. “It was a kind of progression: I went from thinking, OK, I’ve had back pain before, and it went away; to searching for that holy grail, that silver bullet; to figuring out that, OK, yeah, this isn’t going away. I’m going to have manage my pain symptoms somehow. And I’m going to start with my brain.”

In recent years, much of the most intriguing work in back-pain research has been devoted to expanding upon an idea originally floated by the physician John Sarno. In the 1970s, Sarno, the director of a clinic in New York, noticed that patients with bad backs seemed to struggle with other maladies, like stomach problems and allergies and anxiety, and theorized that these ailments had a common root. In his best-selling self-help book “Healing Back Pain,” he proposed a mantra to be recited by sufferers any time they felt pain: “I must think psychological at all times, not physical.” Before his death in 2017 at age 92, Sarno claimed to have reduced pain levels in 90 percent of his patients.

Today, his reputation among orthopedic specialists is mixed. He is widely appreciated for his insistence on addressing the brain-based causes of back pain, and modern research has substantiated many of his theories: In 2023, the journal Pain published a paper showing that many people dealing with chronic back pain are also at risk for other stubborn inflictions, including irritable bowel syndrome, migraines, fibromyalgia and arthritis. But an important aspect of Sarno’s work — the focus on psychological trauma as the cause for back pain — is now viewed as misleadingly oversimplistic. Although mental-health problems do sometimes seem to correlate with back pain, the most recent research indicates that biology and genetics are considerably better predictors of who will end up with a perpetually sore lumbar — and for how long.

Imagine, for a moment, you’re walking around the house, and you step on a Lego block that your kid forgot to put back in the bucket. You squeal, curse and instinctively reach down for your foot, since your foot is where the pain seems to originate. In reality, it is being produced in the brain, in a cluster of nerves known as the pain matrix. Without the pain matrix, humans would never have survived as long as we have. We would walk around bumping into things and putting our hands into open flames; our foot would stay planted on the sharp edge of a Lego.

But recent science, says Jane Ballantyne, a pain expert and anesthesiologist, shows that pain signals aren’t transmitted in just one direction. “You could have an acute injury, and the signal will go up to the brain, where you perceive it,” she said. But the brain is also capable of misfiring. It can send pain signals to parts of the body “where there may be nothing going on — no inflammation or torn ligament, nothing at all.” She went on, “It’s a breakdown in the system.”

In 2013, Apkar Vania Apkarian, a professor at Northwestern Medicine and the eponymous director of a lab that studies chronic pain, published the results of a study of 100-odd individuals with newly diagnosed low-back issues. At the outset, each participant had the same level of pain, but over the course of a year, a sizable subset saw symptoms fade, while others experienced no relief at all. The members of the second group, M. R. I. scans showed, had especially strong connections between two key sections of their brains: the medial prefrontal cortex, which regulates how we think about ourselves, and the nucleus accumbens, which translates thought into action.

“The brain was creating a value judgment about the injury out of past memories and learning processes, and that culminates in a risk factor for those subjects,” Apkarian told me. Translation: The neurochemical makeup of their brains apparently led to a sort of fixation on the pain. “What’s important,” he went on, is that we can use brain scans to “predict by something like 80 percent accuracy who will develop chronic pain a year after diagnosis.”

In recent months, Apkarian has begun “noodling” on a pharmaceutical treatment that could prevent an injury from evolving into a chronic condition. “We think we have a window, and it’s about three months from the initial event,” he told me. “Within that window, if we have the proper treatment, we can stop chronic pain from setting in.” It’s easy to see how it might work: A patient tweaks his back picking up his grandchild and visits his doctor, who prescribes a pill that reduces the communication between the medial prefrontal cortex and the nucleus accumbens. Still, such a drug, should it ever make its way onto the market, would have limitations. “We won’t cure long-term persistent back pain that’s already been there for years,” Apkarian said. “You could miss the boat — the brain would already be reorganized into a new state.”

In the meantime, there are a growing number of treatments that aim for the same effect, albeit with the assistance of a pharmaceutical compound. “Pain can be a false alarm, and you can unlearn that pain over time,” says Tor Wager, a professor of neuroscience at Dartmouth and a proponent of a technique known as pain reprocessing therapy, or P. R. T., a variation on cognitive behavioral therapy in which trained therapists encourage patients to “recontextualize” their experience through steady habituation.

The ideal patient is one for whom surgery is not recommended, or a person who has undergone surgery and is still in pain. “And you’d start with an M. D. sitting them down and saying, ‘That bulging disk — it’s not the issue,’” Wager said. “You tell them it’s OK to move, and then they go to a therapist, and the patient learns that they can do the things they thought would hurt them. They’re learning that, Yeah, you’re going to feel some pain, but it’s not permanently damaging you.”

In 2021, Wager was an author of a paper on the efficacy of P. R. T. on 151 patients with chronic nonspecific low-back pain; after four weeks of treatment, 60 percent of the group reported being nearly or entirely pain-free. And the effects were enduring: A follow-up study, released last year, found that 55 percent of the group was still largely pain-free, compared with 26 percent from the placebo group and 36 percent of those receiving standard-issue therapeutic care.

This year, Ethan Blumen, the writer and editor, signed up for an eight-week chronic-pain program provided by Mass General Brigham and credits his improvement to its pain reprocessing therapy. He stressed that his condition was not gone; it would most likely be there forever in one form or another. “But you learn to accept it. Like, I’ll be on a walk with my wife in the park, and I’ll get a shot of pain. But I use my brain. I say: You’re going to keep going. You’re strong enough. And I’ll think positively. I’ll say, It’s beautiful outside. I’ll say, Hey, body, I’m getting the message, but I’m OK.” He laughed. “It feels like sorcery or something, the way I’m describing it. But it’s not. It’s just practice.”

Blumen told me that one of the biggest epiphanies he had during his recovery involved the understanding that back pain was part of life and that he was better off acknowledging it, rather than exhausting himself with a futile fight to escape it. Swift, in our conversations, agreed. “You have to accept that there isn’t going to be one specific fix,” he told me. “You have to get rid of that notion, because back pain is so complex, right? It’s psychological, and it’s structural. It’s environmental. It involves the muscles, the brain, the bones — every aspect of your lifestyle.” He paused. “I don’t know. Maybe that might make some people pessimistic. But I think it means there are so many ways you can teach yourself to get better — an entire world of possibilities. And I hold onto that.”

Matthew Shaer is a contributing writer for the magazine based in Atlanta. He has written about the loneliness epidemic, efforts to reanimate brain cells and a rise in driving fatalities.
